#8148. The Best Climbing Skins for Skis of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: This gear guide covers the five best climbing skins for skis, tested last season by our experts. The best climbing skins overall are the Pomoca Tour Pro for their excellent glide and reliable tail clip. The most durable climbing skins are the Black Diamond Glidelite Tour for their longevity and lightweight construction.

Unless you’re one of the lucky few who go catskiing or have a helicopter at your disposal (give us a ring, if so), backcountry skiing almost always involves a fair amount of climbing. And while climbing skins—the adhesive-backed strips of fiber that glide up but not down (like fish scales), then get removed for the descent—might not feel like the most exciting piece of gear in our closet, they have the power to make or break our day.

Last winter, our testers took to the hills (worldwide) and put eight different pairs to the test to bring you our favorite climbing skins for 2027. We indulged in deep powder days in the Tetons, dropped pillows in BC, explored wide-open glaciers in the Swiss Alps, and traversed the rugged mountains of Kyrgyzstan, all the while evaluating each pair of skins for grip, glide, durability and packability.

Pros and Cons + Excellent glide + Reliable tail clip – Plush needs break-in period

If we had to choose one skin to accompany us on all of our backcountry adventures, the Pomoca Tour Pro is an easy choice. After big missions in Grand Teton National Park, short dawn patrols on Teton Pass, and quick skins out the gates at Jackson Hole, testers said the Tour Pro blends excellent grip, glide, and packability, checking all the boxes for a trusty pair.

The Tour Pro features Pomoca’s Power Hook metal tail clip, an update last season to their plastic tail clip that was frequently an early fail point on the skins. Testers who’ve been using Pomoca skins for years all commented on the small but crucial update—which “essentially added seasons to the life of these skins,” reported one tester in the Tetons.

Underneath, Pomoca’s dual fiber plush technology is designed to walk the line between grip and glide, placing grippier fiber blends at the edges of the skin (more nylon), and fiber blends with better glide (more mohair) in the center. The result is solid edgehold on firm, refrozen skintracks, while maintaining the energy-saving glide skiers have come to love from Pomoca. “A great choice for everyday ski touring,” said one tester after a season in the Tetons. “They’re no skimo skin, but they easily handled everything I could throw at them.”

While the plush layer proved to glide well on long days in the mountains, testers noticed they took a tour or two to break in. Still, give ’em a few days and these skins will be your companion for years to come.

Pros and Cons + Excellent glide + Super packable – Finicky tail clip – Hard to peel apart at first

Skins don’t have to be boring. Atomic’s MultiFit Bent Chetler skins feature tip-to-tail artwork by celebrated artist and professional skier Chris Benchetler, making a solid case for sprucing up skin design. But they’re more than just pretty: After rigorous testing in the Tetons, Alps, Kyrgyzstan, and Alaska, these skins, which feature a 70/30 mohair/nylon blend, boasted the best glide.

“After a few tours, they were super fast,” said one tester after three weeks of ski guiding a mixed bag of conditions in Kyrgyzstan, ranging from deep powder to alpine variable. “And they packed up neatly so I could stash them in a pocket.”

A few drawbacks: One tester said the tail clips felt larger than necessary and easily slid off his skis if he wasn’t careful. And while the glue was incredibly reliable, even on sub-zero days, it took some muscle to peel them apart for the first 10 or so tours before getting progressively easier. Despite the sticky nature of Atomic’s Hot Melt glue, they never left residue on the skin.

Pros and Cons + Excellent grip + Solid glide + No breakdown in stickiness over multiple laps – Glue needs a break-in period

There’s hardly a better testing ground for skins than a spring hut trip in British Columbia, and one of our testers put G3’s new Alpinist Universal skins through the wringer while ascending wide-open glaciers, heavy isothermal snow, and bulletproof re-frozen crud. “An awesome mid-point between pretty packable, extremely durable, and super reliable,” reported the tester after he returned from Blanket Glacier Chalet in the Monashee Mountains.

G3 completely overhauled their skin collection this season with a redesign of their ChannelBond glue adhesive, which you’ll find in the new Alpinist Universal, Alpinist Grip, Alpinist Glide, and Alpinist Speed. A vertical channel pattern of adhesive on each skin provided a super solid hold around the edges of the ski, which is where we typically see snow sneak in on long tours.

The glue was ultra sticky at first, but after four or five tours it got significantly easier to peel them apart. The updated glue also maintained performance during multi-lap tours, even in deep snow. It’s easy for skin glue to start to fail when you repeatedly pull them on and off but testers found the Alpinist Universal to be just as solid on lap five as lap one.

Pros and Cons + Highly packable + Durable design – Glue takes a few tours to break in

Our favorite skins for longevity, Black Diamond’s new Glidelite Tour skins replace the Glidelite Mix (our longstanding favorite for durability), with a lightened up version of the reliable construction skiers have come to know and love.

“The glue had excellent hold on skis, even during multi-lap days where the snow really starts to cake up,” said one tester after a week of skiing on Teton Pass. Testers noted that the Glidelite Tour felt lower profile than the previous Glidelite Mix skins, making it easier to fit them in a pack. “These skins folded up really nicely, so I could stuff them in a jacket pocket for quick laps where I didn’t need to do a full transition,” said one Jackson, Wyoming-based tester.

A solid metal tail clip provided a secure hold, while the wide reinforced metal tip loop fit a variety of skis, from fat powder sticks to narrower spring skis. While we still found the glue needed a tour or two to break in, it was nothing like previous iterations of the Glidelite Mix, which a few testers had found to need five to 10 days in the backcountry for the glue to mellow out.

Pros and Cons + Super packable + Reliable glue in a variety of conditions – Plush is less durable – Middle of the road glide

The Kohla Freeride Air Skins were a rock-solid midwinter companion this season. They were packable, lightweight, and easy to peel apart right out of the box. We were impressed with how well the glue held up on a seven-day hut trip in the Selkirks, where we’d frequently complete at least ten transitions while lapping short pillow runs.

Packability is thanks to a thin construction, which does result in a small hit in durability. “I usually wouldn’t throw skins in my jacket for laps since they are just so bulky, but I find myself shoving these in my jacket pockets since they lie so flat,” said a tester after a week of nonstop skiing in British Columbia.

The rubbery tail clip was our favorite of all the ones we tested this season, stretchy yet secure, and easy to slide between sizes for adjustments on the fly. The glide is solid, but nothing to write home about—it felt pretty middle of the road compared to the other skins we tested. We’ve had one pair for two seasons now, and so far the glue has held up, though we see the plush deteriorating a bit after 100 days on them—so you might look elsewhere if you tend to beat the crap out of your gear. You can get these skins from Kohla, but brands like Head, Faction, Fischer, and others also brand Kohla skins with their logo, pre-cut to specific skis.

When choosing skins, the first thing we look at is plush material. Mohair (a fiber made from angora goat hair) provides glide, while nylon provides grip. Skins heavier in nylon will feature more grip than mohair-heavy skins. Most of our favorite skins worked out to be in the middle ground range, with a pretty standard 65/35 blend of mohair and nylon respectively. If you’re newer to skinning and looking for extra grip, the Black Diamond Ascension Skins will provide extra security, albeit at the cost of weight and bulk.

We also look for packability, since there’s somehow never enough room in our packs as it is, and skins that fold up nicely (like the Kohla Freeride Air Skins) make it easy to stuff them in a jacket pocket for quick laps.

Some skins come pre-cut to your skis if you buy them as a package, which can be nice if you’re not into cutting them yourself. Buying skins to match your skis isn’t essential (most skins come with a skin-cutting tool), but will guarantee a precise fit and often a tail clip that lines up well.

Tail clips vary in shape and look but work mostly the same. Most backcountry skis already have a flat spot or notch for a tail clip to hold skins in place, but if you have rounded rockered tails it’s worth checking on how they integrate before buying.

Last winter, we put ski climbing skins to the test all over the world, seeking out the full gamut of backcountry conditions. Our testers put eight pairs of climbing skins to the test in Jackson, Wyoming, Victor, Idaho, the Swiss Alps, Washington’s Cascade Mountains, Kyrgyzstan, Alaska, the Monashees and Selkirks of B.C. and Mammoth Lakes, California, evaluating skins for grip, glide, packability and ease of setup. We sorted through which skins felt like trusty companions lap after lap, and which skins felt more finicky. While testers enjoyed plenty of backyard missions, we believe truly putting skins to the test involves taking them along on multi-day trips and missions, gliding along windswept ridges, refrozen chunder, through deep powder and across questionably frozen lakes—all the while taking note of how they did day after day.

Lily Ritter is a freelance journalist and ski guide based in Victor, Idaho with work featured in The Ski Journal, SKI, Powder Magazine, Freeskier, Teton Gravity Research, and Ascent Backcountry Snow Journal. She spends winters backcountry skiing in Grand Teton National Park and riding lifts at Jackson Hole Mountain Resort, with the occasional trip to the Alps (for the food, obviously).

Jake Stern is a writer and editor based in Mammoth Lakes, California. Formerly an editor at Outside and Powder, he fits boots and writes freelance. He spends his free time exploring the Eastern Sierra backcountry and perfecting his pizza dough recipe.

Morgan McGonagle first dipped her toe into the industry as a professional ski patroller at Crystal Mountain, Washington. These days, she balances her time as a patroller with work as a ski guide and avalanche educator. In the summer, Morgan is a full-time mountain guide working primarily on Washington’s glaciated volcanos, so she spends 12 months of the year walking and sliding on snow. One of her favorite things to do while in the backcountry is plunging into a pristine alpine lake or river.

Ariel Kazunas is a freelance writer based in the Teton Range on the Wyoming and Idaho border. Her favorite ways to recreate (on protected public lands) include skiing, biking, hiking, and backpacking. Ariel believes deeply in questioning the status quo and advocating for both people and planet. Other hobbies include baking sourdough, babying her houseplants, making tailgate cocktails, and scanning Zillow obsessively to see if the US’s wealth inequity problem has been addressed so she can afford a home.

#8146. The 10 Most Accurate Rifles We’ve Tested (Plus, the Most Accurate Rifle Cartridges)

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

The number one trait everyone wants in a rifle is dime-splitting accuracy. The truth is that for the vast majority of hunting situations, you don’t need a rifle that shoots itty-bitty groups. But you still want one—just in case you need to shoot across the canyon or thread the needle on a quartering shot, and, most important, because a tack-driving rifle builds confidence, which makes you a better shot.

Here at Field & Stream, we’ve tested hundreds of rifles over the years, and we always subject them to rigorous precision/accuracy testing. Granted, just because our test rifle shot great does not mean if you buy one like it, it will shoot the same. But if a rifle performed well in our test, it should give you some buying confidence.

Below is a rundown of the 10 rifles we’ve tested that delivered the best on-target precision based on multiple five-shot groups at 100 yards with multiple loads of hunting ammo. All but one of these rifles shot average group sizes of less than an inch with multiple loads. Their out of the box weights ranged from 4.8 to 8.6 pounds, and they cost from $769.00 to almost 10 times that much. There’s bound to be one that will fit your hunting style and budget.

This rifle is hellaciously expensive, but extreme light weight and extreme precision do not come together in the same rifle at affordable prices. This Glacier Ti uses a carbon-fiber stock, a carbon-fiber barrel, and a titanium action. It’s also a full-custom rifle, so you get to specify barrel length, stock color, length of pull, the color of the Cerakote finish, and whether it is a left- or right-hand action. That level of customization comes at a price as well. Bottom line: If you want the best and don’t mind paying for it, here it is.

Related: Check out a full review of the Proof Glacier Ti here.

This rifle is one of the least expensive rifles on our list, but it turned in the second-best overall precision, and it also won out Editor’s Choice award in our 2025 rifles test. It features a carbon-fiber-wrapped barrel, a Flash Forged Technology carbon-fiber stock and is available in a variety of color options. It is also available in 24 popular big-game cartridge chamberings, starting with the 22 Creedmoor, and now for 2026, going all the way up to 375 H&H. For hunters looking to extend their reach with a rifle that will not weight them down or bash their wallet, the Ridgeline FFT is one of the best buys on the market.

Related: Check out a full review of the Ridgeline FFT here.

Not only did this rifle deliver consistent sub-MOA performance, but it is also the lightest bolt-action rifle we have tested to date. The Model 20S sort of proves what shooters and hunters have been saying for years, and it’s that the NULA rifles are pound-for-pound the best shooting hunting rifles ever made. The Wilson Combat NULA Model 20S is a modernized factory mini-action version of the full-custom New Ultra Light Arms rifle that Melvin Forbes made famous. This rifle is offered for centerfire rifle cartridges like the 223 Remington, 300 Blackout, 300 HAMR, and 350 Legend and comes with a carbon-fiber stock, floor plate, and a threaded muzzle.

Related: Check out a full review of the NULA Model 20S here.

The Alpine CT rifle is built on Weatherby’s new 307 action that is compatible with many Remington 700 accessories, and it comes with a lightweight PEAK 44 rifle stock that weighs only 24 ounces. It is also fitted with a BSF carbon-fiber-wrapped barrel and comes with a Trigger Tech trigger. At just over 6 pounds, it’s not the lightest rifle on this list but it is a shooter. Weatherby offers’ two action lengths for the Alpine CT with five big-game cartridges, including the 25 Creedmoor, that are available in the short-action version, and 11 in the long-action version to include Weatherby’s new fast-twist 25 RPM and the innovative 7mm Backcountry.

Related: Check out a full review of the Alpine CT here.

We selected the Nosler Model 21 rifle as the best rifle in our 2022 rifle test. We’ve tested a lot of rifles since then, but only four still currently offered have turned in a better average group size for on-target precision. The Model 21 feature a carbon-fiber stock and a fool-proof action with a bolt that’s outfitted with a M16-style extractor. It is currently offered in 10 big-game rifle cartridges starting with the 6.5 Creedmoor and including five Nosler cartridges, the 280 Ackley Improved, and the 375 H&H. Back in 2022, we called it one of the best all-around big-game rifles we’ve ever tested, and that remains true today.

Related: Check out a full review of the Nosler Model 21 here.

Of all the rifles on this list, the Premier MG Lite is the least-traditional looking. It is built around the Bergara action, but the action is fitted into a magnesium chassis, and it features a carbon-fiber-wrapped CURE barrel, carbon fiber grip, and a folding carbon fiber butt stock with an adjustable cheek piece. Even with the ARCA rail for bipod/tripod attachment, the Premier MG Lite rifle balanced very well for offhand shooting. It is currently offered chambered for seven big-game rifle cartridges from 6.5 Creedmoor to 300 PRC, and even the heaviest of these rifles still weighs less than 7 pounds.

Related: Check out a full review of the Premier MG Lite here.

The new Evoke from Christensen Arms is their entry-level rifle, and while our test rifle could not break the one-MOA mark with two of the loads tested, it shot so well with the third load that the rifle’s overall average was just shy of an inch. The Evoke is fitted with a 416R stainless barrel, a synthetic stock with a short section of rail at the tip of the forend, and it feeds from a detachable magazine. It is available in 10 different chamberings from 22 Creedmoor to 300 PRC, including the brand new 25 Creedmoor and the 7mm Backcountry. It is the second-heaviest, and second-least-expensive great shooting rifle on our list.

Related: Check out a full review of the Christensen Arms Evoke here.

The Ruger American Gen II rifle we tested in 2024 was the standard model, but now Ruger is offering six variations of the Gen II to include a Scout model. This rifle features substantial upgrades over the original Ruger American rifle with only a small price increase, but what really got our attention was how well this 6.5-pound rifle shot, with two of the three test loads averaging less than 0.90-inch. The Ruger American Gen II rifle might not be the most precise shooting rifle we have ever tested, but in our 2024 rifles test it received the best value award, and it very well might still be the best value rifle now two years later.

Related: Check out a full review of the American Gen II here.

Although during our testing the Stag Arms Pursuit rifle did not break the magic 1 MOA mark, it comes in as the 10th most precise rifle we’ve tested that is still being manufactured in 2026. Additionally, this chassis rifle is a bit unique. The butt stock is removable with a single pin, the comb is height-adjustable, it has a free-floating forend with M-Lok slots and a free-float rail for bipod/tripod mounting. As the heaviest rifle on our list, it is also configured more like a target/precision long-range rifle than a hunting rifle. It performed flawlessly but it is only available in two chamberings—6.5 Creedmoor and 308 Winchester.

In 1985, West Virginia gunsmith Melvin Forbes introduced the Model 20 custom rifle for short-action cartridges. Weighing right at 5 pounds and shooting like a bench-rest rifle, it set the standard for lightweight hunting rifles. Wilson Combat purchased the company in 2022, modernized the Model 20 with a threaded, custom tapered barrel, a new carbon-fiber stock, a lightweight floorplate, and a Timney Elite Hunter trigger. In our 2023 rifle test, it took home our Editor’s Pick award. The Model 20 is currently offered in five popular big-game chamberings, and the and 22 and 25 Creedmoor are coming in 2026.

Related: Check out a full review of the NULA Model 20 here.

There are two terms shooters use when talking about how well a rifle shoots. The first is accuracy, which relates to the variation between point of aim and point of impact. With a very accurate shot, the point of impact will be the same as the point of aim. Precision is the term that best describes a rifle’s ability to consistently direct bullets to the same or very nearly the same spot every time. The two terms are very similar but do not mean the same thing.

If you shoot a sub-inch group that is in the center of the target, you’ve demonstrated accuracy and precision. If the sub-inch group is not at the center of the target, you have precision without accuracy. If the group is centered on the target but not very small, the shooting was accurate but not very precise, and if the shots are sort of sprayed all over the target the shooting lacked accuracy and precision.

In hunting, accuracy is paramount because your goal is to put a bullet in the kill zone. Precision means your rifle can do that every time. However, as distance increases, precision diminishes. A rifle capable of shooting a one-inch or smaller group at 100 yards will likely shoot a five-inch group at 500 yards, and at a certain distance the rifle’s intrinsic level of precision might exceed the size of the kill zone. For this reason, hunters attempting long-range shots on big-game animals want rifles that will deliver extreme precision. It’s generally accepted that a rifle capable of consistent sub-MOA performance—five shot groups averaging less than one inch—is a very precise-shooting rifle.

The ability of a rifle to shoot with great precision hinges on the quality of all the rifle’s components and how well the rifle was put together. That said, ammunition quality is also very important. The cartridge case, bullet, powder, and primer, and how well they were assembled and work together matter too. And some rifle cartridges tend to consistently deliver good precision better than others.

The rifle cartridges often considered to be the most accurate tend to reflect the characteristics of our most modern cartridges. These characteristics include powder capacities that are not overly large when compared to bore diameter, sharp shoulder angles of 30°, a cartridge neck that is longer than bullet diameter, a minimally tapered case, and a specified fast-twist barrel that will stabilize high-ballistic-coefficient bullets. Many modern cartridges like the Creedmoors, the PRCs, the 6.5 Grendel, 224 Valkyrie, and the 7mm Backcountry reflect these design parameters.

That said, a number older cartridges with only some of these characteristics have a great reputation for precision, including the 222 Remington, 6.5×55 Swede, 260, 7mm-08, and 308 Winchester. While both modern and the older cartridges might have a reputation for precision, there is no fixed rules for a precision cartridge. Great precision can be found with any cartridge using good quality ammo fired from a rifle put together right with quality components. My first custom rifle was a 5-pound New Ultra Light Arms (NULA) chambered for the antique—120 year old—35 Remington and was a consistent sub-MOA performer. The bottom line is, if you get a high-quality rifle known for driving tacks, and you try a variety of good hunting ammo with it, you are very likely to find the combination that gives you first-rate accuracy and precision.

Editor’s Note: Richard Mann’s new book, Rifle Cartridges for the Hunter: A Hunting Journal Spanning a Half-Century details 50 rifle cartridges through real hunts, practical insight, and hard-earned lessons. It is essential reading for serious hunters and riflemen who appreciate ballistic science and authentic outdoor adventure.

Richard Mann was born and raised in West Virginia and has hunted from the Montana mountains to the green hills of Africa. In 2015, Mann began contributing to Field & Stream to cover guns, ammunition, ballistics, and hunting. In 2022, he was named as the brand’s Shooting Editor. Highlights Education Mann has a degree in criminal justice and is a graduate of the West Virginia State Police Academy and the Southwest Law Enforcement Academy of Virginia. He is also graduate of the NRA’s Tactical Law Enforcement Firearms Instructor School as well as multiple courses at Gunsite Academy. As a high school senior, Mann was failing English and his teacher told him, “Choose another career path, because you’ll never write for Field & Stream.” Experience Because his mother was a hunter, Mann was hunting before he was born. He has traversed the world in pursuit of small, large, and dangerous game. He was a member of the 1995 West Virginia Police Pistol Governor’s Twenty, won the 1999 WV National Guard State Pistol Match, and the 2004 WV Muzzleloader Metallic State Championship. Mann established a Scout Rifle training course for Steyr and assisted Gunsite Academy with the development of their Laser Integrated 250 Pistol Course. Mann has worked with many bullet manufacturers conducting ballistic experiments and has a patent for a bullet testing media and a scope reticle. He’s contributed to many periodicals, presented reloading seminars for the NRA, appeared on the Discovery Channel as a firearms expert, and was the executive producer of WildCraft: South Africa, on Amazon Prime. In 2019, Mann was awarded the Bill McRea Lifetime Achievement Award for his writings. #8144. How Two Bored Belgians Broke the Backyard Ultra World Record

Trail Runner contributing photographer Jacob Zocherman drove 15 hours from his home in Sweden to document the Belgian team at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship in Retie, Belgium. Unlike a typical race with a predetermined finish and a predictable narrative arc within it, backyard ultras only end when there is one runner left. Zocherman spent the five days and four hours of what ended up being a world-record-breaking run on the course, sleeping in a camper van when he could. He spoke with managing editor Abby Levene during and shortly after the race.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts had been running for 98 hours at the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, and they were bored. Never mind they had each run over 400 miles on the same 4.167-mile course. Never mind they hadn’t gotten more than a few minutes of sleep at once in over four days. They looked fresh, the nights were long, and blah blah blah, on-the-ground photographer Jacob Zocherman reports. But with the 100th lap on the horizon, something clicked.

“You could see something happen to them, like a spring flower waiting through winter,” Zocherman tells Trail Runner. “Suddenly the sun comes and nothing happens, nothing happens, and then in a specific moment everything happens and the flower comes out in bloom. That’s what I saw in them—suddenly they were happy to be there, cheering with the audience, laughing with each other and joking.”

It was like colleagues going out to the bar on a Friday afternoon: They’ve found their happy place, Zocherman says. Except in this case, their happy place was a park in Retie, Belgium, aka the middle of nowhere.

“It’s very touching to see, because they are so humble and so easy to like,” Zocherman says. “At that point, I felt like the race would go on forever. But it also feels very fragile—when there are only two runners left, there is no room for error.”

Per backyard ultra rules, runners must run the 4.167-mile lap on the hour, every hour, until only one runner remains and is declared the winner. In case that isn’t nutty enough, the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship is an even nuttier spinoff of this format: Each participating country (of which this year there were 67) simultaneously conducts its own backyard race with 15 participants, and the country with the most cumulative laps wins. This backyard team world championship now alternates every other year with the individual championship, held on the original backyard ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee.

Team USA would go on to win the team world title, with Mark Dowdle leading the stars and stripes to a collective 1,120 laps, also known as “yards,” for its second world title in six years. Australia took second, 51 yards behind, and Belgium took third, 11 yards off of them. While the team competition inherently shaped the dynamic of the race, with runners sacrificing their own best interests to slow down and pull teammates along, Steyaert and Geerts had several additional goals on their minds.

They’d each run over 100 laps multiple times—four times for Steyaert and six for Geerts. But neither had ever run through a fifth night. Belgium’s fourth-place runner Kenneth Vanthuyne was long gone after hallucinating that he was at work when Steyaert and Geerts put on their headlamps for the fifth time.

“That was the critical moment,” Zocherman says. “It was the one thing they had always wanted to do.”

As the sun rose over the dewy fields surrounding the dirt road of the race course, they both looked unscathed.

“I was like, ‘OK, nothing can stop them,” Zocherman says. They turned their attention to the Belgium national backyard ultra record of 115 laps, held by Jan Vandekerckhove. They checked that off and reset the goal to the world record of 119 laps, set by Australia’s Phil Gore at Dead Cow Gully in Queensland last year. That, too, proved to be seemingly no problem.

At 5:00 p.m. on Thursday, October 22—over five days after they started running—Zocherman heard rumors that Steyaert and Geerts were setting out on their final lap.

“I think they could have continued. They looked fresh, they looked really good,” Zocherman says. “But I also know they wanted to finish together. And the longer you go, the smaller the margins are that something will happen and one will finish over the other. And they wanted to avoid that. But they wanted to finish together.”

Sure enough, when the pair returned to the start/finish arch at 5:57 p.m., they did not go back out when the clock reached the top of the hour. Instead, the two friends, standing side-by-side in matching red shirts, grinned to the crowd of cheering onlookers, each raising a hand and joining them together over their heads in the shape of a heart.

Together, they had accomplished what no one had done before: Run 124 laps of a 4.167-mile course every hour, on the hour, for a total of 516.7 miles and a new backyard ultra individual world record.

“They are like brothers and have run many times as the two remaining runners,” Zochermans says. “So to them, it is not a competition that late in the race. They are doing it together. And they want it to remain like that. It’s kind of beautiful. It’s poetry.”

From the start at 2 p.m. local time on Saturday, October 17, until Steyaert and Geerts concluded their record-breaking run five days and four hours later, Zocherman was on the ground to document it all. It’s a stroke of good fortune that of the 67 backyard ultra team competitions happening around the world, Zocherman—who lives in his native Sweden—chose to go to Belgium. It’s also not a coincidence.

In fact, Zocherman almost didn’t make the 15 hour drive to Retie after his mother was unexpectedly diagnosed with an aggressive form of cancer two weeks before the race. The only reason he did go, Zocherman tells Trail Runner, is because that random campground in a foreign country is like home. Zocherman had been at the same course in April for the Legends Backyard Ultra, and the mini-universe environment of these events bring people together in a special way that’s hard to describe.

“It was an emotional rollercoaster and a logistical battle,” Zocherman says. “I wouldn’t have gone if it wasn’t this backyard ultra. It was a personal reason to be among people I know and like. I didn’t think it would be the crazy result that it was.”

Zocherman made the trek with his dog Balou, who he says keeps him grounded at these events with no predetermined end, or even rhythm. (She’s now witnessed three world records and could not be less impressed.) They did two laps of the course every day and got a decent amount of sleep for the first few nights before squeezing in 20 minutes at a time between loops by the end.

“I also know it will be a very long race and I have to drive home for 15 hours after so I can’t be crazy wasted,” he says. “Although you become crazy wasted anyway.”

Here’s how this world-record-setting run unfolded, through Zocherman’s eyes and words.

The first out of 372 whistles marks the start for the team world championships, by whistler Eilis Lanclus.

Matthias Pelgrims, one of the top runners the Belgian team is preserving his energy during the first loops of the competition.

Never a dull moment for the crews in between the loops. Always something to worry about.

The hula skirt. Once in a while there is a loop with someone wearing a hula skirt in order to break the monotony.

Resting runners in-between the loops with the watcher waiting to collect.

The puzzle. Whatever brings joy to the table and something to do during the early days is welcomed.

Approaching camp on day three. It’s a misty and cool morning after a very wet and challenging second night of the race.

The runners don’t fear the rain so much during the race, they say. It’s the wind ripping over the exposed night loop that they worry about.

Willem De Troyer is suffering from pain in his legs and is screaming out in pain at every step during what would be his last loop before timing out.

The emotions are rising as the race continues.

Jelle Tielemans is having a hard time during day three, moments before he quits. After 45 hours of racing, only 13 runners of the 990 who started in 67 countries remain.

As the race goes on, usually runners move closer to the start area in order to save time in between the loops.

Bert Verbist on his way back to the camp after yet another successful loop.

Common duties by different hands. Although the race is repetitive, the things that need to be done are endless and carried out by volunteers throughout all the hours of the day and night.

The remains of a celebration for Merijn Geerts, who turned 52 during the race.

Evariest Callens gets a massage on his throbbing legs after 69 hours of running.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

Matthias Pelgrims, who just timed out after 68 loops, receives an emotional hug from his partner Jody.

The intersection of the two loops. The night loop is more open and exposed, while the day loop is more sheltered but also a bit more technical in the forest.

Merijn Geerts takes a micro-nap in between loops.

Tanja Steyaert crews her husband Ivo throughout the race.

The control center with the camera feeds from different parts of the loops, as well as the race broadcast and other tracking sites.

A tense wait for the remaining runners to finish their loops and go out for another.

Sleep is grabbed when you can and where you can. Nothing is certain in a backyard ultra, other than knowing you will get little sleep.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts run through the fifth night. They are the only remaining runners of the 15 who started for Team Belgium.

The party is getting real in the Belgian countryside.

Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert’s backyard ultra world record is celebrated with the power cutting out (and the start/finish arch falling down) after heavy rain broke the electric circuits. But nothing, seemingly, can stop their progress.

The remains of the previous days. A lot of food, drinks, and beer.

Ultimately, Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geert ran 124 loops—and set a new world record—before stopping.

In running and in life: Ivo Steyaert and Merijn Geerts celebrate with their wives as well as crews after setting the world record.

#8143. Where Did the Midweight Ski Touring Boot Go?

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The men's Tecnica Zero G Decoy Pro, staged and ready to go for a backcountry adventure in Cooke City, Montana. (Photo: Rick Sorensen)

Overview: Midweight ski touring boots, historically three buckles and 1,300 to 1,500 grams, can handle the whole range of backcountry skis, yet the class has stagnated while lightweight and crossover boots got most of the industry’s R&D. Writer Bergen Tjossem, a former ski-shop employee, argues the next big touring breakthrough should come from the midweight category.

It’s 4 a.m. and the biting cold plunges into the open garage as I stuff my partner’s idling Forester with gear. But I stall, hovering over my collection of ski touring boots. Big boots or little boots? Neither seems right for the day. I throw my thrashed 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots over my shoulder, snap on my headlamp, and lug my skis to the car. I don’t know why I still hesitate at the start of every backcountry ski day—I end up picking the workhorse boot over the specialists most of the time.

Why, then, is the industry trying to squash this midweight ski touring boot class? Even the Maestrale RS, my beloved midweight archetype, is graduating toward the next class up this season, with a fourth buckle and more heft.

Owning a quiver of boots and skis is fun; it gives you options. But if you already own a pair of alpine boots like most skiers do, one dedicated touring boot could accomplish the vast majority of your needs. Yet where backcountry skis fall on a neat bell curve of dimension and weight, the boots we can buy to pilot them are bimodally distributed: ski shapes cluster in the middle, touring boots at the extremes. The evolution of midweight ski touring boots—the ones that best serve the majority of backcountry skiers—has stagnated compared to their cousins at the ends. It’s the “missing middle” problem every ski town knows from housing.

There’s no rule or buckle count dividing touring boot classes, but allow me to split them for the sake of the rant: lightweight boots typically have two buckles and top out around 1,200 grams, like the La Sportiva Kilo. Midweight boots historically use three buckles and weigh 1,300 to 1,500 grams. Then there are crossover boots that blend touring and alpine: four buckles, around 1,500 grams, typically with a GripWalk sole compatible with tech and alpine bindings, like the Dynafit Tigard.

Ski touring dogma says the optimum backcountry quiver is two pairs of ski touring boots and two pairs of skis: one lightweight and distance-oriented, the other beefy and fun. But here’s the catch—lightweight boots struggle with big skis, especially in poor snow, because they lack progressive flex and damping. And the opposite is also true. Crossover boots are a real drag on lightweight skis. Aside from the cumbersome ROM, the added stiffness, high cuff, and heft quickly overpower lightweight skis. Yet midweights can handle the whole ski spectrum.

When I worked in ski shops in the early 2010s as ski touring took off, midweight boots were the benchmark. Dynafit’s Vulcan and the Scarpa Maestrale were the choice for skiers who wanted to climb efficiently without giving up too much on the descent. What followed that workhorse boot era was an explosion of lightweight options, as almost every company in the business invested in svelter chassis while skis got lighter and less demanding. The rise of resort uphilling and Skimo racing only fueled the growth. Lately, lightweight boots such as La Sportiva’s Kilo XTR have been beefed up to claim more of that middle segment without overtaking it completely. But lightweight two-buckle designs with sturdier components still come up short on the leverage and suspension big skis demand.

Crossovers got the next round of R&D in the name of capturing the massive resort-hybrid buyer. Scarpa’s 1,500 gram 4-Quattro XT with a legit 61 degree range of motion (ROM) revolutionized the segment in 2022. All of a sudden, boots with alpine-like skiing capability unlocked a bigger ROM, while better materials and design brought weights down to 1,500 grams per boot or less. It also introduced freaky new levels of “quiver overlap” for skiers who already own alpine boots with a walk mode.

Smooshed between the crossover and the lightweight segments is that increasingly scant boot group, the midweights. It’s not that these midweight boots don’t exist—the Scott Cosmos Pro and Fischer Transalp prove they do—but rather that they’ve gotten the shaft on R&D over the last decade. Most of the remaining midweights are just stale, longing for a refresh, a trickle-down of new tech, and a burst of innovation.

A radical solution would be to have fewer skis, and I can’t believe you’d even suggest that. I’ve got a better idea: Give me one boot that can cover the entire ski quiver: three buckles, a camming power strap, over 65 degrees of ROM, under 1,400 grams, and minimal fiddle factor. Oops, I just mostly described the Scarpa Maestrale that’s been around for sixteen years. That’s because the industry is barely competing to refine that basic formula into its state-of-the-art form.

As a skier of many setups, I can say there’s a mismatch between the boots I want and those available. Lightweights and crossovers have had their run. My hunch is that the next big touring breakthrough will be, and should be, in the missing middle. Until then, you’ll catch me clinging to my 2023 Scarpa Maestrale RS boots like the gear troll I am.

#8141. We Need to Move Past the “Shut Up And Die Like a Man” Mentality in the Mountains

Will Gadd (left) and his friend, the late Ken Wallator. (Photo: Will Gadd)

“Shut up and die like a man!” sounds like a line from a bad action movie, but we all heard it on the radio from the paragliding competition director. The director was yelling at a terrified pilot who thought he was falling to his death. The pilot had accidentally keyed open his radio’s shoulder mic, allowing his frantic screams to be broadcast across the competition frequency.

The unfortunate pilot begging to god to not die had collapsed his wing and plummeted in front of my eyes. Twenty-one years later, the memory of this sight and soundtrack is unforgettable, and so was the director’s barking, because there was clearly no sympathy for what the pilot thought was his final, horrific ride. Miraculously, the pilot recovered his wing and flew out to land and reflect on his life choices alone.

Most pilots didn’t think the competition director’s statement was out of line for the time. Many still don’t. I see terrible parallels between flying culture and some facets of climbing’s; in alpinism especially, some see death as an attractant, or an inevitability. Over my 40 years as an alpinist and 35 as a pilot, I’ve watched climbers experience gut-wrenching trauma—then do their best to ignore it, too scared or proud to deal with the ugly, messy truth. This avoidance sends a message to younger climbers, much like the competition director’s statement so long ago: Suck it up, move on, and die with honor if things go bad.

But living with trauma doesn’t have to be that way.

When my late friend Ken Wallator was 21, he climbed Mount Belanger in the Canadian Rockies with his girlfriend Heidi. They reached the top of the difficulties, unroped, and walked along a low-angle snow ridge to the summit of the peak. But the snow ridge was actually a massive, overhanging cornice of windblown snow, and it collapsed as they stopped to take a photo. Ken somehow managed to leap to safety but Heidi fell hundreds of meters down the face.

Ken, a brave bear of a man, downclimbed the face, found Heidi somehow still alive, and started carrying her out to a distant hut. She died before they reached it.

In the aftermath of Heidi’s death, I watched Ken receive a surprising amount of blame from grieving members of the climbing community. Didn’t he know better than to walk on a cornice? Why weren’t they roped up? Ken was already wracked with guilt from the accident. When his community piled on, their condemnation lit an internal firestorm.

Thirty years later, in 2019, Ken helped me re-roof my house. He still had the strength of a bear and I watched him haul 100-pound loads of shingles up my rickety ladder. In a rare moment of emotionality, he told me how he still hadn’t gotten over Heidi’s death, or the climbing community’s blame. We talked more about trauma, and I realized only then how that day on Mount Belanger broke my friend in a way that never healed.

As two young, hungry alpinists, Ken and I didn’t know what mental “help” looked like 30 years ago, and Ken was too much a product of his culture to take it 30 years later. Despite his immense physical and mental strength, Ken died by suicide a few weeks after our talk.

More recently, Will Stanhope’s death has brought to mind this idea of “asking for help” once more. For years Stanhope had battled desperately with alcohol. He was facing various charges at the time of his death—including assault and sexual assault—while still succeeding on difficult routes as a professional climber and mountain guide.

In our last real conversation, Stanhope talked about needing to “harden up and stop letting the carnage get to me” one minute, then sobbed about the “death camp” of hard alpine climbing the next. Like Ken and me, he had lost many friends in the mountains.

“You and I [watched] our mentors and friends die, one after another, as if everyone around us was climbing their way to oblivion,” his friend Kieran Brownie wrote in an obituary. “We couldn’t return to the mountains, we couldn’t return to each other.”

Stanhope carried a heavy weight in the final months of his life, made even heavier by grief, guilt, and irreversible mistakes. After a lifetime of hard solos and even scarier roped climbs, it seemed impossible that Stanhope would ever fall off an easy 5.11. But when he did just that last April and succumbed to a head injury, to me and other friends, Stanhope’s death felt more related to the weight he carried in his head than the climb itself. His family and friends made truly profound and sometimes wrenchingly difficult efforts to help him, but, like falling, the weights of addiction and trauma develop their own momentum.

Hard drinking, hard living, and celebrating dangerous acts—usually lauded as “bold”—are hallmarks of every mountain sport I’ve ever done, from kayaking to flying to skiing to climbing. Our literature is full of stories celebrating those who climbed hard, drank hard, and died silently.

I can’t help but wonder if our literature strives to make these deaths seem somehow valiant and necessary, like dying in the mountains is a noble sacrifice rather than the tragedy it really is. The classic mountaineering texts rarely explore the trauma that comes after seeing a friend die. They barrel ever onward to the summit.

Military veterans and first responders have a trauma-treatment framework that climbers should strive to adopt. Soldiers are not considered “weak” if they are affected by bloody combat. Paramedics are not ridiculed for taking leave after responding to a grisly car wreck. These are normal human responses, and professional groups typically have protocols for helping those involved in traumatic situations. These groups have no other choice; a traumatized team simply cannot function.

Those professional protocols weren’t there for Ken, Will, that terrified pilot, or many others, including me.

When I was 19 I tried with every tool I knew to save a fellow kayaker stuck just inches from the surface in his boat. I couldn’t reach him, and he drowned in front of me as I tried to remember how to rig a better haul system. I had nightmares for years of the paddler chasing me in the dark beside that river.

Only decades later did I seek help, after a divorce and a lot of behavior I understood even less than that terrible accident. I’m lucky I survived and sought belated help. Ken and Will and many others didn’t. Many more in our community—your friends and mine—are barely standing today, carrying crippling loads. They need help putting those loads down.

The pain of trauma does not disappear with six or 600 beers. Doing dangerous climbs or flights or other high-stimulus experiences temporarily distracts from the weight, but doesn’t solve it. There is no pack heavier than one filled with trauma you can’t put down.

One of the smartest things I’ve ever heard about trauma came after we failed to resuscitate a dying man at the base of an ice climb a few years ago. A professional responder on the scene could tell I was shaken, and looked me in the eye and said, “Post traumatic stress is normal; post traumatic stress disorder is optional—if you get help. Get help.”

I see real change today, from my wife Sarah Hueniken’s Mountain Muskox foundation to the American Alpine Club’s Grief Fund, two organizations built to support mountain-trauma survivors.

But I also still see a lot of the “Shut up and die like a man” attitude, and the celebration of “bold” yet physically unimpressive climbs that are often little more than Russian Roulette. Huge, low-angle alpine routes with immense serac and avalanche hazard are not that cool, in my book. And I see many climbers who still romanticize the wrong parts of climbing, whether that’s meaningless objective hazard or the very idea of “suffering silently.”

We need to recognize that a mountain death doesn’t end with the funeral; often that’s just the start of a very long and difficult process for everyone involved. In climbing more people die on the descent after the summit than on the climb itself.

At times I’ve felt deeply angry about our outdoor tribe’s celebration of “bold” hazards, and our denial of the after-effects of engaging in high-risk sports where participants die regularly. We often celebrate the bold free solos or dangerous alpine routes where everything clicked into place. We never celebrate the dead parent who doesn’t show up for their kids’ birthdays.

But the truth is that I laughed when the paragliding competition director said his infamous line. I promised myself that if I was in that situation in the future, I’d shut up. That became my normal. Today, I hope I’d speak up on the comment, and reach out to the guy who almost died that day. Because I’ve been him, and it sucks, and I’m trying to do better.

I’m less angry today when I think about Ken, Will, or others who have left the game, and just hope that our culture continues to evolve in the same way the first responders did, and that we ultimately celebrate survival more than dying silently. We can do better, if we want to.

Finally, if, like me, you’ve been through the trauma wringer, it often takes help to sort it out. We’re not tougher than the veterans or first responders even if our culture says we “should” be—we’re just less educated about intense trauma.

The goal is to return to full function and fly in life, not get stuck in the inevitable mental dust devils of mountain death. Peace to those hurting, it can get better with help. Substances and more dangerous living may distract us short term, but long term the combo is deadly despite the romantic words we historically place on both. I write these words for the future Wills and Kens, they are me, you, our friends.

Shutting up is not a solution, because silence is death.

#8139. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8137. There Are Over 40 Resorts Planning To Open In November—Here’s Where Experts Say Conditions Will Be Best

Mammoth Mountain opening day 2025 (Photo: Courtesy of Mammoth Mountain)

Some folks may think skiing in November is crazy: the snow is rarely good, and the mere thrill of lifts spinning often attracts crowds larger than downhill capacity should allow.

It can be difficult to know where, if anywhere, it is worth skiing in November. While resorts are making snow around the clock, the decision to open boils down to weather.

For Colorado skiers, the weather may finally be on your side. According to Open Snow meteorologist Joel Gratz, November is set to start with a “bang.” He predicts a storm arriving Sunday will drop 6 to 12 inches on nearly all mountains, with some spots seeing up to 20. Did someone say powder day?!

Several Colorado resorts are opening their lifts before Halloween is over. Arapahoe Basin opened Oct. 28, Keystone follows on Oct. 30, and Wolf Creek on Oct. 31. Snow is thin at all three for now, but their high elevations should set them up for a stronger start to November.

Breckenridge and Copper Mountain are planning to open on Nov. 6, and if the snow comes in like Gratz is predicting, their opening days could feature more than just a white ribbon of death.

A little later into the month, Vail and Eldora are both planning Nov. 13 opening dates. It’s too early to tell if temperatures will preserve the snow from earlier storms, but as long as cold air remains, these are resorts to keep on your radar for potentially decent skiing.

Neighboring Utah resorts aren’t expected to receive as fruitful a snow bounty. They’ll see the same storm as Colorado, with the highest accumulations on Sunday, says Open Snow forecaster Evan Thayer. “Cooler air will eventually lower snow levels, with some decent accumulations possible up high.”

As of the time of publishing, Brian Head is planning on opening on Nov. 6. If Thayer’s prediction is accurate, the Southern Utah resort could see “decent accumulations” on its highest peaks. Alta, Park City, and Solitude are all planning on opening on Nov. 20. It’s too early to say how these resorts will fare, but cold temperatures will be the biggest asset.

California skiers will have to wait a bit longer. Open Snow forecaster Bryan Alleretto predicts the Tahoe region’s snowy start will likely come after Nov. 10, which could be good timing for Mammoth Mountain, set to open Nov. 20. Mammoth isn’t a Tahoe resort, but it tends to share weather patterns with those to the north.

The East Coast has had a warm fall, but that could change. There’s no official snow report yet, but Maine’s Sugarloaf plans to reopen Nov. 20, likely making it the region’s first resort to welcome skiers back. Vermont’s Sugarbush follows on Nov. 21, while nearby Killington, which often opens early, hasn’t announced a date as of press time.

#8136. How to Hunt the Best Day of the Rut No. 3: November 3

Last fall, a tall 8-point Michigan buck showed me just how good—and lasting—the action can be during the first few days of November. The buck hit my mock scrape twice during daylight, which tipped me off that it was time for a strategic hunt where a small woodlot met standing corn. Between my hunt that evening and another the next morning, I had nearly a dozen encounters with the buck as he zig-zagged his way through the broken acres of timber and ag fields, feverishly seeking a receptive doe. The flurry of activity finally ended when he stepped into one of my shooting lanes at 11:10 am.

Bucks are transitioning into full-blown seeking mode right now, and I’m betting that this coming Tuesday will be one of the best days of the year to be on stand. Of course, it is a big election day across the country, so hopefully you voted early or sent in that absentee ballot, because this is a day you’d probably rather be hunting over a scrape line than standing in line waiting to cast a ballot. Here’s what to expect and how to proceed for your best shot at tagging out on Tuesday.

Related: The Best Days of the 2026 Whitetail Rut

Rut hormones are starting to peak in bucks across much of whitetail range, and more and more does are showing signs that they are ready or nearly ready to breed. It should all add up to great hunting. Bucks, young and old alike, are in seeking mode now, often visible in daylight hours and moving more with each passing day.

This is the height of what I’d call the late pre-rut, with bucks largely still hitting scrapes, but possibly your last chance to catch up to a homebody buck before he abandons those scrapes and gets wildly unpredictable in the all-out chasing phase of the rut. Now, more than ever, bucks are susceptible to a wide range of calling and decoying tactics, as their default safety mode is being overridden by their urge to reproduce. This makes setting up “close enough” a viable strategy for bowhunters with a grunt call in pocket and a set of rattling antlers in hand. So, on this Best Day of the Rut, elect to pack a lunch, sit long, and be ready to shoot on a moment’s notice, because bucks are sure to be on the move.

Things change fast in the whitetail world, and staying on top of current sign can make or break your pre-rut hunting. Hopefully you’ve been scouting as much as hunting since our last Best Day. A big mistake many hunters make is thinking more time on stand will mean more opportunities, while ignoring the scouting that actually leads to high-quality sits. At this time of year, a scrape that was smoking hot last week may be stone cold when you show up, so use a weather event or midday break in your schedule to speed-scout for the latest sign and use that info to direct your hunting decisions. This could be checking a low-intrusion camera or cruising those scrape lines to confirm recent activity. Just try to minimize your impact and keep it as low key as possible.

For your morning hunt, think like a buck and focus on the does. Look for a transition area near known doe bedding where you can catch them returning in the morning hours. Bucks will be close behind. Focus on zones with numerous attraction factors or lines of travel to increases your chances. These factors could include a scrape line, convergence of well-used trails, a fruit tree, or multiple edges of cover necking down to one location. These things will steer deer traffic right past a carefully placed stand and multiply your chances of encountering a doe-seeking buck.

With my 2025 Michigan 8-point, the only standing corn in the area, just 30 yards from my stand, was prime doe bedding. This kept the tall 8 in the area and constantly moving, attempting to see if a doe was just behind the next stalk. The block of woods created four edges where it met a neighboring chunk of timber, encouraging deer to naturally move past my stand as they followed these edges. The last factor was a mock scrape the buck had taken over, which I set in August with just this time frame in mind.

Find a similar transition zone near does and stick it out. Even if a buck happens to sneak by you, there’s a good chance he’ll be back soon to re-check the area. Be sure to avoid areas where the deer will travel as you enter. For this killer morning ambush to work, you’ll need get settled early—like and hour early—to make sure you beat the deer back to their bedding transition. And don’t be in a hurry to leave either. Remember, I shot that tall 8-point at 11:10 am last year.

Related: 50 Expert Tips for Hunting the Whitetail Rut

You can’t go wrong with an evening sit at a food-plot, ag field, or other prime feeding area that you know does are hitting consistently. They will essentially be your real-life decoys. Nearby bucks will have a hard time resisting coming into the open to check on any mature doe they see, even if they aren’t quite in estrus, giving you an opportunity if you’re ready. And speaking of being ready, it’s a good idea between and just before hunts to practice getting drawn quickly, fast target acquisition, judging distance at a glance, and stopping a buck with a mouth grunt or bleat.

As for the evening hunt itself, this is prime time to employ a 3D decoy and deep-sounding grunt tube. I say 3D because, in my experience, 2D decoys at close range can spook deer that can’t see them from certain angles. A realistic 3D decoy can change this, signaling to a passing buck that something has this strange buck’s interest which requires his investigation. Bottom line, if a buck is seeking does in daylight, he’s probably sufficiently amped up to be vulnerable to these ploys.

What about scent? Using a fresh estrus scent now (where legal) could add the realism you need and make decent setup irresistible. Use a drag rope but add this trick: Don’t drag but dab your scent-filled rag on the ground like deer footsteps, exactly what a buck would be tracking. And speaking of scent, yours should be accounted for; use rubber boots to minimize any scent you leave and do your best to allow your scent on stand to blow just off from where bucks are likely to enter. This gives them the ability to scent-check the plot while also feeling safe enough to enter it.

For the diehard public-land hunters out there, this Tuesday could thin out the rut crowd a bit and allow for some natural deer movement patterns, especially in the morning while most people are at work. From my experience, catching up to a buck on public land is still a tough task, especially in pressured areas. Being highly mobile is the fix. If you’re stuck in permanent stands, you may be left out of the action happening just a few yards away in thick cover.

Public-land bucks checking and pushing does tend to stay in denser cover for safety. The solution is to pack that mobile stand or saddle and sticks and adjust to the activity you’re seeing on the fly. If there are no trees big enough for that where the action is, consider a ground sit in exactly the right spot. Use natural cover so you don’t tip deer off to obvious changes to their bedroom or by setting up a blind. Instead, execute a quick, low-impact ambush on a rut-crazed buck on November 3rd.

Adam Lewis is a contributing writer for Field & Stream. A full-time science teacher, Lewis is a Michigan-based outdoor writer and videographer who also hosts the Deer IQ podcast and blog. His how-to articles have appeared in a variety of outdoor publications, typically focusing on finding unique angles and practical strategies for public- and private-land whitetail deer hunters. Highlights Education Lewis earned his BS in Science Education from Olivet Nazarene University, Songwriting School of Hard Knocks, Nashville, TN. Experience Born in the hunting-rich state of Michigan, Lewis grew up around deer camp with his father and uncles and picked up a bow to start chasing whitetail as soon as legally possible, on his 12th birthday. After college, Lewis set his sights on a new pursuit—singing and songwriting, which led him to the neon-lit corner bars of Nashville’s famous strip. He returned to his home state in 2010 to focus on hunting and writing and soon began penning outdoor articles for local and then national magazines. Along with teaching, Lewis currently, writes, produces video, and hosts his podcast and blog, all aimed at educating hunters for improved success in the field. Notable Work

#8135. Vanja Matijevec Gave Up His Own Everest Summit to Save Three People

Vanja Matijevec on the Lhotse wall during his 1981 Himalayan expedition (Photo: Aleš Kunaver, kept by the National Museum of Contemporary History of Slovenia)

Vanja Matijevec belonged to a generation of Slovenian alpinists who pushed onto some of the biggest walls in the Himalayas, but one of the defining moments of his climbing life came when he chose not to summit.

On his legendary 1979 expedition to Everest, Matijevec gave up his own planned summit attempt to help Stipe Božić, Stane Belak and Ang Phu, who had become stranded above 8,000 meters during their descent. Božić later remembered Matijevec’s selflessness as helping him survive after he lost a crampon high on the mountain.

Born in Ljubljana on October 14, 1946, Matijevec first encountered the Slovenian mountains as a child, tending cattle on pastures above Tržič. He came to alpinism later, after meeting climber Jože Hočevar through his field work, and began training as a mountain guide in 1975. In 1979, Matijevec, Lado Vidmar and Blaž Oblak made the first ascent of Lucifer (WI4+), a roughly 200-meter frozen waterfall in Gozd Martuljek. The climb, completed with equipment Matijevec later remembered as rudimentary, helped usher in the era of modern ice climbing in Slovenia.

But Matijevec’s ambitions stretched far beyond Slovenia. In 1981, Matijevec and Franček Knez climbed to the rim of Lhotse’s immense South Face, then considered one of the great unsolved problems of Himalayan alpinism. Over the course of his life, Matijevec accumulated more than 30 first ascents, including a direct new route up the West Face of Trisul in 1987. Despite his achievements, his peers remember his kindness more than anything. Fellow Slovenian alpinist Viki Grošelj, who had known Matijevec since their early climbing days, remembered him after his death as a distinctive personality and, simply, “the right man in the right place,” he told Slovenian newspaper Delo.

#8134. Last-Minute Costumes for Trail Runners

It’s Halloween week and you still have no idea what you’re going to be. Trail or ultrarunning is your entire personality, but you can only toss on some last-minute split shorts and a fake beard to go as Forrest Gump so many years in a row. Everyone is “pretty tired” of you responding to what you are with an exhausted, “I just felt like running” in a goofy accent. It’s OK; we’ve all been there. And Trail Runner’s resident doodler and creative character costume expert, Bobby Peavey, has your back. He’s put together a curated list of archetypes from your local run club and Instagram feed that are sure to be a hit this spooky season.

This costume is perfect for your most bonk-vulnerable friends.  Dress them up as Bonkenstein and enjoy a night of constantly bringing them back from the dead with salty and sweet snacks.

Do you have the patience of a saint and the multitasking skills of Leslie Knope? Then the Race Director costume is the perfect choice for you. Your night is going to consist of making sure there are ample snacks for all, that trick or treating/holiday party schedules stay on track, that everybody stays safe and healthy, and about a dozen other things that everyone else surely overlooks.

When you select this costume for the spookiest night of the year, the assignment is clear: only speak in the past tense for the entire night. You’re full of nostalgia and cynical disdain for anything modern. You’re basically the Uncle Rico of the evening.

Time to update your watch to the current model, recharge your heart rate strap, and cover every inch of exposed skin with wearable storage.  Because the funnest part of your Halloween is going to be teaching all your friends about the newest and techiest gear on the market.

For this costume, it is crucial that you log more photos than miles.  You are in this costume purely for the likes and kudos. If you exit Zone 1 at any point, you’re doing it wrong.

No pacer or muling needed with this costume. Thanks to your vampire diet and a steady dose of nipple chafing, you’ve got all the nutrition you need to conquer any ultra distance!

#8132. Why Québec is the Ultimate East Coast Ski Destination

Owl's Head Ski Resort at sunset. (Photo: Cantons-de-l'Est © Cantons-de-l'Est/BBT Productions)

Nope, it’s not too much to ask: You can get great snow, both natural and man-made, wild terrain, incredible food, historic architecture, and rich cultural immersion all with just a short drive and no time zone change. That’s right. In Québec, winter is so good it feels like it should be hard to get to, but it’s just across the border.

Let’s start with the snow. Canada’s French-speaking province boasts some of the nation’s highest annual snowfall, with up to 250 inches per year. And you’ll find it in every form: deep powder, groomed tracks, and perfect corduroy, spread across terrain that varies from steep and wild to mellow and peaceful. And all that snow comes with dozens of vibrant mountain towns and more than 70 ski resorts—all within a stone’s throw of the Lower 48. (Montréal is just a 90-minute flight or six-hour drive from Boston, and New Yorkers can reach Québec City in less than two hours by air.)

Next, enjoy the rewards of going wherever the path of adventure takes you. The size of the province means you have lots of choices, but rest assured you can’t go wrong: in Québec, skiable terrain unfolds in nearly every direction. The only question is what kind of ski experience you’re looking for. Here’s what you’ll find in the four ski regions featured here—plus which resorts to hit to make the most of it

Looking for spectacular scenery? Unbelievably long runs? Buttery maritime snowpack coming in off the St. Lawrence River? Northeast of Québec City, you’ll find all three in Charlevoix, where the steep slopes of Le Massif de Charlevoix hover over the water, serving up mountain-meets-river views that are totally unique, and plunging valleys and sweeping bowls attract skiers looking to test their skills amid the serene quiet of a Québécois winter. Le Massif serves up the biggest vertical drop east of the Canadian Rockies, while Mont Grand-Fonds offers a compact layout, laid-back atmosphere, and terrain for all ability levels.

Use Québec City as your base camp and you won’t have to choose between good skiing and vibrant arts and culture. The province’s capital is an enchanting maze of European architecture and historic neighborhoods. An evening walk downtown feels like a wander through a snow-draped fairytale. The food and bar scene reflects a similar blend between time-honored traditions and modern flair. And at just 30 minutes from Mont-Sainte-Anne, it’s close enough to the slopes that you can fully immerse yourself in the true Québecois lifestyle without cutting into your ski time.

Close to Montréal, the Laurentian Mountains are speckled with charming, Alps-style villages—complete with classy accommodations, spas, bistros, and microbreweries—that support a robust après-ski tradition. Mont Tremblant offers a stunning variety of terrain, including both gentle runs and enough steep-and-deep to challenge the experts. Meanwhile, Mont-Blanc and Sommet Saint-Sauveur boast quieter settings, family-friendly atmospheres, and five-star night skiing.

The lush, forested mountains southeast of Montréal are densely packed with ski areas, making this the perfect region for some serious resort-hopping. Even better: with the L’EST GO Pass, you can nab discounted lift tickets on four of the zone’s best hills. If you like night skiing, head to Bromont, a local favorite that opens more than 90 runs after sunset. Prefer the solitude of the deep woods? Head to nearby Mont Sutton for world-class tree skiing and a far wilder feel. Laid-back resorts like Owl’s Head cater to families, while Mont-Orford’s high elevation makes it a motherlode of high-quality snow.

Each of the four ski regions featured here has its own distinct personality. What connects them is Québec’s unmistakable joie de vivre: a love of local flavours, lively après-ski, and taking fun seriously. It’s what makes a ski getaway here so full of character.

Québec isn’t far from America’s East Coast, but it feels like another universe. The province boasts a unique culture defined by its French language, historic neighborhoods, local cuisine, and a dynamic craft beer scene. In its urban areas, you’ll find 17th-century colonial architecture, complete with narrow streets, turrets, and flagstone courtyards.

Leave the urban centers, and historic brick quickly gives way to winter’s snow-flocked evergreens and white-blanket pastures. Barns and silos dot the countryside, and just beyond, mountains rear into the skyline like 5,000-foot beacons calling skiers home.

Québec’s unique combination of proximity and novelty make it one of the most unique ski destinations in North America. And yet it’s not nearly as pricey as some of the other life-list destinations you might have on your list. With the American to Canadian Dollar exchange rate, accommodations and food in Québec tend to offer a strong value on a complete ski trip, especially for U.S. travelers. To make the most of that value, explore ski packages and resort offers across Québec on maneige.ski to find the right getaway for your next winter adventure.

Between its vast and varied terrain, deep snow, rich culture, easy access, and affordable prices, Québec has everything skiers need to squeeze more adventure out of winter. Whether you’re looking for more terrain, more culture, or more discovery, you’ll find it here.

Ready to take your ski adventure further? From breathtaking mountain views and exhilarating runs to vibrant après-ski and charming resort villages, Québec offers much more than great skiing. Explore the regions and plan your winter getaway with Bonjour Québec.
