#8120. 4 Backcountry Field Repairs That Can Save Your Trip (When Duct Tape Isn’t Enough)

No matter how well you’ve prepared or how careful you are with your gear, at some point, whether by cactus spine or sheer volume of trail miles, you’re going to tear a piece of clothing. Or, if you’re me, you’re going to flop down on your sleeping pad, which is on top of your toiletry bag, which holds a pair of impossibly vertical tweezers, and punch an irreparable hole in your mat on the first night of a 225-mile backpacking trip.

You can’t fix every gear problem in the field—a melted down jacket is going to need professional attention or replacement—but with a few simple supplies and some know-how you can handle more of them than you think. Here are four field repairs beyond taping your down jacket you should know, along with a minimal repair kit to get you to the next road crossing.

The glue line that attaches the bottom package—the midsole and outsole—to the shoe upper is the most common structural failure in footwear. While you can manage a few days with a blown-out upper or worn-down outsole tread, the bottom of your shoe flapping in the breeze is a problem.

If you’re close enough to town or have a sense of humor, you can wear your Crocs as hiking shoes. For the rest of us, use a combination of lacing, zip ties, and duct tape to keep your kicks together long enough to get back to civilization. The most secure way to reattach the bottom of the shoe to the top is with an X pattern, similar to how you’d wrap a sprained ankle. If you have a spare set of laces or shock cord, begin at the front of the shoe and criss-cross over the bottom and top in a series of figure-eights until you reach the top of the laces. From here, you can cover the lacing with duct tape in the same pattern. If you brought zip ties, you can punch through the outsole/midsole (be sure to punch far enough in that it doesn’t wear through the side) and the edge of the upper where it won’t rub or cause blisters. Secure it tightly, then finish with the duct tape in a figure-8 pattern.

I typically don’t carry single-use items in my pack aside from the core components of my kit, but a tent pole splint is an exception. Tent poles carry high amounts of tension from taut pitches and are under even more strain in high winds, and the tape-a-stake-to-the-pole simply does not work. A tent pole splint (or sleeve) is a tube made from the same material as the pole, and simply slides over the bent or broken section to create an unbroken line.

Before you do anything else, straighten the bent pole as much as possible or line up the two broken sections as close as they can get. Once the sleeve is centered over the break, secure it with plenty of duct tape. The pole splints are typically not much wider than the pole itself, so it should hold in place fairly well until you can get a replacement pole section.

I’ve slapped plenty of patches onto my down jacket and sleeping pads, but tearing your fly is trickier because you’re relying on the material for waterproofing. I ripped a 10-inch hole in my Big Agnes Copper Spur tent a few years ago, and my attempt at a duct-tape repair held up for about six minutes before condensation separated it again. This is where the Tenacious Tape comes in handy, with its flexible nylon, vinyl, or ripstop material and aggressive adhesive backing. It sticks better than duct tape and can fend off a decent amount of moisture for a surprisingly long time.

Be sure to clean the area around the tear as thoroughly as possible (alcohol wipes come in handy here) and dry it thoroughly before applying the tape. GearAid also makes an incredibly waterproof Aquaseal adhesive compound that can act as a seam sealer or smooth on over raincoat tears.

I must be cursed with backpacking stoves, because I feel like my ignitor stops working after my first few trips. I try to remember a lighter for this very reason, but if you didn’t and the finicky ignitor stopped sparking, you can try repositioning the electrode tip. This works if you can hear the igniter clicking but not lighting the gas—the delicate metal electrode wire likely bent away from the port.

Use your multitool pliers here and position the tip five millimeters (just under 1/4 inch) from the center ring, which should be enough for the spark to jump. The wire on the popular MSR PocketRocket tends to slip out of its guide tube, and if you know what to look for, you can slide it back into the alignment sleeve to restore contact. This video demonstrates replacing the ignitor on a similar stove. (Alternatively, just remember your lighter.)

Some items, like load-bearing pack straps or buckles, will need to be tied together until you get to town, but there are a few things that are handy to take into the backcountry.

The short answer is tape, tape, tape, tape. I wrap a healthy dose of duct tape (bonus points for weird patterns) around my trekking poles or a prescription bottle to cobble together many repairs. I also bring a few inches of Tenacious Tape, designed to patch waterproof fabrics like rain jackets and tent flies, and a NoSo Patch, which works wonders for keeping the feathers inside a torn jacket or sleeping bag.

For thru-hikes or longer trips where I’m going to be way in the backcountry, I bring a tiny sewing kit, a lightweight knife with grippy pliers and a screwdriver end, a few zip ties for holding a backpack together, a tent pole splint, and several safety pins. Finally, your inflatable sleeping pad likely came with its own tiny repair kit, including an alcohol wipe and a matching repair patch with adhesive optimized for the pad material. This whole kit weighs three ounces and can help prevent some serious headaches.

#8119. How I Got Benighted (Twice) on Yosemite’s ‘Lost Arrow Chimney’

In the first installment in our Benighted series, Shino Jomoto shares with Climbing the weird and spooky tale from her night in the chimney on September 17, 2023—and what all climbers can learn from her epic.

With over two decades of climbing experience, Jomoto specializes in epics, which she defines as getting sandbagged on adventure multi-pitch climbs and big walls that take far longer than anticipated. But her biggest epic of all occurred in the storied chimney route (5.10a) up Lost Arrow Spire in Yosemite.

Earlier this week, a Yosemite Climbing Association (YCA) newsletter detailed the history of the Lost Arrow Spire, including the chimney route. First ascensionist John Salathé himself bailed near the top in 1946. The next year, he came back “for an all-out effort” that took over five days. “Pushing through the claustrophobic shadows of the Lost Arrow Chimney, Salathé and [Anton] Nelson endured searing heat, dehydration, and brutal physical exertion,” the YCA shared. “They spent four bivouacs dangling from crude hammocks tied to pitons driven into the wall.”

The Lost Arrow Chimney is also believed to contain a human skeleton. On March 19, 1961, 17-year-old Irving Smith died in a rappelling accident from the top. An American Alpine Club trip report shared that Smiths’ body remains in the chimney: “While a ranger and volunteer rescue party was preparing to attempt the difficult and dangerous removal, Smith’s parents and Park authorities determined that no further life should be risked, and that the body should remain at rest where it lay.”

A comment on the Mountain Project page of Yosemite’s Lost Arrow Chimney (5.10a) foreshadowed what was to come: “Don’t let the moderate grade fool you. After pitch 7, you are halfway done.” The Lost Arrow Chimney is 10 pitches.

Poor fitness, dehydration, and sleep deprivation conspired, and by pitch eight we needed headlamps. Too tired to continue, we did the only sensible thing: slept inside the chimney.

I started climbing in 2005, mostly out of a hatred for my corporate job. That led to years living out of a station wagon, trying to figure out how to rock climb. Fast forward decades later, I’m in the business of going on epics—a lot.

Jim Herson said you could write an entire print edition on just my epics alone. I’ve had near-death epics like lightning and hypothermia on a big wall. But I’ll put it this way: I can climb El Cap faster than I can climb the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The reason why I wanted to share this is that nine out of ten climbers will have an epic on the Lost Arrow. You might be able to climb 5.13, but try to climb 10 pitches of old-school chimney—see if you can still call yourself a 5.10 climber. I think everyone goes in with the confidence of the grade. Then they just get gut-punched by the old-schoolness of the climb.

On my Lost Arrow Chimney epic, we weren’t in danger. We never called YOSAR (Yosemite Search and Rescue). You’re just humbled in a silly way because it’s such a silly grade.

Aside from the likes of Chuck Pratt or old-school climbers, I don’t know anyone who’s ever redone this route. When you do a climb, you usually redo it. You want a redpoint or you go back again. Nobody is dumb enough to redo this climb. We’ve done it three times, so it really goes to show either how incredibly stupid we are, or how memorable of an epic it was that we just needed to clear the record.

The lore that Jim Herson shared with me was he knew a guy who climbed the Lost Arrow Chimney and then never rock climbed again. The reality is he went to med school and gave up climbing. But that was his last-ever climb. It just embodies the spirit of the Lost Arrow Chimney.

The first time John and I did Lost Arrow Chimney in 26 hours on October 5, 2019 as a party of three, and we were actually in decent shape.

The time we slept in the chimney a few years later, we were a party of two. We thought we were fit. But we did all the classic gumby moves. We got up too late and got lost on the approach. To get back on route, we had to rappel. It’s obvious on a topo where you should go, but at four o’clock in the morning, you get lost. And we didn’t bring enough water.

On the climb, we started losing daylight. My boyfriend started dry heaving from dehydration and lack of fitness. He stopped mid-pitch in a chimney—he couldn’t go on.

There’s nothing you can really say in the dark. We’re not Rocky Talkie people. We have too much pride for that. So we just had to communicate with a rope. Finally, I was on belay. I went up to him. We were mid-chimney—this wasn’t even a belay station.

John was like, “I can’t. I can’t do this anymore.” And he’s a 10-times better climber than I am. So I was like, “All right, I’ll go.” He was like, “Are you sure?” I was like, “We can’t sleep here. We can sleep in a lot of places. This is not a place to sleep.”

It’s always scary when a very experienced person says, “I’m scared.” John rarely says he’s scared. It takes courage to say that. When you’re in the dark, there’s nothing you do. You can’t start yelling and placating, you know? You just realize in that moment like, it’s a serious climb. And you’re still having to reconcile that with 10a.

So I went questing and found this chimney that was adjacent to the climb. It wasn’t a chimney you go through on route, but everyone goes by it.

We were two pitches from the notch. Should we suffer for six hours, then rappel and call it a day? Or suffer through the whole night? You make those calculations. We decided we might as well stay put, rather than burden resources to call for YOSAR or any sort of search and rescue. I think that’s the number one thing: Can you self-rescue?

We had brought a salad that we thought we were going to eat at the base. So we ended up at the bivy with a salad, but no water. It’s kind of hard to eat a salad without water. So all of my swear words were salad- or foliage-related. It doesn’t matter if you have a whole buffet, if you have no water, you don’t want to eat anything. So we were just staring at this salad in the chimney. It’s one of those things with the Maslow’s hierarchy—if you don’t have water, you can’t do anything.

We laid out both climbing ropes so that we were a little bit insulated from the ground. We did the bivy dance. It was flatter than most bivy spots I have slept on. We were really depressed, just waiting for daylight.

Back sleeping was impossible, so we were relegated to side sleeping for the next six hours. There was no way to sleep besides big spoon, little spoon. The walls were very cold. I put a giant sad face in chalk where I was. Another group went and did it later and said, “We knew where you bivvied ’cause there was a giant sad face.”

But we were so thirsty, the epic wasn’t over. We could hear Yosemite Falls. Our brains went: Maybe we can just hike over there. Another lesson is you’re not rational when you’re having an epic. So we lost another half day going to the falls. We were sitting in a pool of water that we couldn’t drink. And we realized we couldn’t cut over. So we had to go back. A day and a half later, we got back to the car.

Finally, on June 2, 2024, we got our redemption. We did it in a day and tagged the summit where people do the Tyrolean. It still took us all day—and we didn’t even free it. We had to pull on gear. It makes you respect the history of the first ascensionists—the lineage of people who have tried it and who have bailed. There’s an insane amount of really, really old bail slings.

You’re in there and it’s a vortex. It’s spooky. I’m not a mystical person, but there are hexes that have been kind of swallowed by the rock. It’s a freaking spooky museum of gear. When you’re in there, you have an appreciation for who climbed this before you and the style in which they climbed it, because it is terrifying.

I feel like I’ve gotten my chimney badge in Yosemite. There should be a club for it: the Lost Arrow Chimney Support Group. If you can summit the whole climb and rappel in a day, I would have mad respect. More people climb the Nose than the Lost Arrow Chimney. Anyone who’s dumb enough and adventurous enough to sign up for that level of masochism will resonate more with me than if you’re C1ing a 30-pitch climb.

If you survive nine or ten pitches of chimneys with your partner, you will be bonded forever, for better or worse. They’ve done all these studies about reality TV shows, like for love matchmaking. You put people in intense situations and they confuse their endorphins as romance, but it’s really just adrenaline. Part of it is trauma bonding. Some couples are more willing to climb the Lost Arrow Chimney than go to couples therapy.

The beauty of epics is there are way more fun memories than sending. Every sending story is so ephemeral. But when you’ve been sucker-punched so hard by something scary, or that requires lack of sleep, or incredible amounts of suffering, you remember those experiences for decades.

If you don’t have some delusional optimism, you will never get off the ground. That delusion will catch up to you at some point. But you have to have a little bit of fuel. As long as it’s not over your head or dangerous for you and others. Can you live well and safely enough to live another day? Go do it.

Delusion meets reality at some point, like when you’re having an epic. Benighted is a subcategory of epics—it’s in the taxonomy. There has to be some darkness involved, generally speaking, but you don’t need to have slept.

The easy way to know is when you end up at the parking lot, you see your best friends, and they’re like, “How was it?” The face doesn’t lie. You actually don’t need to say words. They see your face and they’re like, “That was an epic.”

John and I have an epic grading scale. It’s the reverse GPA.

Every time we finish, we rate them. The Lost Arrow Chimney was like a 5.0.

As told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

Got your own tale of getting benighted? Submit it here.

#8117. I Hike With a Flip Phone. Here’s the Tiny Camera I’m Bringing Along.

Over the past few years, I’ve learned I’m much happier when I don’t have my smartphone on me—I’m not sure the human mind evolved to have 24-hour access to all of the Internet’s information on demand. In an effort to disconnect and be more present, I took a page from the Gen Z playbook and started carrying a flip phone instead. It’s been great—except for the camera.

A while ago, I started testing a potential solution in the Life Camera S168, a thumb-size digital camera built to compete with the Kodak Charmera. How did it actually perform on the trail? Check out this video to see what kind of photos and footage this $30 gadget is capable of turning out and read our full review for more.

A while ago, I swapped out my smartphone for a flip phone. I was getting tired of how distracted I was—doomscrolling, checking my emails—and I wanted to simplify things. This has really done the trick. On the trail it’s pretty much everything I need. It can send messages, make calls, if I need to get a hold of 911 in an emergency, it can do that. It has an MP3 player, so I can listen to podcasts at night, and it even has a rudimentary mapping app, although I’m not sure I’d trust it, I always bring a paper map and compass as backup.

However, it does have one big shortcoming: the camera on this thing really sucks. The pictures are grainy, blurry, and usually blown out. It’s not how I want to remember my trips. I often find myself hiking with my smartphone just so I can get better pictures and video. I’ve been looking for a solution, since that kind of defeats the purpose of ditching the smartphone, and I think I’ve found one.

This is the Life Camera S168. It’s part of a crop of new thumb-sized digital cameras that are designed to appeal to the retro crowd, they’re kind of like old digital cameras or old film cameras, you know, the disposable you used to take to summer camp with you. The most familiar one is the Kodak Charmera, you may have seen that in stores.

However, according to a lot of online reviews, the Life Camera’s photos and video quality is significantly better, and it has, from what I’ve seen, a fairly decent camera, you’re not going to confuse it with an iPhone or anything, but it may be enough for my purposes.

So, is the Life Camera a gimmick or a game changer? Well, that depends on you. If you’re like most hikers and you have your phone in your pocket most of the time, it’s definitely a gimmick. Your phone can do anything the Life Camera can do, and probably in better resolution.

If, however, you’re part of the small subset of hikers like me, who find they’re happier when their phone is off and in their pack, or if they’re just carrying a flip phone, you might give the Life Camera a try. No, the resolution isn’t anything to write home about, but it can capture your life on the trail in adequate detail, and if you don’t mind that retro vibe, it’s kind of fun. I’ll be carrying one on my next hike.

#8116. After Testing 122 Pieces of Gear, We Found the Best Climbing Gear of Fall 2026

Gear testing above 12,000 feet on the golden granite of Chamonix's Aiguille du Midi. It's a hard job, but someone's got to do it. (Photo: Anthony Walsh)

Rock climbing season doesn’t end when snow hits the high country. Some of the best conditions of the year are right around the corner: cool temps, ample shade, and just the right amount of humidity in the air. Unless you’re sharpening your ice tools, don’t give up on the rock (or plastic) season just yet—with the right gear, you’re in for the best season of your life.

Climbing’s gear-testing team has spent all summer sweating it out with the latest and greatest so you don’t have to. We tested 28 harnesses, 27 pairs of climbing shoes, 30 pairs of approach shoes, 9 ropes, and 28 backpacks—a healthy mix of new items and longtime favorites. Some of the gear was good, some was great, and a lot of it missed the mark: bruised hips, sore feet, exploding packs—it’s all part of the gear-testing game.

2026 was the year of the hyper-specific shoe. Although notable all-arounders made it onto our list, the real highlights were the shoes who didn’t try to do too much. One shoe felt about as stiff as a crampon, with its new-age carbon insert, and powered us up numerous vert testpieces; another had about as much support as a woolen sock (but, like, in a good way!); and the best shoe I’ve ever used for offwidths is absolutely terrible for finger cracks. Perhaps 2026 is the year of the shoe quiver.

The harness is the one piece of gear that will make or break your day on the wall. In an effort to find the best climbing harness available, we put everything from fast-and-light alpine G-strings to beefy big-wallers to the test this year, taking them on trips from the cold Canadian alpine to the steep walls of Devil’s Tower to overhung sport routes at The Red.

Unlike this year’s crop of rock shoes, my favorite climbing packs worked hard to serve multiple niches. One versatile alpine-climbing pack carried anywhere from one to four days of mountain kit with ease. And a new haul bag might just be the last pack (and airplane carry on) a rock climber will ever need.

The best climbing ropes are a tough category of gear to review because, these days, almost all are well made and perform great right out of the package. It’s only after hard wear—climbing pitch after pitch in rain, snow, and ice, coiling and uncoiling on dirt and sand, and taking some big whippers—that a rope reveals its true colors.

Helmets are our best defense against rockfall and weird whippers while climbing outdoors. And after years of writing accident reports—often of climbers who took a seemingly benign fall, before something weird happened—I regularly note how fortunate the climber was to be wearing one. When shopping for a helmet, take the time to find one that’s comfortable, lightweight, breathable, and fits properly—because actually liking your helmet makes you far more likely to wear it.

#8115. The Supreme Court Will Decide Whether Border Construction Can Cut through Big Bend

An excavator and bulldozer sit near Santa Elena Canyon in Big Bend National Park, Texas, on August 13, 2026. The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to allow border construction to resume after a federal judge halted the work. (Photo: FangXiaNuo/Gett Images)

The fight over border construction in Big Bend National Park has reached the U.S. Supreme Court after the Trump administration asked justices to override a federal judge who had ordered work to halt.

On October 29, plaintiffs in an ongoing lawsuit over the border construction, including the Center for Biological Diversity, Friends of the Ruidosa Church, and a local Rio Grande river guide, urged the justices to keep construction on hold. They warned in a 50-page filing that roads and barriers could permanently scar the fragile Chihuahuan Desert ecosystem surrounding Big Bend National Park, threaten river access and local livelihoods, and damage historic sites. The document cited earlier testimony from local residents, environmental researchers, and other officials who oppose the construction.

“If this actually occurred, I think it would destroy the tourism that Terlingua, Presidio, Marfa… all those towns depend on,” Billy Miller, a local rafting guide who takes tourists on sections of the Rio Grande river, said in the document. “I don’t think they’ll have an experience anymore. I think it will be a tour of the military-industrial complex, not a tour of the wilderness.”

The Supreme Court’s decision could determine whether construction resumes across a vast stretch of West Texas that includes Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and protected stretches of the Rio Grande.

The construction plans vary across the region. Inside Big Bend National Park, Customs and Border Protection has proposed access roads, surveillance technology, and roughly 17 miles of smaller vehicle barriers designed to stop cars and trucks from crossing. Elsewhere in the Big Bend Border Patrol sector, the government plans to build 30-foot walls.

The question at the heart of the lawsuit is whether the government can bypass environmental reviews to build in Big Bend.

U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone halted construction on October 2. She noted that Border Patrol had recorded more than 89,000 apprehensions across the 517-mile sector over five years, yet Big Bend had the lowest apprehension rate per mile of any sector along the southern border.

Towering 1,500-foot cliffs, the Chisos Mountains, and waterless desert expanses make travel through Big Bend exceptionally punishing, leading Customs and Border Protection to acknowledge in May that the topography of the area naturally deters foot traffic across the border.

On October 21, the Trump administration pushed back, arguing in a filing sent to the Supreme Court that delaying construction imperils national security.

“The Sinaloa and Juarez cartels operate south of this sector across the Mexico border and seek to exploit any vulnerabilities in United States border protection to traffic humans, drugs, and weapons,” Justice Department attorneys wrote in the filing, saying that leaving a “300-plus-mile gap in border defenses” could attract criminal organizations.

In an October 30 reply, the administration maintained that the judge lacked authority to halt construction and reiterated that the injunction threatened border security.

Opponents argue that allowing work to resume before the lawsuit is resolved could cause irreversible environmental damage.

Jeffrey Renfrow, an ecologist and director of Rio Bravo Restoration who has worked in the Big Bend region for more than two decades, testified that the damage already done could outlive generations.

“My opinion is that there’s been significant harm to hydrologic function, vegetation and soils and that that harm will probably persist for decades if not centuries, and, in some cases, never recover,” Renfrow told the court.

Bulldozers and other heavy machinery can crush biological soil crusts, delicate living mats that bind the desert floor together and prevent erosion. According to a U.S. Forest Service report, some organisms in these crusts can take around 100 years to regrow.

Local rancher Bill Guerra-Addington testified that construction traffic had already increased wildlife deaths along access roads. He also described the emotional toll of watching the landscape around his home change.

“I’ve cried a river of tears seeing what they’ve done to my home,” he told the court. “I just see this kind of like a dystopian nightmare in my very home, a place that I hold sacred.”

The administration had previously used special legal exemptions to begin construction without completing certain environmental reviews and meeting other legal requirements. Cardone’s order blocked further work under those exemptions.

If the Supreme Court lifts her order, construction could resume while the lawsuit continues. If the justices leave it in place, the government must comply with applicable laws before restarting the disputed work.

#8114. 9 FREE Online Workouts for Pregnant Women

Being pregnant means your body goes on a whirlwind adventure of hormones, cravings, and more. From morning sickness to exhaustion, it can make working out and staying healthy a bit of a challenge. But keeping your body moving is one of the best ways to head off pain and also prepare for labor and childbirth. So get the green light from your doctor about exercising during pregnancy and check out these 9 free online workouts.

What it is: This 24-minute workout starts with a warm-up yoga flow before getting into the more challenging resistance exercises. Expecting mamas can expect to work everything from their back and shoulders to glutes and thighs, even engaging pelvic floor muscles and core stability when crunches just aren’t an option.

Why you’ll love it: Depending on where you are in your pregnancy and how fit you’re feeling, there are modifications you can choose from, which is ideal for changing bodies. You can also use an exercise band, free weights or no equipment at all. And what mama-to-be doesn’t love plenty of restorative stretching?

What it is: A very full 20 minutes of all your favorite yoga poses, including chaturanga push-ups and triangle pose. The approach is straightforward and fuss-free, with reminders for breathing and visuals of modified poses.

Why you’ll love it: A consistent yoga practice can not only keep you strong and limber, but may aid in postpartum recovery too.

What it is: Celebrity trainer Andrea Orbeck helped Heidi Klum stay healthy and fit during pregnancy. Here, she leads a 10-minute workout with plenty of reps and a focus on keeping posture in check.

Why you’ll love it: You’ll get your heart rate up for sure, but this workout is so quick that you may not even break a sweat. Squeeze it all in before or after work, or anytime you have a handful of minutes and want to check exercise off your to-do list!

What it is: A series of basic, simple movements kicked up a notch, thanks to the help of a kettlebell. Each exercise is about 45 seconds of movement and then 15 seconds of active rest.

Why you’ll love it: It works well for all three trimesters, especially the third because all the core work is from a standing position, not lying down on your back.

What it is: Twenty minutes of free-weight work with the added challenge of the stability ball, which forces you to engage your core. You’ll do a little bit of everything from bicep curls (good practice for holding a growing baby) to squats (perfect for picking up a dropped pacifier).

Why you’ll love it: If you exercise frequently, then these exercises might be a nice break from your ordinary routine. Save that stability ball for easing the pains of labor, and for lightly bouncing a fussy baby who needs some rhythmic movement or help getting to sleep.

Related: 8 FREE YouTube Workouts You Can Do With Your Baby

What it is: A high-intensity interval training workout (HIIT) combining five warm up exercises; ten are relatively intense, and five focus on core and cool-down. Each move is 40 seconds with 20 seconds of active rest, like marching in place.

Why you’ll love it: The workout is intense but low impact with none of the big, dramatic jumps typical of most HIIT routines. Plus, Nancy’s energy and positive attitude are infectious.

What it is: An at-home barre experience full of super-low-impact moves and enough pulsing to feel tons of burn.

Why you’ll love it: All you need is a chair, which you can even skip to make it more challenging during the first and second trimesters. But it’s a good idea to pull one out for the third.

What it is: Focus on your lower body with tons of lunges, squats, and kick-backs. The goal is to burn your way through 20 nearly non-stop minutes of exercise, with or without the “booty band” for added resistance.

Why you’ll love it: The beach setting and upbeat music will have you feeling motivated and as if you’re anywhere else but your home gym.

What it is: Ten calming minutes of moderate stretching to gently open your neck, chest, hips, and back.

Why you’ll love it: This routine is full of fluid but controlled movements that will make you feel great in the moment and alleviate any persistent discomfort.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8113. Nearly Half of US Hikers Use Cannabis, And Other Strange Findings From the ‘Hiking While High’ Survey

Most hikers have experienced a natural high at some point in their outdoor adventures. Whether it’s the buzz of an athletic flow state or being straight-up stupefied by an amazing view, we’ve all been there. Endorphins fire, oxytocin floods the brain, and you’re overwhelmed with energy, good vibes, and a general sense of peace.

It’s also not news to anyone that some hikers use drugs in nature. People smoke weed on the trail, eat edibles, drink beer, and even take psychedelics. Every year it seems like we publish at least one story with a headline like, “Hikers Rescued After Mushroom Trip Goes Bad” or “Two Hikers Reported Their Friend Dead. It Turned Out They Were Just on Mushrooms.”

But how many hikers are actually hitting the trail under the influence? Those questions and several others led the team at Climbing Kilimanjaro, a Tanzanian guide company, to conduct its “Hiking While High” survey. It polled U.S. adults who hike to find out once and for all how many of them use cannabis, mushrooms, alcohol, and other substances, and importantly, in what circumstances.

The results surprised the folks at Climbing Kilimanjaro. Not just because of how many hikers admitted to using substances on the trail, but because those who do are “surprisingly disciplined about where and when,” Brian Raffio, Kilimanjaro consultant for Climbing Kilimanjaro, says.

“On one hand, we expected to get some respondents who were very into using substances while hiking, and others who were as sober as sober gets,” Raffio says. “What we ended up with was much more of a grey area.”

For the survey, Climbing Kilimanjaro polled 1,008 U.S. adults between September 1 and 3, 2026. The sample was 52 percent women and 46 percent men, all of whom counted hiking as a core interest or hobby. They also grouped respondents by experience level. Hikers self-reported as casual hikers (people who hike a few times a year), regular hikers (people who hike roughly monthly), or avid hikers (people who hike weekly or more).

Of the 1,008 U.S. hikers surveyed, 44 percent said they have hiked under the influence.

Cannabis is far and away the most popular trail substance. A notable 35 percent of respondents admitted to having used it while hiking. Of hikers who take anything, 80 percent said they are reaching for weed. Behind cannabis, alcohol was the second most popular, with 23 percent percent admitting to having drunk beer or liquor while hiking. In third were magic mushrooms, with 15 percent admitting use (and another 24 percent saying they are curious to try psychedelics in nature but never have).

However, a majority—56 percent of hikers—said they have never used any substances on the trail. And while 7 percent of hikers who enhance their hikes say they have felt judged for doing so, surprisingly more of the sober hikers (9 percent) said they have also felt judged, but for their choice to abstain.

“Hikers feeling judged for staying clear-headed rather than for using something was a bit of a head-scratcher for sure,” Raffio says. “Apparently ‘no thanks, I’m good’ raises a few eyebrows.”

What surprised the Climbing Kilimanjaro team even more wasn’t these reported use rates. Instead, it was the level of caution users claim to have when they’re hiking high. More than half (51 percent) said they seek out shorter, easier hikes, and would never try to hike under the influence at high altitude. And nine out of 10 who hiked under the influence said: “There’s at least one place they would never use a substance.”

“In the end, hikers seem to be a fairly self-policing bunch,” Raffio says. “The summit push is where folks want to stay sharp and have their senses fully alert. Whatever [substance] a hiker packs, the trail rewards you when you know the terrain, and you understand your limits.”

The final result that stuck out to Raffio was how many people use hiking to recover. Roughly half of the hikers surveyed said they hit the trail sometimes “to reset after drinking or a night out.”

According to the Outdoor Industry Association (OIA), there are roughly 63 million hikers in the U.S. That makes this sample size anything but definitive. The most obvious takeaway is that people like to enhance their hikes with substances—whether it’s cannabis, magic mushrooms, or something else.

Climbing Kilimanjaro’s results also suggest that hikers are fairly split when it comes to substance use on the trail. While the majority of the respondents had never used anything while hiking, a 56/44 split isn’t that wide of a margin.

For those who do partake, it’s clear (and unsurprising) that cannabis is hikers’ substance of choice—by a long shot.

The Hiking While High survey didn’t poll hikers on their feelings around the topic, and that was intentional. The guide company didn’t want to present opinionated data. It just wanted to open up an honest conversation around the rates of drug use on the trail.

“We asked ourselves: What if this was discussed more openly?” Raffio said. “We wanted to come from a place of curiosity, not judgement.”

#8112. A Conversation Between Alex Honnold and Jim Morrison on ‘Everest: The Other Side’

At first glance, it might not seem like Alex Honnold’s free solo of El Capitan has much in common with Jim Morrison’s first ski descent of Everest’s north face, which is documented in Jimmy Chin’s new film Everest: The Other Side, which releases today, October 30.

But in a conversation during a live recording of Climbing Gold in May, it became clear that several parallels exist between these historic firsts:

Despite their shared sky-high risk tolerance, both Honnold and Morrison also agree with the general public on one thing: They consider each other “crazy.” Morrison called Honnold’s ropeless ascent of El Cap “totally insane.” Meanwhile, Honnold struggled to identify the line one might ski down Everest’s north side in a photo. Once Morrison pointed it out, Honnold declared: “That seems like death.”

The Hornbein Couloir on the northern Tibet side of Everest has taken the lives of several climbers, including the snowboarder Marco Siffredi who attempted to make the first descent of the couloir in 2002; his body has never been found.

Two Americans, Thomas Hornbein and Willi Unsoeld, made the first ascent of Everest’s north side in 1963. The north side’s first ascent came just 22 days after Jim Whittaker became the first American to climb Everest via the south side. The 9,000-foot couloir they took to the top was colloquially known as “Hornbein’s Avalanche Chute.” Jimmy Chin also attempted an ascent of Hornbein’s in 2003, but was caught in a near-deadly avalanche.

At the age of 50, after two failed attempts and the staggering loss of Hilaree Nelson, his partner in life and mountains, on Manaslu, Morrison skied down Hornbein’s Couloir on October 15. He pulled it off just four months after undergoing a partial knee replacement. Before Morrison’s ascent last fall—which included a 12-person team of Sherpas, Ecuadorian fixers, and filmmakers—no human had successfully ascended the line since 1991.

Honnold’s conversation with Morrison about his historic ski descent was part of the first-ever live recording of Fitz Cahall’s and Honnold’s Climbing Gold podcast. The interview took the stage at Outside Days on May 31 in Denver, CO. The podcast episode dropped today, alongside the release of the film. You can watch an excerpt above, and read on for Honnold’s and Morrison’s thoughts on grief, the question they dread most, and risking their lives for sport.

Morrison conceived of the goal to ski down Everest’s Hornbein Couloir with Hilaree Nelson. The two ski mountaineers met on Makalu (8,463m) in 2015 and fell in love.

“We were on a tear,” Morrison told Honnold and Cahall, “ticking off these dream runs all over the planet.”

The two had been trying to get to Everest to attempt their ski descent. But COVID delayed their plans, making it impossible to get to the Chinese side of the mountain. To stay in 8,000-meter-peak shape, in 2022, they headed to Manaslu (8,163m) where Morrison recalls they “had a pretty incredible day all by ourselves up on the mountain.” He started skiing down first; Nelson followed, but when Morrison stopped to wait for her, she never appeared. She had set off a small avalanche. “What ensued was a multi-day, horrific rescue of her and trying to find her,” he said. “And it changed my life.”

At first, Morrison wanted to hang it up—never ski or head into the mountains again. But eventually, he began to realize “this is part of me, this is in me.” And he returned to the goal they’d started together. “I wanted to do it for her, and her legacy, and us.”

On the summit, Morrison spread some of Nelson’s ashes. “It was a really emotional moment for me, looking off at mountains I had skied with her, Lhotse and Makalu,” he reflected. “I really felt like she was there.”

In 2011, before losing Nelson on Manaslu, Morrison’s wife, daughter, and son passed away in a plane crash. While he has experienced unfathomable loss, he continues to try to push past the grief to keep living. On stage, he shared a metaphor he uses to grapple with loss:

I’ve described grief as a big heavy wet blanket that gets put on you. It’s just really hard. You go through a process of losing a loved one or spouse or child and it’s a really heavy weight. I like to think over time you take that blanket and you dry it out and you begin to fold it up. And eventually, you put it in a backpack and you carry it with you.

After free soloing El Cap, Honnold said his life became “a crazy whirlwind.” A week and a half later, he was on an expedition in Alaska. Then the film came out, thus marking his “six month deployment to Hollywood” of screenings and award ceremonies.

The effect was that his memories of free soloing El Cap blurred with the scenes from the film as he watched himself on the big screen, again and again. What he’d set out to do for himself became a messy, public experience. As Chin releases his film, Morrison may undergo a similar experience of distorted memories and mayhem.

Honnold also recalled the dreaded question punted at him on his Hollywood deployment: What’s next?

Morrison received the same question after his Everest descent and gave an answer Honnold wished he’d come up with years ago: Isn’t this enough?

“I just achieved this 10-year life dream,” Honnold joked of receiving the “what’s next” question. “I don’t have another life dream lined up on the back burner.”

Morrison called achieving his Everest ski descent goal an “incredible journey” and noted that he appreciated the team that supported him throughout the process.

Cahall teed up his last question by warning that “some of this is triggering to some people.” Meaning, this talk of visualizing fatal falls, of risking it all for the goal. But, Cahall wondered: Are we mistaking complacency for safety?

Morrison said that he doesn’t really see it as complacency versus risk. It’s not an either/or situation. “This is what I’m drawn to and this is what my life’s goals have been centered around,” he said. “I’m not going out there to make a mistake and not come home.” He added that while his ski descent might seem like a “horrendously risky thing,” it was the culmination of extensive planning and preparation, just like Honnold’s El Cap free solo.

“It’s really hard to look at you climbing El Cap without a rope and rationalize it and understand it and be able to relate to it because it is so totally insane,” Morrison said. But at the same time, he said he held “deep respect” for all of the preparation and focus Honnold put into ticking the goal.

“Without taking some amount of personal risk, you just can’t lead a rich and fulfilled life,” Honnold added. “People watch the film Free Solo or a film like that and they’re like, ‘Well, that’s crazy!’ Yeah it’s unusual, not the sort of risk taking you normally see, but it’s still making smart choices in their life in order to lead the most fulfilled life that they can.”

#8111. Why Outdoor Athletes Can Benefit From the Cozy Cardio Trend, According to a Personal Trainer

(Photo: Woman outdoors: Raul Ortin/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva)

The term cardio often elicits grumbles as people picture punishing treadmill sessions and trail runs. But add the word cozy before it, and cardio is suddenly…a lot more palatable. That’s the gist behind the “cozy cardio” trend, which took off on social media in 2024 and resurfaced in 2026. The concept is simple: perform low- to moderate-intensity workouts in a comfortable, inviting environment.

Cozy cardio could look like setting out a few candles in your living room, dimming the lights, and turning on your favorite Netflix show while you stroll on a walking pad. Or it could involve donning a comfy velvet sweatsuit and sipping a delicious beverage while going for an easy walk on your favorite trail or through your neighborhood.

Cozy cardio looks different for everyone, according to Hope Zuckerbrow, the TikToker credited with starting the trend. But no matter how you practice it, the overarching objective is the same: take the pressure off exercise and actually enjoy movement.

As a certified personal trainer, I wholeheartedly support that notion and think there are several key benefits that outdoor athletes could reap from embracing the trend.

When it comes to exercise, many people have an all-or-nothing mindset—especially athletes who take their outdoor sport seriously. They have a set workout plan—for example, a five-mile run or an hour-long strength session—and when something thwarts it, they might throw in the towel and do nothing at all.

But staying consistent with your workout routine is key to reaping the mental and physical benefits of exercise. So a better approach is to still do some form of movement even if it looks different than what you’d originally envisioned. That’s where cozy cardio can come in.

Because the trend is all about lowering the stakes on exercise, it can feel really doable, even on those days when life gets in the way, or you’re not in the mood to do anything.

Plus, cozy cardio creates an environment that makes working out a pleasurable experience. And that’s important, because actually enjoying exercise is associated with actually sticking with a workout routine, according to research.

Another benefit of cozy cardio is that it can serve as active recovery in the wake of long, hard workouts. Research suggests doing even six to ten minutes of active recovery after a workout may boost overall performance.

So engaging in a short cozy cardio session after a big hike, ride, or run could inject a little more energy into your next outdoor adventure.

A 2026 study found that low-intensity exercises improve both aerobic fitness and cardiometabolic health, which refers to factors involving the heart and metabolism, including blood pressure and cholesterol.

If you choose a steady-state form of exercise for your cozy cardio session, such as walking or a bike ride, and keep your effort low, you’ll likely tick the box for Zone 1 or Zone 2 cardio—both of which, when done consistently, can help build your aerobic fitness, or your VO2 max. VO2 max describes how efficiently your body takes in oxygen and transports it to the rest of the body so that your muscles can use it during physical activity. The higher your VO2, the better your aerobic fitness.

Overall, one of the biggest benefits of improving your aerobic health is going longer and having more energy during your favorite outdoor sport.

#8110. This Sound Map Will Transport You to the PCT From Anywhere

Most backpackers memorialize their trips through photographs. But when LA-based hiker Tom Kelly hit the PCT in 2023, he wanted to document a different, more sensory experience of the trail. Kelly, a nature sound field recordist, composer, and musician, toted 40 ounces of audio recording equipment during his 2,650-mile thru-hike, pausing along the trail to capture the acoustics of the journey. Kelly set up his microphones along burbling creeks and amid chirping insects; he recorded the rustling of grass in the wind, rain on a tent fly, or the chatter of passing hikers. Upon completing his thru-hike, Kelly spent two years compiling his recordings into an interactive and freely accessible sound map.

Reporter Amelia Arvesen spoke to Kelly about his project, the challenges of capturing sound in the backcountry, and what he hopes listeners can gain from the map.

Tom Kelly: It was beautifully calm, really nice day. And we all went to bed, and I woke up to the sound of a great horned owl calling across the lake. And so, the last thing I want to do is wake up and do something, you know? It’s hard enough to wake up to go to the bathroom, much less take your recording equipment, go hike, set up, and you know, do the whole recording process.

I’m a nature sound field recordist, I’m a composer, and music performer based in Los Angeles, California. What led me to recording sound on the PCT is kind of the natural history I have of recording sound in spaces that I would travel to in general. Leading up to the PCT, I’ve always had a field recorder with me because it is just very natural for me to bring it along as my way to interface with the space that I’m in. Getting to the Pacific Crest Trail, I knew that this was going to be my method of creativity while I was hiking. When I set out, I didn’t necessarily know what the project was going to be, or if there was even going to be a project to begin with. But I knew that I wanted to engage in the practice of listening and recording sound along the trail.

In the Mojave Desert, on the north side of the LA Aqueduct, I just sat down on the ground, pulled out my recorder, and started listening. And it was in that moment that I became very aware of where I was and what I was doing. And honestly, I could not be happier in that moment. Comparing the scale of these things—like this massive trail, and then here’s like this little moment—and it’s just, for me, taking in kind of just the depth of those small moments all along the trail is something that’s been really rewarding for me, and has been something I’ve worked through this project to try and convey, and offer as a gift to everyone. I hope that when someone sets out to interact with the sound map that I’ve put out there, that they’re able to get just a little piece of what I was able to experience out there. And that is just the ability to slow down and just really experience nature along the Pacific Crest Trail in this kind of embodied sort of way.

#8109. Baby Sign Language 101: Baby’s First Signs

Well before they utter their first words, infants as young as six months can learn to sign. Baby sign language is thought to reduce baby’s frustration levels, boost self-esteem, and bolster language development. And you don’t need to be an expert. Begin with three to five signs, saying the word as you sign it. Encourage other caregivers and siblings to join in. Then repeat, repeat, repeat. Your little one’s motor skills may not allow them to perfectly mimic the sign, so watch for hand gestures that indicate she’s trying, usually within two months of being introduced to it. Here are some great baby sign language starter signs.

Show your little one the sign for a person they know, like mommy, daddy, brother, grandma, or baby. It doesn’t matter if you plan to use mommy, mama, mother, or mom; the sign is the same — using an open palm with fingers spread, tap your thumb on your chin. For “daddy” and its variations, use the same hand position; only tap the forehead. Remember to point to the person as you sign.

Food is a great motivator. Teach your little eater the sign for their favorite food or the ones for eat, milk, or bottle. When Baby’s plate is empty, “more” and “all done” allow them to set the pace for the meal. To sign “more,” press the thumb and fingertips of each hand together, and then tap the fingertips of the two hands together several times. Look for baby to put their fists or palms together as they start to get the hang of this sign.

Animal signs are fun because they often mimic some aspect of the animal. Baby will love learning the signs for her beloved pet or for the animals around the neighborhood. Dog, cat, fish, and bird are all good candidates. You can even have a favorite stuffed animal act out the motions for its sign. The baby sign for “dog” is patting your hand to your hip, as if calling a dog. This is a slight modification from the American Sign Language version, which includes a snap that is too difficult for emerging motor skills.

It’s never too early to introduce your little bundle to being polite. “Please” is a great word to start with. Try this technique when it’s clear your baby desires something specific, like a toy or a drink, and he’s not upset or in any distress. Say that you will get it and ask if they can say “please,” demonstrating the sign as you do so. Then give them the item, regardless of whether they do the sign or not. Eventually the concept will begin to sink in, and they’ll be doing it on his own. With a flat hand and thumb extended, sign “please” by moving the palm of your hand in a circular motion in front of your chest.

Use the repetition of baby’s routine as an opportunity to teach her the signs of daily life. Learn “sleep” for naptime and bedtime. Let baby know it’s playtime by signing “play,” and then show her the sign for whatever you are playing with, be it a ball, blocks, or a book. The sign for “bath” mimics the act of washing. To do this sign, simply move both your fists up and down in front of your chest as if scrubbing it.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8107. The Dean Fidelman Interview: 6 Photos, 6 Decades

A portrait of Dean Fidelman in 1971, the year he arrived in Yosemite. (Photo: Warren Shelton)

Dean Fidelman arrived in the Yosemite Valley in 1971 as a teenager. Yosemite has been his home ever since—except for a blip in the ‘80s, when he set aside his passion for climbing to become a fashion photographer in New York City and Los Angeles. But a phone call saved him from what was, for him, soulless commercial work.

It was Lynn Hill who called, asking Fidelman to start making climbing photos again. She invited him to come shoot her on some climbs in Europe, where he also first met Chris Sharma. From there, he doubled down on his life’s mission to show “the art of rock climbing,” in his words.

Fidelman spent the first half of his career shooting in black and white on film cameras, including a Pentax 6×7. He processed his own film and developed his own photos—sometimes by night in the historic Yosemite darkroom of Ansel Adams. Eventually, he caught up with the times when filmmaker Renan Ozturk gave him a Sony a7R II mirrorless camera and he made the switch to digital—and full color. “In my viewfinder, I set the preview to black and white, but the capture contains full color,” Fidelman told Climbing.

Now, 55 years after arriving in Yosemite, Fidelman still calls the area home and continues to shoot climbers around Camp 4. Perhaps best known for his work capturing the Yosemite Stonemasters and Stone Monkeys, Fidelman has also sat down for interviews in a couple documentaries released this year, including The Dark Wizard about Dean Potter, and a film about the weed plane that crashed in Yosemite, enriching many of his friends.

Fidelman is also known for his Stone Nudes, nude portraits of climbers bouldering or free soloing. He started the series in 1999 and now estimates it runs 300 images deep. At least a few times a year, he still receives requests from climbers to shoot a Stone Nude—a phrase which he has tattooed on his hands.

We caught up with Fidelman to discover the changes and throughlines he’s observed across six decades of Yosemite photography, the challenges of revisiting his relationship with Dean Potter for The Dark Wizard, and the next iteration of the Stone Nudes project. For this retrospective interview, we also asked Fidelman to select one photo for each decade of his work, which you’ll find below.

This interview has been edited for clarity and concision.

Dean Fidelman: As the decades have progressed, the way that I think about making a photograph has changed. But the people haven’t changed as much. With the Stonemasters, I was just making photographs of my friends doing cool things in the desert. I wasn’t really thinking about anything besides trying to make the best photograph I could—and finding out what a good photograph was.

With the Stone Monkeys, from the late ’90s until 2010 or 2015, I was simply living in Yosemite in the meadow, sleeping down by the river. So I fit in financially with this group of people really well. When I asked someone to make a photograph with me, there was no hesitation.

Recently, I’ve done some photographs for Summit Journal of people on YOSAR [Yosemite Search and Rescue] and at Camp 4. The first thing someone would say when I asked if I could make their photograph was, “I’d be honored.”

That kind of put me on the back foot in a weird way. If I ask to make a photograph of you, it’s because I respect you, or there’s something about you that I really enjoy being around or seeing. So it’s more like you’re honoring me, because you’re going to be vulnerable in front of my camera for a moment. Once we get over that, it’s just like working with the people I’ve always worked with.

Fidelman: When Lynn reconnected with me, it was pretty much immediate—”there it is.” You think of your path in a linear way that leads to being the best at something, but that’s not how it works. I was doing my photography much more personally than commercially. When Lynn connected with that, I thought, “Oh yeah, the personal aspect of photography, I can do that.” She definitely sponsored me and opened that world back up.

Fidelman: Charles Cole at Five Ten and John Bachar at Boreal both used me for ads. But Charles especially would say, “Here’s $500, here’s $1,000. Here’s my camera. Just give me some photos, but make what you’ve always made—no pressure.”

When I got back into Yosemite, one of the first people I met was Dean Potter. He was super open to me. I met him through Bachar because they were giving him shoes at the time and wanted to make some photographs. We had an immediate kinship, and that brought me deeper in with the Stone Monkeys. Then you had Cedar Wright, who was just starting off at that moment in time, and everyone else just came out of that.

With the people who survived—and the people who didn’t—I realized I was making this visual record of friends, trying to express them in the moment. That’s what I’ve hopefully continued to do.

Fidelman: Honestly, my opinion hasn’t changed since the ’70s. It wasn’t like I just happened by when Bachar or Yabo [John Yablonski] or somebody was doing a solo. Sometimes Bachar would say, “Hey, I’ve got this thing figured out now and I’m going to do it. I want you to make the photographs.” Three or four of us would jump in his van, go down to wherever the solo was, and make these photographs.

Even back then, climbing magazines did not want to publish [free soloing photos]. I didn’t take it personally. The first publication that published my work was the National Enquirer. It was a picture of Bachar soloing with a headline like “Man Climbs Rock” or “Daredevil Climbs Rock.”

So I experienced both ends of the spectrum early on. I realized that what you’re making isn’t going to be universally accepted. But you’re doing it for the people who are doing these solos and the people who appreciate it. I wasn’t making all this stuff happen; it was happening in front of me and has continued across generations.

Fidelman: When film crews called 10 years after Dean Potter died to make a film, I was really kind of conflicted, but I approached it as professionally as I could. They showed me a rough cut of all four episodes. After I watched, I went into this horrible depression that I just got out of in the last couple months.

Fidelman: It made him very real again. Suddenly, I still think he’s alive. He’s existing. I can feel his presence, trying to come up really close to me and intimidate me—his voice and everything. Obviously, it’s storytelling, but it’s made me really question a lot of what happened and a lot of who I was. I think hopefully I’ve gotten that straightened out.

Fidelman: It means having a high respect for unspoken boundaries—how you carry yourself in that moment, what your objective is, and what you can ask of the person in front of you. With Stone Nudes especially, they are naked and vulnerable. There’s all kinds of trust going on there. You respect unspoken boundaries by observing someone to see how open they are to direction. But I’ve also found women have been mansplained with men trying to tell them how to climb.

And then with your friends, you’re on an intimate level because they know you, but suddenly there’s a camera up. They’ve seen your work and they’re honored. So you need to try to get rid of that awkwardness by bringing your energy back and refocusing.

Fidelman: I’m still working on the Valley Muse book. I made some new Stone Nudes this March that I really like, so I’m looking at calendars or possibly a book, gathering for another five or six years, traveling to favorite spots and places I’ve always wanted to go to.

Fidelman: There are a couple of photographs I want to make in Patagonia. It’s just a boulder in the middle of nowhere—and there was so much nowhere. There’s also a cool volcanic place in Venezuela. But next, I’m heading to Spain to work on deep-water soloing nudes in Mallorca.

Fidelman: Probably 2018, right when I stopped with the Stone Nudes calendar and Renan [Ozturk] gave me that camera. That’s probably the last time I went into a darkroom, unless the darkroom had a scanner in it and I was scanning my negatives. With a lot of my original black and white photography, I would process the film myself. I used to find these traditional photo labs up and down the coast.

After the last lab closed, I used Ansel Adams’s darkroom in Yosemite. They would let me use the darkroom from 10 at night until midnight. What was left of it was just a long sink and a heavy dark curtain. I’d be rattling cans at midnight and I look over and there’s a portrait of Ansel looking at me like, “What are you doing in my darkroom?”

Fidelman: Once I was shooting in the middle of the Merced River by the 120/140 junction. A friend was on top of the boulder posing while I was waist-deep in the river. Suddenly, a big tour bus pulled over and a bus-load of tourists piled out, pushing each other trying to take photos with their phones.

One time I was making photographs in Eldorado Canyon on that boulder right in the middle of the river with my friend Anora, a hippie. I went back to Yosemite and processed the film in Ansel Adams’s darkroom. I’m hanging out at the lodge and this person comes up to me—obviously a climber, but very clean-cut. He goes, “Excuse me, are you Dean Fidelman?” And I go, “Yeah.”

He sticks his hand out, with this big smile on his face and goes, “I want to shake your hand. You were in Eldorado Canyon about a month ago and you were making some photos. We were on the Bastille and oh my God, she is so beautiful. That was the most amazing day. My partner went home and bought a calendar even though he knew she wasn’t going to be in that one. But is she going to be in the next one?”

Then I made a Stone Nude of my friend Brian Ludovici, who’s a wonderful human and a super cool boulderer. He asked if I would make a photograph of him on Midnight Lightning (V8) with his clothes on. So I show up there and he’s just got this pair of short shorts on, right? This is his favorite boulder problem. He loves it. He worships it. And he goes up it and down it. I say, “Hey, man. You think you could do it nude?” Maybe four or five of his friends are there, all egging him on. He gets to where he’s pressing out the mantle, but he couldn’t do it. He put his shorts back on.

Then there’s this guy running full blast toward me from 100 yards away. He looks really closely at Brian. Then he stops and goes, “Dude, this was the most amazing day of my life. I looked from over there by the kiosk and there was a beautiful nude woman doing Midnight Lightning, so I started running to get a closer look. But it’s a dude.”

Fidelman: One fall. My friend Joey was like, “Let’s make a photograph.” I first met her when she was 16. She goes, “I want to make a photograph.” I go, “No, no.” Same with [Chris] Sharma. I go, “No, you have to wait until you’re 18.”

A couple years later, she’s in Joshua Tree and wants to climb the White Rastafarian (V2). First, I tell her she has to do it with her clothes and shoes on, so I can see that she can do it. She does it perfectly. But she can’t do it barefoot. So, she took her clothes off and we had a bunch of pads down, hidden by the bushes. Three of her friends were spotting.

She gets up to the crux and starts to bring her hand up and she blows. Her friends didn’t even touch her. She hit the pads, but sprained her ankle fairly badly. I felt really horrible, but I did put it in [a calendar]. I always make certain that [climbers] can do it at least with their clothes on first. Now I always tell the spotters, “If you’ve got to get in the photo, don’t even worry about it. Put your hands on them, even though they’re naked!” Unless somebody wants to solo something, but it’s not going to be outside the limits—ever.

Fidelman: I’m working on two books. One is a history of the Nose with John Long, Hans Florine, Ed Hartouni, and Sarah Conley. The other is a book on the Stone Monkeys with James Lucas. We’re getting the manuscripts and photo selections organized, with plans to publish over the next couple of years.

Fidelman: I’ve been working on archiving all the stuff from the ‘60s and Glen [Denny] was a huge influence on me, as well as Tom Frost and and a few others.

I understood two things very early on. One is if you’ve tied into a rope with people who have climbed with people like John Salathé and Royal Robbins, you’ve tied into a rope with all those other people, too. I tied into a rope with [Jim] Bridwell and lots of people that probably go back all the way to Salathé.

When John Long and I made the Stonemaster book, it was a fulfillment of my dream to make a book, but also of the understanding that if we allow those stories to die, we have no magic. All our beliefs are based on those stories and those legends.

I’m hoping maybe someone shows up, and I don’t care who they are. If I can see that passion and they’re really looking to provide that rope that we can all tie into, then my work would move forward.
