#8106. These Guys Are Searching the Pacific Northwest for Bigfoot. I Tagged Along.

Tanner Hoskins, the de facto leader of the Pacific Northwest Bigfoot Search and the Pacific Northwest Missing Persons Project (Photo: Emily Halnon)

The forest sounds empty, but I know it’s not. Earlier today, I’d walked along the lakeshore and seen hoof prints, a cougar track, and coyote scat.

The trees have all turned black beneath the night sky. The only light comes from the full moon creeping through clouds. I’m deep in Washington’s Gifford National Forest and it’s so quiet I can hear my own heartbeat.

No creature is giving its location away by making noise—but we certainly aren’t alone as we stand on the edge of a lake, its waters as dark as midnight. I look at the shadows between trees and wonder what’s hiding in the forest.

Beside me, Tanner Hoskins raises a thermal scope to his eye and scans the trees to look for heat signatures. He pauses as he sweeps to the far corner of the lake.

“I think I’ve got something moving,” he says.

For the last six years, Hoskins and a group of friends have been searching the Pacific Northwest’s wilderness for an answer to that very question: What else is out there?

And I’m tagging along for a weekend to see what happens when I go looking for evidence of the unknown.

About two miles away, as the crow flies, a dispersed campsite is tucked into a grove of pine trees.

On a July night in 2020, decades-long buddies Kelly Stolp and Mike Palagi sat around a fire with Stolp’s sons and Palagi’s fiancée. Flames licked the black sky as they laughed into the night. It was a familiar scene for the friends, who met in the Army in 2005.

Stolp retired to his tent while the fire was still crackling. Deep in the night, he heard a loud, guttural howl—it sounded like a car engine trying to turn over. Then, footsteps. Slow and steady, getting closer to his tent. They seemed too loud to be human. More stomp than step. He could feel each footfall hit the earth. But he knew, without a hair of doubt, they were coming from a two-legged creature.

Stolp grew up on a 35,000-acre ranch in Montana. He’s hunted for decades and recreated outside since he could walk. He went on his first backpacking trip at the age of 12. He’s an avid outdoorsman and familiar with all of the wildlife that roams the West. A grizzly bear once came into his camp. But in that moment, he knew he wasn’t hearing a bear, nor a cougar, elk, or coyote.

Stolp listened as the creature approached his tent, brushing up against the huckleberries just feet away. It was only 50 degrees, but he was covered in sweat. Then, he heard the footsteps disappearing up the dry creekbed that winds past the campsite.

The next morning, he told Palagi, “Something came through camp last night.” It was large and two-legged, he went on. Palagi laughed, said he didn’t hear anything, and pointed at the empty bottle of whiskey as an explanation. Stolp dropped the topic for the rest of the day.

But at 3 A.M. that night, Stolp heard the footsteps again. Thump. Thump. Thump. The same guttural howl was now coming from two different spots.

He heard a gun racking, then: “Kelly, I’m up.”

They rolled out of their tents. Stolp shouted, “We’re armed, show yourself.”

Palagi and Stolp both trained as military snipers and knew how to clear a space. They moved through camp, weapons ready. They found nothing, but the two men, who don’t scare easily, passed the rest of the night in their cars.

“I’ve spent my entire life outdoors and encountered everything the wilderness has to offer,” said Stolp. “But I’d never slept in my truck, not even when a grizzly came through my camp.”

They tried to recreate the stomping sound in the morning. They were not small men. Palagi played football in Montana as a defensive lineman, and Stolp looks like he could have been on a team, too. But even when Palagi jumped with his full body weight, he couldn’t come close to what they’d heard.

Stolp headed to the Shriners Children’s Hospital in Portland the next Monday, where he worked as an electrician alongside Palagi, a maintenance engineer. He pulled his coworker, a security guard named Hoskins, aside.

“But you have to promise you won’t tell anyone,” he told Hoskins. He knew how ridiculous the story sounded. He didn’t want anyone to think he believed in Bigfoot.

But Hoskins was more of a believer. While he was growing up, his great-grandmother had warned him about “hidebehinds,” a large, mysterious creature that was blamed for the disappearance of loggers in Idaho. Stolp’s story, when added to ones told by his great-grandmother, made him wonder if the Pacific Northwest was home to similar creatures. Hoskins swore he wouldn’t say a thing. Then he went home and built a website for the Pacific Northwest Bigfoot Search, telling anyone who found it about his friend’s story—and inviting others to share their own.

Tales of large, mysterious, forest-dwelling creatures have swirled around the world for centuries. Bigfoot’s other most-used moniker, Sasquatch, is an anglicized version of “Sasq’ets”, a word from the Coast Salish People, a tribe that lives in British Columbia. Versions of this mythical being, which goes by many different Indigenous names, have traveled across generations of stories, as both a large, hairy animal and a spiritual guide.

Today, Bigfoot has grown into something else entirely—as has the hunt to prove Bigfoot exists. Its likeness has been slapped on stickers, shirts, and road crossing signs. The Bigfoot subreddit boasts nearly 300,000 members. There are Bigfoot podcasts, conferences, symposiums, and a seven-night Bigfoot cruise that features daily lectures with Bigfoot researchers. Animal Planet released 11 seasons of the popular show Finding Bigfoot, and the Travel Channel has aired 59 episodes (and counting) of the docuseries Expedition Bigfoot.

There’s no question that Bigfoot has captured the imagination of many, but whether Bigfoot has any foothold in reality remains a mystery.

There are thousands of reports alleging Bigfoot’s existence; most of them focus on one creature, though the common belief within the Bigfoot community is that Bigfoot encompasses an entire species, like wolves, bears, or cougars. The Bigfoot Field Research Organization has collected more than 5,000 sightings through its online database. Washington state leads the charge, with over 700 reports. For decades, people have circulated grainy photographs, videos, and stories. But if Bigfoot is real, he (or she) remains elusive and incredibly camera-shy.

Bigfoot hunters, like Hoskins and crew, want science to back them up. “Science wants a body” is a common refrain in Sasquatch circles. Most aren’t actually rooting for the death of Bigfoot, but if he happened to peacefully pass away in an easily findable location, that would really help them out.

Bigfoot hunters might be lacking scientific proof, but they do have some trained scientists on their side, including tenured professors like the late anthropologists Grover Krantz and Jeffrey Meldrum, who both spent years researching the creature. Even Jane Goodall said she was open-minded about the existence of Bigfoot, and believed some of the stories she heard, adding that it was compelling that every continent has stories about a Bigfoot-type creature.

When Hoskins launched the website for the Pacific Northwest Bigfoot Search, he invited people to submit tales of their own encounters. He shared the site widely through social media channels and online Bigfoot groups, as well as in more general outdoors, fishing, and hunting forums. He also used geotags on Instagram during the group’s early searches, which generated some of the first reports from people who’d experienced supposed encounters near the same areas.

Since 2021, Hoskins and the rest of the Pacific Northwest Bigfoot Search have received 287 reports via the website and social media, covering everything from footprints and vocalizations to alleged sightings. “You have to take a lot of them with a grain of salt,” he told me. But he finds some reports compelling, especially the ones from people who want to remain anonymous, like loggers, law enforcement, and government employees.

The Pacific Northwest Bigfoot Search has grown beyond solely an online database. The crew has headed out regularly, every month or two for the last five years, looking for evidence of unknown, large, bipedal creatures across the Pacific Northwest. The four men behind the Pacific Northwest Bigfoot Search include Hoskins, Stolp, and Palagi, who all once worked at Shriners together, along with Alberto Quinones, a warehouse manager who married Hoskins’ cousin. They’ve all become best friends, Hoskins says.

At 30 years old, Quinones, who usually sports a black hoodie and mustache, is the youngest of the group. Stolp, 48, is the oldest and a father of two, who commutes to Texas where he manages a multibillion-dollar construction project. He’s been out of the Army for over a decade, but his haircut could probably still pass a military inspection. His Army buddy, Palagi, likes to challenge his friends to cook-offs and lives with his three cats and dog at his home outside Portland. And Hoskins, also a father of two, is the de facto leader. He doesn’t relax until everyone’s made it to camp and always requests texts to make sure everyone got home safe after a trip. He likes to say that he “looks like a cop,” though he was denied a career in law enforcement because of severe scoliosis and an amputated right leg.

The four men don’t seem like typical Bigfoot hunters. For starters, half of them don’t think Bigfoot is real. Palagi calls himself the greatest skeptic of the group, saying, “I’ll drill holes in their theories all day long.” And Stolp is quick to clarify that he “doesn’t believe in that shit.” As for that camping trip in 2020, Palagi has an explanation: “A deer pouncing with both legs.”

And the loud, guttural howl: “A territorial bullfrog on the deer’s back.”

Even Hoskins, who spearheaded the formation of their Bigfoot search, says he’s only at 80 percent on the Bigfoot-believometer until he sees one for himself.

A washout pitches my car sideways at a precarious angle. A tunnel of overgrown bushes and trees scratches at my van. The rutted old logging road I’m following, full of creek crossings and potholes, turns my drive into a carnival ride. Hoskins warned me I’d need the right rig to get into camp to join the crew for a two-night Bigfoot search. I’m driving my 2011 Toyota Sienna, to which, Hoskins tells me, “I’ve never seen a minivan on that road.” But it’s all-wheel drive and equipped with an aftermarket lift kit and beefier tires for extra clearance. So far, it’s getting the job done, even if my heart rate is accelerating with every ditch I have to drive over. I wonder if this will be the scariest part of the weekend.

As I drive farther into the Gifford Pinchot National Forest, the trees seem to grow taller and thicker as the road narrows. I’m 47 miles from the nearest gas station, and each washout feels like a “do not enter” sign. I can’t help thinking that this densely wooded forest in the shadow of Mount Adams is where I’d come if I never wanted to be found.

I’m not a Bigfoot believer. But I’m curious about some of the stories I’ve heard that don’t have an easy explanation. Like, what exactly stomped through the guys’ campsite in 2020, howling like no creature they’d ever met.

The 1.3-million-acre Gifford Pinchot, where I’m meeting Hoskins and crew, is a hotbed for Bigfoot reports. It’s home to the aptly named Ape Canyon, where gold prospectors allegedly encountered seven-foot apelike animals in 1924. There’s also Skookum Meadows, where scientists found a body imprint left in the mud in 2000 that they attributed to an “unknown primate” because they couldn’t connect it to any animal. There were so many Bigfoot reports around here in the 1960s that Skamania County passed an ordinance to protect Bigfoot from harm, punishable by jail time or a hefty fine, which still stands today. The original ordinance acknowledged the increasing volume of “well-armed” Bigfoot hunters and expressed concern that said firearms could threaten both Bigfoot and humans traveling through the area.

Finally, the narrow road opens to a small clearing in the trees, where two vehicles are parked a stone’s throw from a fire ring. Hoskins and Quinones are tossing wood onto a campfire. The ground is damp from 24 hours of rain. This summer’s fire ban has been lifted, and the group is taking full advantage.

At five-foot-two, Hoskins is about a foot shorter than Quinones. His work pants hang loose over his prosthetic leg, and he holds a walking stick in his left arm. He moves around the campsite with confident steps as he grabs his chainsaw and returns to the pile of firewood.

I walk over and see that a folding table is covered with their go-to supplies for Bigfoot hunts: thermal scopes, drones, casting materials, trail cameras, and audio recorders.

Hoskins has a handgun on his hip. Quinones has a shotgun in his car. They’re always armed, says Hoskins, though more for humans than Bigfoot. He mentions the Green River Killer, who murdered 49 women in the Pacific Northwest in the eighties and nineties, and left some of the bodies in the forests, which were later found by hikers.

It’s not unusual for campers to be armed in the woods this time of year. It’s hunting season in Washington. I’ve got a bright pink fleece and neon orange hat packed, thanks to Hoskins reminding me to bring colorful gear. He, on the other hand, is wearing a camouflage jacket and light brown pants. Quinones is dressed in all black.

As Hoskins fiddles with the thermal camera, he tells me that it took four years after that first encounter for them to find anything that could be pinned to Bigfoot. Fittingly, it was a big footprint, measuring 16 inches from heel-to-toe and 7 inches wide, that they stumbled upon in the woods. That’s roughly equivalent to a U.S. men’s size 26.

“That’s a long time to keep looking with no results,” I say.

“Well,” Hoskins starts. “There are only 2,000 Bigfoot creatures across North America.”

It’s unclear how exactly that estimate was generated, considering there isn’t definitive proof of a single Bigfoot. It’s also unclear what the plural of “Bigfoot” is. Bigfeet? Bigfoots? Bigfootuses?

“There are 30,000 bears in Oregon,” he goes on. “How often do you see one?”

I think back to the last bear I saw. It was in May. And the only one I’ve seen this year, despite spending most weekends, and plenty of weekdays, on trails around my home in Oregon.

“Bigfoot hunting is like playing the lottery, and the only way to really play is to go camping,” says Hoskins.

“I mostly said yes to my first search because I love camping,” says Quinones, who tells me that he grew up in a family that sees the outdoors as more of a threat than a fun pastime. When he moved to Sherwood, Oregon, from Los Angeles as a teenager, his main social options were hanging out in parking lots or around trees. “I chose trees,” he says and gestures at the many pine trees towering over us.

“I’d stopped getting outside until Kelly shared his encounter,” Hoskins adds.

Hoskins says he used to love driving deep into the forest and spending the night outside. But in his twenties, he fell into a different routine. Most of his friends preferred video games or dive bars to camping trips.

After Stolp told him about his 2020 encounter, Hoskins seized the opportunity to drive his rig back into the woods and set up camp. He also lost his great-grandmother in 2021, who was a parental figure through a childhood affected by addiction. He found himself even more drawn to the outdoors after her death.

“I spent weekends in the trees just screaming, crying, and staring at the fire,” he says. “I think being out here is the best thing for you when you’re going through shit; your mind actually has space to process what you’re feeling.”

He’s not the only one in the group to use these camping trips to process grief, stress, or other hardships. “Some weekends, we’re all just sharing the tough things we’re going through around the campfire,” he says.

“It feels like the only place we can talk about everything, down to the really, really hard stuff,” says Stolp.

“The news is garbage, social media is garbage, everything is garbage,” Stolp continues. “The only thing that feels real and meaningful, other than my family, is going into the woods with my buddies. I think a connection with the outdoors is probably what a lot of the world is missing.”

Hoskins sweeps his arm around the campsite, which, short of the thermal scope and casting materials, looks like any weekend campsite, with camp chairs, packed coolers, and plentiful BBQ fixings. This location is a favorite of the group, I’m told, both for its idyllic setting on an alpine lake and for the ideal Bigfoot terrain that surrounds it: remote wilderness, very few humans, and thick forests. Also important is what they all describe as “weird energy.”

“Something about this camp is just creepy,” says Palagi. “At night, there’s just a weird feeling, maybe it’s because you can’t see very far. But the energy just shifts after the sun goes down.”

They’ve been to this particular spot so many times that they constructed a makeshift outhouse on a tree stump downhill from camp. Though Hoskins warns me not to use it, thanks to the local fire ant population taking a liking to it.

“I think it’s incredibly important to be good stewards of the land,” Stolp tells me, adding that they often pack out more than they pack in.

Hoskins checks the battery on the audio recorder. We’ll leave it out overnight to see if it captures any “vocalizations,” like the howl heard back in 2020. Bigfoot is also rumored to be a wood knocker, screamer, and whistler, depending on whose accounts you read or hear.

“Witching hour is from 11 P.M. to 3 A.M.,” he says.

I pull my hood up as the rain picks up. The shadows are growing long on the forest floor.

Hoskins tells me he was thrilled to see rain in the forecast for the weekend—not just because it’s good for campfires, but because “rain is great for prints.”

Last month, the group found a 12-inch footprint in the forest adjacent to our campsite. That’s equivalent to a size 14, which is less outrageous than the size-26 print, but still suspicious, according to Hoskins.

“I assume they aren’t born eight-feet tall,” he says. “That would be a very painful birth experience.”

He promises to show me where they found the footprint tomorrow.

“Tonight,” he says, “We’ll go down to the lake after it gets dark.”

The Gifford Pinchot isn’t just a hub for Bigfoot activity.

In 2021, a family reached out to Hoskins because their loved one, Glenn Austin Oldfield II, had gone missing in 2015 while camping alone in the Gifford Pinchot. When they saw the group was spending so much time in the same area, they asked if the Bigfoot hunters could keep an eye out for any sign of him.

Inspired by the request, Hoskins reached out to the Washington State Patrol, and they sent him a list of 34 people who’d been reported missing in the Gifford Pinchot since 1979.

It was then that the group launched the Pacific Northwest Missing Persons Project to look for evidence of missing persons and bring closure to cold cases. They realized that the same skills they use to look for abnormal footprints and disturbed soil could help them find scraps of clothing or human bones. They search in the Gifford Pinchot and beyond—wherever their hunt for Bigfoot takes them—or wherever there’s a family in need. Hoskins compiled the names of 500 people missing across Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Montana, and California. Every time they go out, they’re armed with lists of clothing and belongings.

They see their work as picking up the trail where search and rescue leaves it, since most SAR squads lack the funding to continue the hunt after a mission moves from a search to a recovery.

“I want these families to get the closure they deserve,” says Hoskins.

Many families have gone years without answers. Some of them tell Hoskins they’ve been moved from detective to detective, while others can’t get anyone to answer their calls.

For Hoskins, searching for missing people gives him the purpose he’s been unable to find in his career. Hoskins was born with severe scoliosis and had 14 surgeries as a kid. His right leg was amputated when he was a toddler. He uses a hiking stick to get around, and has to physically lift his amputated leg over many of the logs that we crawl over throughout the weekend.

He wanted to serve in the military or go into law enforcement, but he couldn’t pass the physical fitness tests. He got within 30 seconds of completing the course Oregon requires for police candidates, but no matter how hard he trained, he couldn’t do it any faster. He was denied by every branch of the military, he told me. When he was young, doctors told him he wouldn’t be able to walk or run.

“I’ve been told I can’t do a lot of things,” he said. “But no one can stop me from being out here.”

The Pacific Northwest Missing Persons Project is currently pursuing three active searches and has a waitlist of over 100 families. They’re mostly limited by time and gas money, Hoskins says; he would take on every case if he could. Last fall, they found human bones during one of their searches. They’re still waiting on law enforcement to identify them.

A curtain of mist shrouds the lake in the early morning. The night before, we’d set up an audio recorder on the shore and searched the forest for heat and sound. I don’t know if it was the campfire stories or the “weird energy” vibes, but I wasn’t upset that Hoskins had that handgun on his hip as we slipped into the shadows of the dark forest. Quinones recounted how they once heard a voice, “clear as day,” saying “hello,” as they walked through the woods. It’s part of the legend: Bigfoot will mimic human voices or animal sounds. We didn’t find any sign of Bigfoot last night. Still, I didn’t get out of my van to pee until the sun was up.

This morning, we climb over the deadfall that guards the lake and bushwhack through its marshy edges. We walk over broken tree limbs, foot-long pinecones, and downed logs, looking for disturbances or anything that seems odd: boulders that have been moved, branches that have been woven together, or footprints that seem too big and too out-of-place to be human.

“Basically anything that looks like nature didn’t do it,” says Hoskins. The crew draws from their many years of military service, backcountry hunting, and outdoor navigation to look for clues during their searches.

“I’m constantly scanning 20 feet in front of me, looking for breaks, looking for grass pushed down, watching game trails, seeing if there’s a track,” says Stolp.

As we hike, the guys point at the foliage, which is starting to change color, and the hillside that rises above us. Quinones offers to take me up to the ridge so I can see the view. “It’s just gorgeous out here,” says Hoskins.

I get the sense that if searching for Bigfoot involved cities, smog, and skyscrapers, they’d quickly lose interest.

After a lot of off-trail hiking, we get to the shore of the lake and scan the softer, more malleable ground for prints. There are hoofprints galore. But after searching banks of mud, we spy something much bigger than a hoof.

“That could be a deer butt,” says Hoskins. “But let’s cast it to find out.”

He pours plaster into each depression in the soil. We’ll pick up the hardened casts tomorrow to see if they reveal anything promising, like toes, or a whole footprint.

Hoskins then leads us to where they found a footprint last month. When they discovered it, they had Quinones try to match it.

“He’s our go-to guy when we’re trying to gauge whether a large human could’ve left the print,” says Hoskins of Quinones’s six-foot-two height and 250-pound build. “He couldn’t come close.”

“Our first step is to try to debunk anything that we find,” he says. “I can’t say that it wasn’t a human.” Then, he gestures to the ground, which is covered in debris right up to the mud, before sweeping his arm over the lake, which is more bug bog than pristine water.

“But would you walk around here barefoot?”

Palagi shifts his gaze towards the canopy and asks, “You ever look up while you’re out here?” His tone suggests he’s gearing up to spook me, not to point out the scenery.

It’s the next morning, and we’re walking back to the lake to fetch the cast. Palagi drove into camp a few hours ago while an owl was still hooting from a nearby tree. He had to work all weekend, so he told Hoskins he’d get here before we woke up to make breakfast. I thought there was no way Palagi would show up, just to cook us some eggs. Our campsite was a two-hour drive from his home outside Portland, each way. But I saw his headlights cutting through the night while I was still in my sleeping bag. Before I was out of my van, he had his entire camp kitchen out, along with fixings for breakfast sandwiches, and more wood for the fire.

“There’s definitely a crisis going on for men right now,” says Stolp, as he talks about why he keeps coming back to these woods. “And we’ve found a brotherhood through going out in the woods and looking for something that may or may not exist.”

I look up at the canopy and ask Palagi: “Does Bigfoot like to hang out up there?”

“There’s definitely mystery out here,” Palagi goes on, as he looks around the trees that surround us.

Palagi tells me he plans to stop telling the tale of that camping trip in 2020. He’s sick of talking about something that he doesn’t believe in.

But he’s still out here—and even the “greatest skeptic of all” thinks about that question when he’s walking around this forest, he says: What else is out there?

It’s like a treasure hunt every time they come out, Stolp tells me, like being a kid again. And, minus the loaded firearms, this camping trip is reminiscent of scenes from my childhood, when I’d wander through the woods of Vermont looking for my next pirate ship or dragon’s den in the trees and boulders. The possibilities felt endless every time I stepped into the forest.

And maybe that’s a big part of why these guys come back again and again. Whether we believe in Bigfoot or not, there’s an appeal to searching for the unknown. We’re wired to stare at the ocean, the night sky—and a dark forest—and wonder what’s out there. We like thinking about that question, even if it comes with goosebumps on occasion. But it’s easy to lose touch with that in all of the other wires of life.

Hoskins grabs a toothbrush and goes to work on the cast. He gives a play-by-play while he dusts off the hardened plaster, “Indent, another indent.”

When he holds it up for its dramatic reveal, everyone stops talking so he can tell us what he found. I want it to be a large and indisputable footprint. But I know it’s hard to win the lottery on one ticket.

“It’s an unidentifiable blob,” Hoskins says. “Most of them are.” I’m disappointed, of course, but I realize that even the biggest, most undeniable footprint wouldn’t really answer anything. Not even another size 26 track would stop anyone from coming back to the forest—between deadlines, commutes, and night shifts—to walk through the trees and look for reasons to believe the world is still full of wonder.

Emily Halnon is a story collector and teller based out of Eugene, Oregon. She’s the author of the bestselling memoir, To the Gorge, and can often be found sharing snacks and trails with her best friend, Dilly Pickle Chip. Some of her most notable runs include setting a record on the 460-mile Oregon PCT, finishing Hardrock in both directions, and traversing every Domino’s Pizza in Eugene city limits. You can find her online at @emilysweats.

#8104. 4 Quick Activities to Try If Your Kid Is Wired at Bedtime

As a parent, you probably know that bedtime can go two ways: one, your kid was so busy all day they’re exhausted and can’t wait to get that story and hit the pillow. Or two, they haven’t had a chance to expel the endless amounts of energy they store in their little bodies. The latter is where a normal nighttime routine can get tricky because that second wind is no joke. They’ll be jumping, singing, fidgeting, and doing everything they can to delay the inevitable “lights out” moment, meaning there’s even less time for you to binge a few episodes of your new favorite show.

If you’re dealing with a kid who’s wired at bedtime, there are a few things you can do to make the transition to dreamland easier. Mom and pediatric occupational therapist Courtney English recently shared a few of her favorite sensory activities that help kids calm down before bed, and they’re simple but effective. Her TikTok video shows what parents can do:

Dr. Megan Anna Neff writes for Neurodivergent Insights that “Proprioception plays a role in body awareness, self-regulation, coordination, posture, and the ability to focus.” Playing a short game of tag in their bedroom will allow kids to realize where they are at that very moment in time, helping them to center themselves and be present.

Massage is known to be a great way to receive proprioceptive input, and what English calls a sensory sandwich (putting your child between two pillows and pressing down) is a low-energy activity that’ll give their body what it needs to relax.

Vestibular input is another important factor for kids who are wired at bedtime. As Laura Petrix writes for the OT Butterfly, it’s “a network of parts in your inner ear that contribute to your sense of balance and coordination.” It allows our bodies to know when we’re falling, move in coordinated ways (like riding a bike), and know the right speed to walk around other people. The combination of singing and rocking helps to calm the vestibular system by providing auditory rhythm and linear movement.

This is another great type of massage or touch activity that provides proprioceptive input to the nervous system. Plus, it’s a great chance to get a few snuggles in there before they close their eyes.

These activities are no secret to occupational therapists, who use them often. In fact, English has offered other sensory activities that are appropriate for bedtime, including tossing around a weighted animal and doing the “clock move.” But they’re something we should all have in our back pockets next time we’ve got monkeys jumping on the bed.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8103. The Gear That Backpacker’s Editors Loved in October 2026

With spooky season behind us, we’re into fall’s final stretch. Here at Backpacker, we made the most of it: A month ago, our editors got together to backpack a stretch of Wisconsin’s Ice Age Trail, then spent October exploring the forests of the Pacific Northwest, strolling our local trails in Vermont, and even notching a few early-season ski days in Colorado. Here’s the gear that helped us do it

I know: How brave of me to pick what must be the most commonly-used sleeping pad in existence. But some things are classics for a reason, and this folding closed-cell pad is one of them. Consider: It’s unpoppable, a big deal when you regularly go backpacking in the desert like I do; it doesn’t need to be inflated or deflated, which eliminates one task from both your nighttime and morning routines; and it’s light, with a regular running just 14 ounces.

Is it comfortable? Opinions on that vary. I’ll admit that it may not be the supportive option available for side sleepers (or, with its R-value of 2.0, cold sleepers) but I’ve found its egg-crate-style design to be comfier than flat closed-cell models like Walmart’s roll-up Ozark Trail. Anyway, if you’re not tired enough to fall asleep the minute your head hits the ground, you could always just try hiking farther. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief

This poncho is the answer to a dilemma I’ve faced since starting to backpack with my dog. I worry about keeping her warm on chilly nights, but a dog-size sleeping bag never seemed like the best solution, and she’s too big to crawl in with me. The Palisades Sleep Poncho from Ruffwear is the first wearable sleeping bag I’ve seen available; it offers more full-coverage warmth than a dog jacket, stays put better than a blanket, all while being less confining than a sleeping bag. Featuring a ripstop shell and packable synthetic insulation, the poncho slips over the dog’s head and drapes over their back so they have the freedom to move around, curl up, roll over or sprawl without compromising coverage.

A cinchable neck baffle keeps in warmth, and soft, adjustable leg loops eliminate slippage (it’s also easy to bundle up the rear of the poncho with a button for potty breaks). On an October night camping in Washington’s Mt. Baker Wilderness, temps dipped below freezing. My dog, who is usually restless in the tent, slept soundly all night curled beneath the Palisades Poncho. Her water dish was frozen solid when we woke up, but she was cozy and content all night long. Paired with a pup-sized foam pad, this poncho makes for a doggy sleep system I can feel confident in. Bonus: It’s extremely cute. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor

I should have mentioned the price of these hiking pants in the video, but I forgot to. So I’m going to lead with it here: $430 for a single pair of pants is a little outrageous no matter how you spin it. That’s about the same cost as weatherproof snowpants. But the Charge Trousers from Thrudark are exceptionally well made, thoughtfully designed, and built with premium materials (some of which I’ve only ever seen in packs and tents). There are three main things I like about these pants. First, the layout is exceptional. There are six pockets (all on the front), but they don’t look like cargo pants. The ankle cuffs have snap-button adjusters to tighten or loosen them depending on preference and what you’re doing. The hips have Velcro adjusters built in, so you can dial in a perfect fit to your waist, and despite that feature, Thrudark still included belt loops. (Some brands don’t do loops if they have the adjusters, and that drives me nuts.)

My second favorite thing is the materials that these pants are made with. Thrudark used a high-tensile cotton and a Dyneema-Cordura blend that is both highly durable and lightweight. The knees are reinforced with that blend, so you can kneel in a bed of nails and would probably be just fine (at least the pants would be). The rear panel has a four-way stretch material over the butt, which offers a lot of freedom of movement. Third and finally, they’re just comfortable. I can’t say that about every brand’s hiking pants. Where do they fall short? The price, obviously. There’s also the question of how well the cotton elements would hold up if exposed to too much rain (or ungodly perspiration from the wearer). Maybe I’d ask Thrudark for one more pocket on the back, but then again, who on Earth needs seven pockets? —Will Brendza, Associate Editor

Polartec, a well-known fabric company that supplies much of the outdoor industry with its fleece, just released two new versions of its popular Alpha fabric that you’ll be seeing in big-name and cottage brands this winter. One of them is Alpha Wool, a fabric that uses a wool base weave with tufts of Alpha polyester insulation on the outside.

Our very first sample is a crew pullover from cycling brand Ornot. It’s not quite as featherlight as pure Alpha, but at 8.5-ounces in medium, still lighter than micro-grid fleece. Because of that base wool layer, it’s totally stink-free. It’s also slightly more wind-resistant, softer, warmer, and more durable than regular Alpha. —Benjamin Tepler, Senior Gear Editor

#8102. What Matters Most to Jimmy Chin? The Oscar-Winning Director on Fear, Parenting, and His New Book.

(Photo: National Geographic/Savannah Cummins)

When Jimmy Chin was in his twenties, living out of a 1989 Subaru Loyale somewhere between Yosemite and the Tetons, he kept trying to explain climbing to his father. His father, a librarian at Mankato State University in Minnesota, would listen, and then say: “Our language is 5,000 years old, and there is no word for what you do.”

Chin has spent the decades since building a vocabulary for it anyway, as a climber, a photographer, and the Oscar-winning director of Free Solo featuring Alex Honnold, and his latest film, Everest: The Other Side, which documents Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson’s attempt to climb and ski down the North Face of the world’s tallest mountain.

His new book, Rules to Live By (Celadon), presents other people’s words, but is also part memoir. It’s built from ten conversations with people who have lived on their own terms: Yvon Chouinard, Yo-Yo Ma, Simone Biles, Ridley Scott, Kelly Slater, Annette Bening, Lynsey Addario, Kris Tompkins, Alex Honnold, and Bill King, a retired command master chief of SEAL Team 6. He asks each of them some version of the same question: In the end, what really matters? And in the end, we learn what matters most to Jimmy Chin as well.

Earlier this month, I sat down with Chin onstage at the Bell House in Brooklyn. It was his first book event, and he confessed he hadn’t reread the book since turning it in. “There’s a reason I’m a filmmaker,” he told the crowd. “Writing is really, really difficult.” What followed covered violin practice, an undisclosed military base, and a missing sock. The conversation has been edited and condensed.

OUTSIDE: You write that you’re “the only son of an only son of an only son.” That sounds like a lot of pressure.

Jimmy Chin: I started violin when I was three, and it became two hours of practice a day. Then martial arts, two hours a day. Then homework. That was my weekdays, and it was all I knew. But I learned discipline, and there was a very high expectation for excellence. My dad always said, “If you’re going to do it, you might as well do it well.” I hated that. Sometimes I still struggle with it.

There’s a scene in the book where you’re practicing violin, staring out the window at the forest. When did the forest win?

Chin: Anytime I did well in school, my reward was running off into the woods. There were no rules out there. My parents were librarians, so I always had a lot of books, and later, when they asked how I ended up doing this, I said, “It’s your fault. You gave me all these books.” I found climbing in college, and it was the first thing that felt like a calling. Growing up, I literally thought there were three jobs: lawyer, doctor, or professor. So after graduation I told my parents I’d take one year off, get it out of my system, and then pursue my real career. Which was a total lie. From 21 to 28 I lived out of my car, or in a cave in Camp 4, or in a chicken coop in Jackson.

Chin: My sister, who went to Stanford and worked at Yale for 18 years, was my huge advocate. I’d ask her how Mom was doing, and she’d say, “Mom just keeps saying, ‘I raised a homeless man.” With my dad, I deeply wanted him to understand me. People see the films and photographs and ask about the greatest risk I’ve ever taken. It definitely wasn’t a mountain. It was being in my early twenties, full of doubt. There are a lot of storm days, sitting in a cave with water dripping, soaking wet, thinking, What am I doing here? Meanwhile your friends are going to grad school and starting careers.

And during this time, you were in a reggae band.

Chin: I dropped violin after high school and picked up the guitar. The furthest thing I could think of from a concerto in D minor was covering Bob Marley. The whole band was classically trained kids. Everybody was technically skilled, so we could play whatever we wanted.

How did you choose the ten people in the book?

Chin: My documentaries take four, five, six, seven years. You have to bleed for them. You can only make so many films in a lifetime, and there are so many people I admire who I’ll never make a film about. I wanted the book to be a constellation: totally different backgrounds, totally different careers. After these extraordinary lives, what have you discovered really matters? What did success look like when you started, and what does it look like now? I had just turned 50, so I was looking back at my life in phases and thinking about what was to come.

Chin: After Meru, producers kept asking what was next. I mentioned to my friend Evan Hayes, who became a producer on Free Solo, that I’d been thinking about a documentary about Alex. I hadn’t even finished his name before he said, “That’s it.” National Geographic green-lit it immediately. I hadn’t even made a pitch deck.

I’d been filming and photographing Alex for ten years. I’ve worked with some of the greatest adventure athletes of our time, people at the pinnacle of their sports. All of them were anomalies within their sport. In my mind, Alex was an anomaly among anomalies. Even athletes at that level were confounded by what he was doing.

So I called him: “Good news, the film’s green-lit.” He said, “Great, because I’m thinking about soloing El Cap.” I said, “No. Not making that film.” I literally called Evan and said, “I’m out. Done.”

Chin: Among his friends, none of us would even talk about that idea. We didn’t want to put it in the ether. We’d seen the trajectory. He soloed Moonlight Buttress, which was outrageous. Then he soloed Half Dome. We were talking about breaking speed records on Half Dome, not free soloing it. It wasn’t hard to see what came after that. We just didn’t want to say it out loud. And then he dropped it in my lap. My fear was obvious: What if filming him causes him to fall? That’s not something I could live with.

Chin: He was going to do it anyway. I knew Alex really well. I took him on his first international expedition, and we’d done so much together. And I trusted him. Alex was the most calculated person I’d ever met. He had instinct, he was extremely smart, and it was never about external validation. He’s also straightforward, to a fault. He’s been well trained by now, with all the awards. But when I first met him, he’d say things and we’d be like, “You can’t say that.” If he isn’t comfortable doing something, he’ll tell you, and tell you why it’s stupid.

So we moved forward, and I gave my crew three rules. They were almost all elite professional climbers, because that’s the only team you could have: a short list of people who are both. Number one, we’re his friends first. Second, we’re climbers; you think like a climber before you pull out the camera. Third, we’re filmmakers. The film’s needs can never supersede Alex’s needs.

People saw the brain scan in the film and decided Alex was superhuman. You write that he resents that.

Chin: Because it’s just not true. He says, “I feel fear. I’ve always felt fear.” One of the reasons he started soloing was that he was so shy he was too scared to ask people to climb with him. So he climbed by himself. His process was to step outside his comfort zone a little at a time, in a regimented, disciplined way, until the things that scared him were well within it. The film took almost four years. But he’d been training for that climb his entire career. We left the brain scan open to interpretation, but that’s his process.

In 2017 you were trying to dial down the risk in your life. Then Conrad Anker and Alex asked you to come to Antarctica, and you went. You argue in the book that children need parents who are alive, but also parents who feel alive inside. Is that an argument or a good excuse?

Chin: Those are really personal decisions. It’s impossible to justify to a child that their parent died in the mountains doing what I do. I don’t know if there’s a right answer. I’ve lost a lot of friends in the mountains, some of them parents. After my friend Hilaree Nelson died, Bill King wrote to me, and I wrote back: “The mountains give us so much life, yet they take so much life away. It never makes sense, but we understand.” He quoted that line in his retirement speech. So it’s not an excuse. I believe your kids want you alive physically, and alive as yourself. For better or worse, this is my calling.

How do you tell fear that’s protecting you from fear that’s psyching you out?

Chin: Fear can sharpen your senses or paralyze you. When things are going sideways, panic never serves you. So you break it down: How much of this is perceived risk, and how much is actual risk? That exercise alone brings you back into the present. You set the perceived risks aside, focus on what’s real, and mitigate it. Then you make a plan and execute.

I love how all Bill King wanted to know was why you turned around 100 meters from the summit of Meru.

Chin: I got a surprise call from SEAL Team 6 asking me to come talk at the base. They gave me a date, a time, and an airport. I got on a plane, they flew me to an undisclosed location, took my phone. I hadn’t been nervous speaking in years, but these guys roll in and size you up. Someone told me every member of Team 6 had watched Meru. When I finished, a guy in the back cut to the chase: “How did you decide to turn around 100 meters from the summit?” I knew the entire reason I was there was to answer that question. That was Bill.

When you’ve put years into an objective and it’s within sight, and things aren’t right, it takes extraordinary discipline to walk away. On Meru we had seven days of food and were on the wall for 19. We crossed so many of our own lines, deliberately. You set a line, reach it, evaluate, set another. The more you do that, the more invested you are, and the harder it is to turn around.

You and the SEALs share a no-asshole rule. Tell me about that.

Chin: I asked Bill what trait gets people through training. He didn’t flinch: “Humor.” If a guy is getting his ass handed to him and he’s still cracking jokes, they’re not worried about him. It’s the same in the mountains. Humor changes the environment and brings you back to good, rational decisions. My selection process isn’t as serious as theirs, but these are the people holding a rope for you. You can’t have people who only think about themselves. And you can feel it. In conversation, it’s “I, I, I, me.”

Yvon Chouinard is the closest thing you have to a guru. He tells you, “It’s so easy to complicate your life. It’s so much harder to simplify it.” Have you managed it?

Chin: On expeditions, yes. That’s part of why I love them: the best version of me comes out. We’re brutal about simplifying, because every ounce counts. Everything is about efficiency, even how much stress you allow, even your heart rate. I can stay really calm in the worst situations. But if I can’t find my matching sock at home, it’s all over. In the mountains, when things are going sideways, I’m like, oh, this is casual.

You have kids. Do you worry about whether the wild places you’ve spent your life in will still be there for them?

Chin: It’s what the last pages of the book are about. I think of it with Yvon on one end and Kris Tompkins on the other. They’ve both had a tremendous impact on my life, and I’ve talked with both of them about this a lot.

Yvon always says, “Everybody has different tools. Whatever tool you have in your toolbox, whatever you’re good at, that’s what you should contribute.” It’s not only activism. His example is that if you’re an accountant, there are a ton of grassroots organizations that need accountants. So you ask: What can I contribute? Contribute what you have.

Chin: Storytelling, and a platform. That’s why I made Wild Life after Free Solo. I had the chance to finance a film about conservationists, which I probably wouldn’t have had otherwise. It’s about Doug and Kris Tompkins, who preserved something like 17 million acres over a 25-year dream of creating national parks. I’ve brought my kids down there. Those are the things I hope will make a difference: telling these stories, and putting them in a book. What Yvon and Kris have to say is so much more compelling than what I have to say about it.

#8101. Meet the French Soldiers Who Get Paid to Climb Hard Alpine Routes

Dream jobs come in all shapes and sizes. Some might consider my job at Climbing dreamy. Others might hope to hangboard their way into professional climbing one day. My former colleague Duane Raleigh once made a very serious list of climber “dream jobs” that included roofers, fast food cooks, and snow shovelers.

I am here to tell you that none of these jobs are the best climber jobs. The actual best job for a climber, without any shadow of a doubt, is to be a member of the French military’s 27th Mountain Infantry Brigade. Why?

Allow me to describe the group’s latest work trip.

Last Wednesday, October 14, Sergeant Konrad Piontek and Corporals Amaury Fouillade and Clovis Paulin stood on the 6,654-meter summit of Peak 41 in Nepal. On the 1,400-meter North Face, they had just opened a stunning new route linking long sections of vertical ice with burly rock roofs and pitches of deep snow. They called the line Bon Matin (ED+ WI5+ M6 A1 90° snow), which translates to “Good Morning.” (Not sure what “ED+” means? Check out this article about international alpine grades.)

The three first ascensionists were part of a team of six from the 27th Mountain Infantry Brigade, better known as the Groupe Militaire de Haute Montagne, or GMHM. They had arrived in Nepal in mid-September along with a military doctor. After a period of acclimatization, the group split into two rope teams according to their skill level and how well each had adjusted to the altitude.

The Piontek-Fouillade-Paulin team eyed an attractive, unclimbed smear running plumb down Peak 41’s north side, to the left of a Korean team’s route from 2016. They began climbing on October 11 and summited after “four days of particularly committed climbing,” according to a statement shared with Climbing.

Over the 1,400 meters of the face, the team had to deal with numerous steep and poorly protected pitches, including sections of vertical snow. “We weren’t expecting pitches as steep as that, especially in snow,” said Corporal Paulin in the statement. But they also climbed what can only be described as truly classic mixed terrain: solid rock and squeaky ice, hanging above tons of exposure.

After summiting, the team descended the peak’s southeastern aspect via 15 rappels and significant downclimbing, turning their outing into one massive loop back to basecamp. “Reaching the summit was a real physical relief,” said Corporal Fouillade. “The mental release came later.”

Officially, France’s 10-person GMHM is tasked with “mastering extreme terrestrial environments, particularly vertical terrain and high altitude,” said a spokesperson to Climbing. This fluency in alpine terrain aims to contribute to the development of the entire French army’s mountain capabilities.

“The whole point of the GMHM is to practice high level alpinism,” said the group’s spokesperson. “What is learned regarding mountaineering or cold weather environments is passed on to the French mountain units, but the GMHM has otherwise no militaristic purposes.”

Similar mountain-military units exist across the globe, but—tragically—nothing so geared toward climbing excellence exists in North America. (If you happen to have a French passport and the pre-requisites, I’d be refreshing this recruitment page regularly.)

As far as we know, there is no fixed contract length for GMHM members; some alpinists have been part of the dream team for years and years.

In addition to one high-altitude expedition each year, the group travels to Greenland to teach the Groupement de Commandos de Montagne (literally: “mountain commandos”) about how to thrive in cold weather. They also take minor trips to develop rock and ice climbing skills, whether that’s locally in the French Alps or abroad to Yosemite. In plain terms, that means that 10 climbers get to occasionally don camo and earn a decent government salary to climb full time, around the world.

Did I mention the GMHM is the ultimate dream job?

#8100. An Oregon Deputy Rescued a Missing PCT Hiker After Following Bare Footprints in the Snow

A deputy saved a lost PCT hiker after discovering a set of footprints in the snow, with one foot bare. (Photo: Marion County Sheriff's Office)

An Oregon sheriff’s deputy rescued a missing and hypothermic hiker along the Pacific Crest Trail after following a set of bare footprints in the snow, the Marion County Sheriff’s Office said.

According to the department, the deputy was patrolling near Breitenbush Lake on the PCT (Mile 2039.4) on the afternoon of October 30 when he came across the footprints and realized that while one of them showed the outsole of a shoe, the other appeared to have been made by a bare foot. The officer, who was “concerned for the individual’s safety,” followed the tracks for almost five miles to Forest Service Road 4220, where he discovered a man in a sleeping bag.

“Thanks to the quick actions of our Forest Patrol Deputy, the man was located and immediately transported to Detroit, where medics were able to treat him for exposure to the elements,” the sheriff’s office wrote. The hiker, who had been lost for 4 days, is being treated for hypothermia and frostbite.

<span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span><span data-mce-type="bookmark" style="display: inline-block; width: 0px; overflow: hidden; line-height: 0;" class="mce_SELRES_start">﻿</span>

The Salem-based Statesman Journal identified the deputy who made the rescue as Derrick Ramseyer, a 19-year veteran of the department.

The sheriff’s office said that Ramseyer had “likely saved the man’s life, and called the incident “an important reminder to always be prepared when heading into the wilderness.” The office urged hikers to carry an inReach or other emergency communicator and keep a close eye on weather conditions, which can shift rapidly at higher elevations.

The northern stretches of the Pacific Crest Trail are experiencing freezing temperatures with the onset of late fall, especially at higher elevations. On October 30, the Boulder Creek weather station, which is located roughly 13 miles from Breitenbush Lake and 2,000 feet lower, recorded a low of 31 degrees Fahrenheit.

While it’s not entirely clear how the man came to be partially barefoot, hikers losing shoes in snow or deep mud is a surprisingly common occurrence during the shoulder season, and can leave them frostbitten and trapped outside in inclement weather. In April 2023, three separate groups of hikers had to be rescued on Colorado’s Quandary Peak in the span of a single week after losing their shoes in soft snowpack.

#8099. The First-Time Experiences Kids Will Never Forget in Citrus County

There’s something magical about watching your child experience something for the very first time. The wide eyes. The nervous excitement. The inevitable “Can we do that again?” And the stories they tell anyone who will listen long after you’ve unpacked the suitcases. In Citrus County, Florida, those moments are practically everywhere.

Welcome to Crystal River, Homosassa, Inverness and Floral City—a refreshingly wild side of the Sunshine State where first-time adventures come naturally. Here, kids can swim alongside gentle manatees, search the Gulf for their own dinner, explore underwater worlds and discover that sometimes the best adventures don’t require a screen, a schedule or even a ticket. It’s outdoorsy without requiring your family to be expert adventurers, educational without feeling like school and relaxed enough that you don’t need a vacation from your vacation.

An easy road trip from many Florida cities and an unexpected nature escape for families traveling from farther away, Citrus County is where your next family vacation can become a collection of unforgettable firsts.

Imagine the look on your child’s face when a 1,000-pound manatee glides through the water nearby. It’s the kind of moment that makes even the too-cool-for-everything tween forget to play it cool.

Crystal River is known as the Manatee Capital of the World, and it’s one of the few places in North America where families can swim with these gentle giants in their natural habitat. Book a certified tour with an outfitter like Explorida, where guides teach families the importance of respectful wildlife viewing, including the all-important “Manatee Manners.” Tours operate year-round, but winter is prime time for seeing larger numbers of manatees as they gather in the area’s warm springs.

Not ready to snorkel? Explorida also offers manatee-viewing eco cruises, so younger kids, grandparents and anyone who prefers staying dry can still experience the magic.

Why they’ll remember it: Because seeing a manatee in a book or aquarium is one thing. Sharing the water with one in the wild? That’s a story they’ll be telling for years.

For little explorers (and grandparents) who aren’t ready to jump into the water, the next best thing might be watching nature unfold right beneath their feet.

At Three Sisters Springs, a boardwalk winds around the crystal-clear spring complex, offering an incredible vantage point for spotting manatees during the winter months. The surrounding wetlands are also home to birds and other wildlife, turning an ordinary walk into an impromptu nature safari.

Give your kids a challenge: How many manatees can they spot? Can they find a mother and calf? What other animals can they discover along the way?

It’s stroller-friendly, wonderfully unhurried and proof that you don’t have to get wet to make a splash.

Why they’ll remember it: The thrill of spotting their first wild manatee all on their own, and the pride of being the one who shouts, “I SEE ONE!”

Forget searching for seashells on the beach. In Citrus County, kids can head underwater on a real-life treasure hunt and bring home something delicious.

During summer scalloping season, families venture into the shallow Gulf waters off Crystal River and Homosassa, armed with snorkels, masks and mesh bags, to search the seagrass for bay scallops. Think Easter egg hunt, except underwater. And instead of chocolate, the reward might end up on your dinner plate.

Never tried scalloping? That’s part of the fun. Guided excursions with operators like Explorida help beginners learn the ropes, with equipment, guidance and plenty of encouragement along the way. And the moment your child spots that first scallop hiding in the grass? Pure victory.

Why they’ll remember it: There’s something incredibly satisfying about finding your own food. Just wait until they proudly announce at dinner, “I caught that!”

Tinybeans tip: Scalloping is seasonal, typically July through September. Check current dates, regulations and tour availability before planning your adventure.

For kids who’ve never tried kayaking and paddleboarding, Citrus County offers a pretty spectacular introduction. Imagine pushing off from shore, dipping a paddle into clear spring water and realizing that, for the first time, you’re helping steer the adventure.

At Hunter Springs Park in Crystal River, families will find a freshwater swimming area, kayak launch, waterfront boardwalk, picnic spots and a playground. The spring water stays around 72°F year-round, and during cooler months, there’s even a chance of spotting a manatee.

Bring your own paddle craft or book with a local outfitter. Younger kids can ride along with an adult, while older children can take a more active role in navigating.

The best part? There’s no rush to get anywhere. Stop to watch a bird, look for fish beneath the surface or simply float and take it all in.

Why they’ll remember it: That first feeling of independence. The realization that they can help navigate a kayak, explore somewhere new and discover what’s around the next bend.

What if your kids could explore an underwater world without ever putting on a swimsuit? At Ellie Schiller Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park, they can. The park’s famous Fish Bowl Underwater Observatory lets visitors descend beneath the surface of the spring to watch fish and, when present, manatees swim past the windows. For kids, it’s a little like stepping inside a nature documentary.

Back above water, shady, stroller-accessible boardwalks lead past native Florida wildlife, including black bears, alligators, red wolves and Florida panthers. Daily manatee programs offer another opportunity to learn about these remarkable animals and why protecting their habitat matters.

It’s an ideal first introduction to Florida’s wild side, especially for families with younger children or anyone who prefers wildlife encounters on dry land.

Why they’ll remember it: Because the first time you see the underwater world from a fish’s point of view, you never look at the water quite the same way again.

Remember the first time you rode your bike somewhere that wasn’t your driveway or neighborhood? The freedom. The excitement. The feeling that you could go anywhere? That’s what makes the Withlacoochee State Trail such a great family adventure.

Stretching approximately 47 paved miles through forests, lakes and charming small towns, the trail is flat, scenic and easy to explore in family-sized sections. No one expects your six-year-old to conquer all 47 miles.

Start in downtown Inverness, where the trail passes through the Depot District, and let your kids help choose how far to ride. Along the way, keep an eye out for birds, turtles and other wildlife. When everyone starts asking about snacks, make The Train Station part of your plan for pizza, pretzels and a well-earned break.

Why they’ll remember it: Their first real biking expedition, complete with the satisfaction of going farther than they thought they could. Bonus points if they proudly tell everyone how many miles they conquered.

You can tell your kids mermaids aren’t real. Or you can take them somewhere that might make them question everything.

At Mertailor’s Mermaid Aquarium Encounter in Lecanto, live mermaids perform underwater alongside fish, rays and other marine life, creating a magical experience that feels straight out of a storybook. But there’s more here than mermaid magic. The indoor aquarium features over 20 exhibits, interactive touch tanks, sharks, stingrays and freshwater animals, giving curious kids plenty to explore.

For children ages nine and up, the separate Discover Mermaid experience takes things a step further, with the chance to put on a mermaid tail and monofin and learn to swim like one. It’s also a great rainy-day adventure or a welcome break from the Florida sunshine.

Why they’ll remember it: Because watching a mermaid swim with sharks is pretty unforgettable. But getting to be a mermaid for the first time? That’s next-level vacation bragging rights.

Not every unforgettable first requires an adrenaline rush. Sometimes it’s the first time your kids experience what it feels like to slow down.

Head to Homosassa for a waterfront meal at Crumps’ Landing, where palm trees, water views and laid-back Florida charm set the scene for a different kind of family dinner. No rushing to make a reservation across town. No squeezing in one more attraction. Just good food, waterfront views and time to talk about everything you’ve done together. Let the kids recap their favorite adventures while you watch the sky change colors over the water.

Why they’ll remember it: It may not be the meal they remember years from now, but they’ll remember the feeling: salty air, sunset skies and everyone together with nowhere else they need to be.

Remember when simply staying in a hotel felt like the most exciting thing in the world? Now imagine staying somewhere that puts you right in the middle of the action.

Paddletail Waterfront Lodge sits on King’s Bay in Crystal River, giving families easy access to the area’s most memorable experiences. With paddlecraft activities, manatee excursions, waterfront dining, a pool and complimentary hot breakfast, the lodge makes it easy to spend less time coordinating logistics and more time having fun. Rooms with refrigerators and microwaves, and select kitchenette options also make traveling with kids a little easier.

Wake up knowing that another adventure is waiting just outside.

Why they’ll remember it: Because when the place you stay is part of the experience, even the moments between activities become vacation memories.

Here’s a first that might surprise you: What if you gave your kids an entire afternoon to decide what the family does? No packed itinerary. No racing from one attraction to another. No pressure to squeeze every last minute out of your vacation.

One of the best things about Citrus County is that it gives families room to explore at their own pace. Maybe your kids want another swim at Hunter Springs. Maybe they want to wander downtown Crystal River, go for another bike ride, find ice cream or sit by the water and watch for wildlife. Let them choose.

Because sometimes the most meaningful first isn’t swimming with a manatee or spotting a scallop. It’s the first time your child discovers that an adventure doesn’t need to be planned to be unforgettable.

Why they’ll remember it: Because they helped create the memory themselves. And those are often the moments that stick.

Someday, your kids might forget what they packed, what they ate for breakfast or how long the drive took. But they’ll remember the first manatee they saw. The first scallop they found. The first time they paddled across a spring or rode their bike farther than ever before. And you’ll remember the look on their faces when they did.

That’s the magic of Citrus County. It’s not just a place to visit. It’s a place to try something new, discover something extraordinary and make the kinds of memories that grow more meaningful with time.

Ready to make some first-time memories? Plan your Crystal River and Citrus County getaway and request a FREE Visitor Guide, or book a certified manatee tour and get ready for an adventure your family won’t soon forget.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8098. How to Car Camp in Your Subaru Crosstrek

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Jackery Explorer 1000 Portable Power Station

Exped MegaMat LuxeWool Auto Sleeping Pad Cover

I’ve always been jealous of people with a kitted-out Land Cruiser or a made-to-order Sprinter van. These #adventuremobiles not only look cool and bestow the driver with backcountry cred, but they also offer the freedom to roam without worrying about finding a place to pitch a tent. Behind the wheel of one, you can venture into the unknown and, when sleepiness starts making your eyelids heavy, pull off the road for some fully prone shut-eye without even stepping outside.

Even if you’re not pulling over at the last minute, these rigs serve as comfy, spacious home bases for drive-in campsites, getting rest before a big race, or road-tripping to a far-flung national park. The major problem? They can be prohibitively expensive, rarely work well as daily drivers, and can be tricky to keep running smoothly. Sleeping in my car comfortably always felt like a luxury I couldn’t afford—until this summer.

In June, I bought a car for the first time in years. Like many outdoor-minded folks, I gravitated toward a small, capable crossover that promised competence on dirt roads alongside decent city gas mileage. For me, that was a Subaru Crosstrek—a car I’ve wanted for nearly a decade. But it could have been an Outback, a Toyota RAV4, or any number of smaller utility vehicles. Since I’d be driving it daily in Los Angeles, the fuel economy and parkability made sense. But I also knew I could take it off the beaten path to road-trip to Mammoth or explore the American West. What I wasn’t sure of was whether I could turn it into my own adventuremobile and spend a comfortable night sleeping inside.

After some research and a few key car camping gear pick-ups, I can tell you that it is indeed possible to sleep in the back of my Crosstrek and fully stretch out my five-foot-ten frame—no scrunching or squishing necessary. In fact, two people could sleep back there quite easily, which I didn’t anticipate when I drove it off the lot. I’ve found car-specific sleeping pads, easy-access roof boxes, and numerous other bits and bobs that make sleeping in the back of a compact car genuinely comfortable.

Since June, I’ve dialed in a basic setup you can apply to just about any small vehicle. Read on for my car camping essentials, plus a few items I hope to pick up soon to make nights in my hatchback even more luxurious. Who needs a van? (Okay, I’d still love a van.)

If you buy only one thing to make sleeping in your car comfortable, make it the MegaMat Auto from Exped. The first time I slept on one was at a friend’s house; they used their original MegaMat as a guest bed. I was skeptical that a camping mattress could match a standard air mattress, but my skepticism was misplaced—it gave me one of the best nights of sleep I’ve ever had on an inflatable bed. When I saw Exped made a car-contoured version, I had to get one.

It fits snugly in my Crosstrek with both front seats pushed fully forward, providing plenty of width for one person and enough room for two to sleep as comfortably as they would in a two- or three-person tent. It inflates quickly—especially if you use the Mega Pump, which tops it off in under two minutes.

Plus, it doubles as a spare mattress for houseguests. For extra luxury, you can also add the MegaMat LuxeWool Auto cover.

I’ve never owned a roof box before, and it’s a total game-changer for car camping when square footage is at a premium. Sure, you could chuck everything from the trunk into the front seats while you sleep, but that leaves zero room for organization. With a cargo box, you can store your sleeping gear up top while driving, then swap it for your extra gear overnight.

The Thule Motion 3 looks sleek (especially in black) and opens smoothly from either side, which is handy on the Crosstrek since I can center the box on the roof and still access it from the driver or passenger side. The Large size fits perfectly on the roof length-wise. Locks and keys are included, and while it’s light enough for one person to hoist or remove, I recommend having a second set of hands. The mounting hardware clamps down without fuss. I pair it with the Thule WingBar Evo crossbars—a bit spendy, but versatile enough to keep on the roof year-round.

There are plenty of ways to manage car storage, but hard-sided crates solve one of car-sleeping’s biggest headaches: the rear footwells. While my back seats fold flat, there’s a wide gap between the folded seats and the front seats that needs support so your mattress doesn’t sag under your head.

My Sidio crate lives in the trunk loaded with car essentials—first-aid kit, blanket, towel, and miscellaneous gear. When it’s time to sleep, one of these crates slides into each footwell to create a sturdy platform. One crate isn’t quite tall enough on its own, so I usually stack a sturdy shoe box on top to level it out. Stacking a Quarter Size Crate on top of the Full Size Crate would likely hit the exact height needed for the Crosstrek.

You don’t strictly need a dedicated camping pillow, but keeping one in the car saves your everyday bed pillows from outdoor dirt. The Luno Packable Camping Pillow lives in my Sidio crate full-time. It doesn’t pack down microscopic, but it compresses enough to justify keeping it in the car 24/7, and the shredded memory foam fill is comfortable enough to use indoors. A zippered inner liner lets you add or remove filling to adjust the firmness.

Any standard blanket works, but a technical down quilt packs down small and adapts well to changing temperatures. I use the Therm-a-Rest Vesper (which doubles as my backpacking quilt), while the team at Backpacker rates the Neve Gear Waratah as a top choice. Choose based on the climate and temperatures you expect to encounter.

I’ve been using a compact Nestout Battery Pack to charge my phone, but a larger portable power station makes multi-day trips much easier. Compact stations like the Jackery Explorer or Goal Zero Yeti tuck away neatly while keeping cameras, headlamps, and laptops powered up.

To read or wind down without wearing a headlamp, interior lighting is a subtle upgrade. The BioLite Luci Solar String Lights add cozy ambient light across the cabin, while a compact lantern like the Big Agnes mtnGLO can easily hang from a grab handle or ceiling hook. The BioLite lights are rechargeable, and the Big Agnes light requires AAA batteries, so keep that in mind when adding accessories that require power.

#8097. 31,000 Miles, 28 Years: Karl Bushby’s Walk Around the World by the Numbers

Karl Bushby walks through a park in Peterborough, England, on October 22, 2026, during the final leg of his 28-year Goliath Expedition. (Photo: Leon Neal/Getty Images)

On November 1, 1998, Karl Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, and began walking north. Ahead of him, the 29-year-old British former paratrooper pushed a modified golf trolley filled with supplies and gear that he dubbed “The Beast.” His goal: to walk as far as a person could in unbroken footsteps on Earth, without using anything but his own hands and feet to make forward progress. His planned route for what he called the Goliath Expedition would take him from the southernmost tip of South America to his hometown of Hull, England, a journey he estimated would take him about 12 years.

Exactly 28 years and one day later, Bushby arrived back in Hull’s Queen Victoria Square to cheering crowds at shortly before noon on November 2, capping off a journey that was much longer—and far more complicated—than he could have imagined when he began. Along the way, he navigated shifting ice floes across the Bering Strait and swam the Caspian Sea to dodge geopolitical tensions and the English Channel after Eurotunnel refused to let him walk through the service tunnels connecting France and the UK. Not all the obstacles were physical, either: Bushby decamped to Mexico to regroup after his sponsorships dried up in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and spent 10 years crossing Russia, stymied by visa requirements and an entry ban. (He finally received the permission he needed in 2014 after walking 3,600 miles across the United States to Russia’s embassy.)

All of that added up to something larger than a hike—a journey that ended up taking almost exactly half of the 57-year-old’s life. (It demanded a commensurate sacrifice, and not just from him. Bushby has a son, now 36, who he’s only seen a handful of times since leaving, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met until finishing his trek; he also had and lost two long-term romantic relationships during the journey.)

For all that, the man behind the Goliath Expedition isn’t inclined to brag. When Backpacker writer Bill Donahue caught up with Bushby in Mexico in 2012, at what would turn out to be the halfway point of his walk, Bushby downplayed his own achievements.

“I’m an average guy,” Bushby said. “I’m less than average. I’m an underachiever. All I’m doing is putting one foot in front of the other.”

Here’s what Bushby’s big walk looked like by the numbers.

The approximate distance that Bushby walked from Punta Arenas, Chile, to Hull, England. That’s equivalent to 14 thru-hikes of the Appalachian Trail, 1.25 times the circumference of the globe, or roughly 13 percent of the average distance from the Earth to the Moon. That distance took him through 30 countries, according to the Associated Press.

The total distance Bushby had to swim during his trip. That included roughly 179 miles across the Caspian Sea in September and October 2024 and 21 miles across the English Channel in October 2026. Bushby did both of those swims in stages, resting on a support boat at night and returning to the coordinates where he had gotten out of the water in the morning.

The amount of time Bushby spent in jail after crossing borders without authorization. That includes 18 days in Panamanian custody after he crossed the roadless Darién Gap from Colombia and 58 days in Russian detention following his crossing of the Bering Strait from Alaska.

Bushby’s average pace across his entire trip. While far slower than other long-distance hikers—the small group of people to have hiked 10,000 miles in a year all had to knock off roughly 28 miles per day—the legal and financial hurdles Bushby faced, as well as his refusal to use transportation to bypass complicated terrain, meant that making miles was significantly more difficult for him.

The number of carts that Bushby used to carry his gear during the Goliath Expedition. The first, the Beast, survived three years before breaking down in Nicaragua. He used its replacement, the Beast 2, for the remaining 25 years. In an interview with The Guardian, Bushby called the cart “my Wilson,” referring to Tom Hanks’ famous volleyball and conversation partner from Castaway.
