#8096. A Love Letter to Flated’s Inflatable Truck Shell

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

For more than a decade, I’ve driven trucks, and always with a fiberglass hardshell topper. The cap transformed the bed of my pickup into a gear shed for all of my outdoor equipment and a tiny cabin for me to crash in on climbing trips and before alpine starts. But, as my hard shell weighed north of 150 pounds, I never—and I mean that literally—took it off.

That’s all fine and dandy for the dirtbag climber and runner, jaunting around New Mexico and Colorado without a care in the world in her twenties. But at this stage of life, as a mom of three kids with a house to maintain, a farm to care for, and loads of bikes and strollers to haul to and fro on the weekends, my truck needs to be a little more versatile.

As its name suggests, Flated shells are inflatable. I blew it up using the plug-in pump reserved for my SUP in just a few minutes. Installation required no further tools. At under 60 pounds, installation is not only simple, but easy to do by myself. I just inflate the cap and lift it onto my truck. Then, I attach it with a handful of tie-downs. In total, installation takes about 30 minutes, but I bet I’ll get faster with practice.

Flated doesn’t skimp on features, either. It’s fully waterproof with a rain skirt built in to repel water from the truck bed. There are two tinted windows, two screens on the side windows, and one rear window. The part of the topper that connects to the truck cab also features a pass-through window, so you can easily access the truck bed from the backseat. Sturdy zippers and Velcro secure window shades while you drive, and a couple of interior mesh pockets on the cab end help sort smaller gear and gadgets. I have yet to camp with the Flated Cap56, but when I do, that’s where I’ll stash my phone and headlamp for safekeeping.

At $1,600, it’s not cheap, but it does cost several thousand dollars less than a traditional hardshell.

I live at high elevation and full sun in northern New Mexico, so time will tell how the new topper stands up against the elements, but so far, I’ve driven it for about a month without any signs of wear.

Last weekend, I had it on for transporting bike gear and keeping it safe from the rain, but I pulled it off the next day to haul home some new trees from the local nursery. This, in a nutshell, is the beauty of the Flated Cap56: it’s versatile and goes with the flow of life, no matter how chaotic my days may get.

#8095. It’s an All-Day Pool Day at Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort

An all-inclusive vacation with kids should make family time easier, not leave parents juggling restaurant reservations, activity schedules, and snack requests every few hours. At Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort, Spa & Casino in the Dominican Republic, families can explore a sprawling resort, splash in pools, and enjoy activities for all ages.

The resort is part of the Lopesan Costa Bávaro Resort, Spa & Casino complex in Punta Cana, a destination known for its white-sand beaches and turquoise Caribbean waters. With family accommodations, supervised kids’ activities, and options for teens who prefer to spend time away from their parents, Lopesan Caoba Lagoon offers a setup that makes multigenerational family trips or vacations with school-age kids easier to plan.

Whether your family wants to spend most of the day in the water or mix pool time with games, dining, and evening entertainment, there are plenty of ways to make the vacation your own.

The largest family accommodation configuration combines a Resort Junior Suite Connecting room with a Family Junior Suite Connecting room. Together, the rooms offer 1,179 square feet of space for up to seven guests, with one king bed, two queen beds, a sofa bed, and two bathrooms.

That layout is especially useful for families traveling with several children, grandparents, or another family member. Two bathrooms make getting ready for dinner much less chaotic, while connecting rooms let parents stay close to younger children without everyone sharing the same sleeping space.

Before booking, confirm the exact room configuration and occupancy with the resort. Connecting rooms can be a practical alternative to squeezing everyone into a single suite, especially on a multi-night trip.

Even on a family vacation, it’s nice to have a little time apart. Lopesan Caoba Lagoon offers a Mini Club for children ages 4 to 12 and a Teen Club for guests ages 13 to 17, giving kids time with peers while parents enjoy downtime.

The clubs operate from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m., with meal breaks to give families flexibility to plan around breakfast, lunch, pool time, or dinner. Parents can enjoy a quiet break, book a spa treatment, or simply spend a little time together while the kids have activities of their own.

For families with younger children who aren’t quite ready for a group kids’ club, babysitting is available 24 hours a day with advance arrangements at $20 per child per hour.

One of the highlights of Lopesan Caoba Resort is its water features. Families can ride the waves in the wave pool, let little ones splash around in the kiddie waterpark area, splash down on the waterslides, or find a spot in the shade to enjoy one of the lagoon pools.

My favorite was the cenote swimming pool, something I haven’t seen at other all-inclusive resorts. This tranquil area never got crowded when I visited, offering a respite from the lively swim-up bars and water aerobics sessions.

For those looking for beach time, the property is adding a beach club, and in the meantime, guests can visit the Lopesan Costa Bávaro Resort beach club. Keep in mind that seaweed can be an issue in the Dominican Republic, depending on when you visit.

One of the main advantages of an all-inclusive resort is not having to figure out every meal. You can plan meals around swimming and activities instead of interrupting the day to find an off-property restaurant. The breakfast buffet was massive, offering everything from fresh fruit smoothies to pastries and waffles made to your liking. They even had a whole section for kid-friendly options and Dominican favorites.

With eight traditional restaurants to choose from, you’ll find something for every taste, from deeply flavorful Indian dishes at Indra to upscale pasta, pizza, and more at Sotto Terra. If you decide to get a babysitter for the night, definitely book a meal at the adults-only steakhouse Brassa Nova.

Evenings can be a highlight of an all-inclusive vacation, especially when there’s entertainment close to your room. Instead of arranging transportation or trying to keep everyone awake for a late dinner in town, families can enjoy the resort’s evening offerings and return to their rooms when the kids are ready to wind down.

The Boulevard, which connects Lopesan Caoba to Lopesan Costa Bávaro Resort, offers a bowling alley, theater, ice cream shop, café, and casino for adults. We enjoyed live music performances and karaoke at the bars during our stay.

Families can fly into Punta Cana International Airport (PUJ), about 20–30 minutes from Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort, depending on traffic. Private airport transfers and transportation through the resort or a third-party provider make getting to the property easy, so you won’t need to rent a car. If it’s busy when you are departing, consider using the airport’s VIP Fast Track service.

Lopesan Caoba Lagoon Resort, Spa & Casino Online: lopesan.com

Editor’s note: This trip was paid for by Lopesan, but all opinions belong to the writer.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8093. Does Anti-Stink Clothing Actually Work? We (Really) Wanted to Find Out

It wasn't easy, and didn't go as expected, but the no stink clothes seemed to work as advertised. (Photo: Sam Anderson)

I boarded a 3-hour flight wearing a T-shirt I’d worn for over three weeks straight.

By this point I only had a vague sense of what I smelled like. Sleeping bag sweat? Iso gas? Hot dog water? I listened to the crew make the “very full flight” announcement again and shifted in my middle seat. It wasn’t just that I had a dirty shirt on—I’d barely showered for the entire trip, and apart from a few bracing dips in rivers and ocean water, I had made little effort to clean myself at all.

Instead, techy fabrics from Patagonia and an innovative startup called HercLéon battled my oils and odors at point-blank.

Except for deodorant, all that guarded the packed flight from trail stank were various items of “laundry-free” or “anti-odor” clothing. My Patagonia pants and sun hoodie were treated with steam-extracted, food-grade mint oil. The HercLéon T-shirt and my boxer briefs were infused with charcoal and woven with copper fibers. I had used exfoliating nylon washcloths from Lunatec that “never need washing.”

When I planned to hike through the majority of Washington state on a former rail grade, I immediately thought it would be helpful to bring only one set of clothes. But if I tried it and anything went wrong, I could be exposed. As is the case on many long-distance hikes, I knew clothes shopping could be a tough ask depending on where I was.

Still, wardrobe weight is real, and weight quickly becomes the enemy of comfort. So could materials like Patagonia’s HeiQ and HercLeon’s HercCopper limit foul smells after days on trail? Could that improve my overall mood, along with the weight savings, and could it all help me with social graces along the way?

My target was a 330-mile segment of the Great American Rail Trail. It links old railroad corridors from the western Cascades to the Idaho border, dividing roughly into two halves that mirror Washington’s geography: rugged mountains west of the Columbia River and sparse deserts to the east.

I quickly realized small-town hospitality would be my only ticket through the eastern deserts. With no infrastructure or known water on the trail for 40 miles in some areas, networking with anyone willing to provide would be key. I knew I’d be more likely to score overnight stays or solid hookups if I didn’t roll into town smelling like Sasquatch.

Early on, though, the hike took a hard turn: I limped off the trail after 60 miles with a foot injury, but decided to stay in Washington anyway. Some supportive offers from friends could give me a runway to rest up until my original bail date, and maybe hit some rock climbing if I could recover in time.

Because that plan would still require a pretty deep level of dirtbagging, I knew I could keep stink-testing my clothes—which had amazed me to this point.

The accident led to a variety of activities I wasn’t planning on.

This demanded resilience and adaptation from me and everything in my kit, including my clothes.

Apart from activities, my clothing was also subjected to heavy chemical factors, including sleeping bag sweat, dehydrated meal sweat, fried food sweat, and beer sweat. Smoky campsites, rampant use of catholes and wag bags, many cups of coffee, and trash bags packed in vans directly alongside gear during rainy spells also played a role.

In short, I believe the textile engineering of several items made it possible to keep the same clothes on my back for the duration—without disgusting myself, visibly offending service workers, or prompting any business owners to kick me out.

To understand this question is to understand why a tiny startup like HercLéon would market a copper-infused T-shirt for $130.

TL;DR: Body odor happens because our skin is a Golden Corral for bacteria. And it’s open 24 hours.

No matter what we’re doing, our skin is always generating natural oils and shedding dead cells. Glands in areas like the armpits and groin constantly leech thicker protein- and lipid-composed fluids onto the skin. The resulting buildup becomes a body-sized feeding trough for potentially trillions of bacteria.

When those bacteria expel waste, that’s where stink comes from. That and the layers of old oil, decaying cells, etc. that accumulate until you wash them off with soap and water.

Imagine flooding this system with sweat, then draping a layer of clothing on top. Sweat itself is generally odorless, but it does help bacteria multiply. And when it touches the clothing, it allows them to swim, slosh, or spill over. If your skin is a microbial Golden Corral, your sweaty clothes are like a swim-up bar attached to the dining room. But not all textiles are equally hospitable.

Polyester repels water but attracts oil. Skin oils can bond tightly to its synthetic fibers, but the fibers naturally reject water, even in the washing machine. The oil, and anything else gummed up in it, gets welded to the fabric. (This is why some of your cheapest workout shirts get “permastink.”)

Merino wool is the opposite: It repels oil and attracts water. The thirsty fibers soak up sweat from the skin, but leave most bacteria behind, stuck in the oil. And because the merino is removing their water source, the bacteria have a harder time multiplying and farting out more odor.

Techy fabrics like those from Patagonia and HercLéon take this equation of moisture and bacterial transfer to the nth degree—they seek to wall off the swim-up bar.

The HercShirt felt great right out of the bag in a size small, and matched my sizing expectations. Field performance proved to be incredible.

The fabric felt slightly heavy, sliding across my skin with a gentle pressure that felt cooling and was never scratchy. I found it fit closely enough to help me look sharp in town, but never lost its shape. After three weeks, the material still felt stretchy everywhere. The collar hadn’t bagged out and even the shirt’s hem under my hip belt wasn’t sagging or creased. By the end of the journey, it was tie-dyed with sweat stains from pack straps, but still passed as a deep navy blue. It never developed pit stains.

Of course, odor did become noticeable. It’s hard to say whether it was on day 12 or 20, but I also made no effort to clean the shirt. So based on my testing, HercLeon’s stated 10-day freshness target is fair—especially if you take the punishing factors of my testing field into account. My shirt endured days of sweaty hiking, exposure to muggy northwestern rainforests, late nights out on the town, cold snaps, and rainstorms that kept me layered up for days on end. It survived nights wadded up at the bottom of a sleeping bag around my heinous feet. I have almost no doubt that 10 days of normal wear with regular showers would be feasible.

My HercUnderwear 2.0 Boxer Briefs were equally impressive. With the caveat that there is a wide spectrum of underwear hygiene tolerance in the population, my findings are below.

First, did I wear the same pair of underwear every day for over three weeks without washing them? No, because there are bacterial realities that command respect. I did take a backup pair of boxer briefs, and I wrung out the HercUnderwear once in a sink with hand soap and once in the ocean. With only this spartan care, the single pair of shorts served for up to nine days at a time. (I used wet wipes consistently.)

For comparison, I did test how long I could make my spare Hanes 92/8 poly/spandex units last. I found four days was my threshold, and wanted to incinerate them after that for the benefit of the trash workers. Meanwhile, crude handwashing rejuvenated the HercUnderwear to a satisfactory extent for the field.

I found fit and roominess to be on the small side. I opted for mediums with my 29-30” waist.

Ultimately, I’ll keep the underwear in my kit for activities except hot-weather hiking. The fabric is a bit heavier than many boxer briefs’, and can feel slightly warming depending on pants choice.

HercLéon’s engineering exists at every level of manufacturing. Instead of using a spray-on coating, the brand mixes tiny particles of copper and charcoal into its raw textile material before spinning that into fibers. It is called a “masterbatch.” Materials are chosen to control odor at three different points: bacterial growth, odor absorption, and moisture management.

The shirt starts with lyocell, a soft, moisture-absorbing textile fiber made from processed wood pulp.

Copper particles embedded in the fibers release antimicrobial ions when damp. This damages bacterial cell walls, limiting their ability to multiply and convert sweat and other food sources into foul-smelling compounds.

The next contingency is charcoal. Their highly porous carbon structure can trap odor molecules that do develop, HercLéon says, preventing them from escaping into the air.

Finally, “plasma modification”—altering the surface properties of the fibers with ionically-charged gases during manufacturing—causes sweat to spread out and evaporate across the garment, rather than accumulate. Less lingering moisture means fewer opportunities for bacteria to multiply.

Stumbling into Cle Elum, Washington, with wobbly legs, an injured foot, and a calorie deficit, I lurched toward the nearest bar (a long, long mile away). It had been a 30-mile day, and I’d been walking since it was too cold to feel my fingers in the morning. The afternoon in the sparse Yakima River valley had reached 93 degrees. I hadn’t stopped to change clothes—I knew I was hurt and no comfort would amount to real relief.

Night fell, and I sat down at a park bench in a fugue state to put on layers. I reached for my shirt collar to pull it off, expecting to wrestle with a sweat-soaked sheet. Instead, it was bone dry.

My Patagonia Capilene Cool Ultra hoody slotted into the “go-to” position on the trip. The lightest of four entries in the Capilene line, Patagonia builds it specifically for summer temperatures. I confirmed this use case in an unseasonably hot, exposed ascent of the west face of Exfoliation Dome. But I also discovered the hoody had just enough weight to take the shiver factor out of a damp Pacific morning.

Features are limited but functional. I found that using the thumb loops didn’t stretch the sleeves beyond recognition, and I liked the single button to tighten the hood. There are no pockets. Wearing the hoody roughly as much as my HercShirt, often layered with it, I got the sense that odor control wasn’t quite as strong. But it did still generally meet the limits of social acceptability by the end of the trip. And since it was easy to rinse and dried fast, I had no problem dunking it and wringing it occasionally.

According to Patagonia’s anti-stink coating provider, this shouldn’t have worked to refresh odor-fighting capabilities. The coating is a handful of botanicals arranged in a bioengineered structure. HeiQ Mint contains essential mint oils and other “naturally derived deodorizing ingredients”—inside capsules the manufacturer claims are capable of trapping the oils and acids that cause odor. This proprietary “encapsulation technology” snatches odor-causing particles and encloses them during wear. Then it releases them during washing thanks to the alkalinity of soapy water. Thus, laundering duds like the Capilene Cool hoody restores them for their next use, according to HeiQ.

On the last day of the trip, we walked down from the base of Blueberry Buttress (5.8+, 1,000 feet). In just a half mile from the foot of the climb to the car, we lost 1,300 feet of elevation. Quads screaming, we reached my borrowed van and flopped. My climbing partner wrestled himself out of his soaking wet T-shirt, now two or three sizes too big, and hung it on a tree branch.

My Capilene hoody wasn’t stinking up the campsite, and it still fit around my shoulders. Plus, it was dry enough to continue wearing comfortably.

Lunatec’s “never needs washing” camp cloths were absolutely clutch in my kit. With no technology on board except a loose weave for fast drying, the two units thoroughly supplemented wiping and cleanup needs without creating their own.

The green “odor-free” dishcloth was abrasive enough to lift stuck-on burnt bits, and highly durable. Its diffuse weave made it economical to rinse after scouring cookware with sand.

The “self-cleaning” washcloth, slightly larger and stretchier, played well for more detailed work. It was minimally absorbent (I didn’t reach for it when I spilled an entire beer into my friend’s van carpet). But viscous bits like snot or soup remnants clung to it well, then vanished when rinsed. The elastic hang tabs doubled as gathering straps, making each cloth easy to pack up.

What is Lunatec’s secret to self-cleaning? According to the brand, nothing. Their washcloths are 100% nylon, and nothing else.

A backpacker’s world is a stinky one no matter what. So if you’re on an anti-gross-out program, how can you tell if your efforts have meant anything? How can you tell if you’ve kept the Golden Corral in the corral?

There is a device used to measure odors in clinical settings called an olfactometer. It works by, basically, establishing a control smell and then upping the ante in increments—approaching the threshold where the subject can’t handle it anymore. In everyday practice, though, you experience moments when you become suddenly aware of an odor. You lift a shoulder to reach an awkward zipper or squat fast to pick up something you dropped—and the wave breaks. A solid mass of stink floods your face, and you wonder how long everyone else has been able to tell.

For many of us, that’s the trigger. “I need to wash, somehow, now.”

Over 25 days living in a pretty dirty corner of the dirtbag life, I never had that moment. River plunges sufficed for bathing. Sink water rinses refreshed the hardest workhorses in my wardrobe. I didn’t take a microscope, but I think the makers of my clothing delivered on their broad promise: Science can help you not stink (or at least, stink less).

The maintenance burden of living outside full-time had been meaningfully decreased. I thrived in my unexpected program of outdoor and social events for over three weeks with a wardrobe that would fit in a McDonald’s bag, and I’d spent zero time doomscrolling at the laundromat.

Boarding my flight, I looked down at my disheveled rags and scratched at an itch in my neck—I also hadn’t shaved for the whole trip. Then, both of my neighbors arrived and settled in, smiled warmly, and relaxed.

#8092. Nike Alphafly 4 Review: Softer & Lighter, But Is It Better?

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

The Nike Alphafly is the flagship marathon super shoe from the company that invented the super shoe—and arguably the most iconic racing shoe ever made. It was on the feet of Eliud Kipchoge in 2019 when he became the first human to break two hours in the marathon, and again in 2022 when he ran his 2:01:09 official world record. It stood atop the podium in Chicago in 2023 when Kelvin Kiptum broke Kipchoge’s record, and again in 2024 when Ruth Chepngetich ran 2:09:56 to break the women’s world record. Over the past six years and three iterations, the Alphafly has consistently carried elites and competitive runners to course records, podium finishes, and PRs.

But despite this consistent success, the Alphafly has struggled to maintain a consistent ride and reliable feel. The original was incredibly bouncy but extremely unstable. The Alphafly 2 fixed the stability issue, but many found it lost its bounce. The Alphafly 3 introduced a continuous sole and repositioned the Air Zoom units, bringing back the bounce in a lighter overall package.

As a competitive masters athlete and full-time running coach, I have a few trusted super shoes I personally race in and recommend to my clients. The Nike Alphafly 3 is one of them; the Alphafly 2 was not. So when I heard rumors of the Alphafly 4 launch, I got anxious about what Nike would change and whether it would be a step back for the stellar shoe.

I’ve now had the chance to run in the Nike Alphafly 4 to confirm or allay my fears. Here’s what I found out.

Weight: 6.6 oz (men’s 8.5; women’s 10) Stack Height: 39-31 mm Heel-to-toe Drop: 8 mm

+ Softer, more cushioned ride, especially in the forefoot + Air Zoom units are easier to engage at slower paces + Roomier, more comfortable upper that’s easier to put on

– Less snap than the Alphafly 3 at faster paces

When I first saw the Alphafly 4, it was comforting to see how similar it looked to the Alphafly 3. However, despite the similar looks, I learned that every component of the shoe, from the upper to the outsole, has been updated. Bret Schoolmeester, Nike’s vice president of running footwear product management, said it was the biggest improvement in Alphafly history.

The biggest change came in the way the Air Zoom units are sealed. The Alphafly 3 used heat to seal the Air Zoom units, whereas the Alphafly 4 uses radio frequency, which creates thinner, cleaner seams and, according to Nike, made the Air Zoom units 30 percent lighter and softer.

The carbon fiber plate keeps the same scooped geometry but has been slightly widened to improve stability. Above the plate, Nike introduced a new ZoomX foam called ZoomX LT. It has the same ingredients as the current ZoomX, but is processed differently, which, Schoolmeester said, makes it lighter and gives it better energy return.

When I had the chance to run in the Alphafly 4, I immediately noticed a very different underfoot feel than the Alphafly 3. It’s much softer and more cushioned, especially in the forefoot. Even a casual walk puts enough pressure on the revamped Air Zoom units to engage them. I wouldn’t call it better or worse, just much gentler.

The Alphafly 3, on the other hand, is more responsive: the more force you put into it, the more energy it returns. The Alphafly 4 takes less force to engage but doesn’t snap back as powerfully. I found that made it more comfortable at slower paces. However, when I wanted to run 10K pace or faster, it didn’t pop off the ground like the Alphafly 3 did.

While I didn’t get the chance to race in them or cover 26.2 miles in a single run, my intuition is that the Alphafly 4’s softer ride would shine in the later stages of the marathon when fatigue plays a crucial role in running form and cushioning takes precedence over propulsion. These changes further distinguish the Alphafly from its firmer and more responsive sibling, the Vaporfly 4, which I wouldn’t recommend for anything longer than a 10K for most runners.

One of the biggest improvements in the Alphafly 4 is a much better-fitting, more comfortable upper. The Alphafly 3 was notoriously tight and hard to put on. Some runners said that as their feet swelled during the marathon, the upper became even more uncomfortable. The new AtomKnit upper is much softer and easier to put on. I also found the toe box had much more volume and room to splay, making it an overall more accommodating shoe.

Usually, when I review a shoe, it’s pretty clear to me whether it is a step forward or backward from its predecessor, but the Alphafly 4 has me scratching my head. Maybe I needed more miles in them for a definitive verdict, but it seems to me that they are both really good shoes, just different.

For the marathon, I think the Alphafly 4 will be better for most runners. The fit and upper are more comfortable over the long haul. Underfoot, it’s lighter and provides more cushioning and rebound at slower paces. But for the half marathon and under, I’d want something that’s more responsive and less soft and squishy—like the Vaporfly 4.

#8090. Do Hikers Need an Off-Season? A Burnt-Out Backpacker Makes the Case.

At the end of every racing season, my high school cross-country coach laid down the same strict decree: two full weeks off. No runs, no light jogs, no cheating. I hated the rule. I spent those two weeks pawing at the gates, desperate to keep moving for fear that I’d lose my fitness.

But last month, as I blearily packed my bags for yet another day in the mountains, I found myself wishing more than anything that Coach Stasko would appear on my left shoulder and tell me to take a break. Then, I told myself to snap out of it. It’s just hiking, I reminded myself. Hikers don’t need an off-season.

For many endurance sports, a designated off-season is a crucial time to rest, heal nagging injuries, and give the nervous system a break from the endless cycle of prep and exertion. Most trail running coaches advise their athletes to take two to six weeks off of running at least once per year, especially after completing a demanding objective. Runners often follow that period of total rest with several months of unstructured outdoor time or cross-training. Cyclists and triathletes are known to take even longer—sometimes up to two full months of rest before they start their cross-training. But what about hikers? Does taking long walks through the woods count as an endurance sport?

In 2021, German researchers tested a group of walkers before and after they hiked 60 miles over a 24-hour period. What they found surprised them: the group’s post-hike health markers were similar to those of ultramarathon finishers. Admittedly, that’s a long way to hike in a single day. But those results indicate that periods of low-intensity, long-duration exercise can create muscular and metabolic stresses similar to high-intensity running events. Even if you’re not doing grueling, single-day forced marches, extended hikes leave a lasting impact. Do enough of them, and your recovery plan might need to resemble that of an ultramarathoner, too.

Physical exhaustion isn’t the only thing an off-season break can solve. Like fatigue, mental and emotional stress can be cumulative, and forcing yourself to take structured breaks from a sport gives your brain time to reset. Regular off-seasons are one of the keys to keeping hiking sustainable as a lifelong hobby. Prolonged rest is also one of the most consistently prescribed fixes for athlete burnout—the very thing I was experiencing when I realized that hike prep had begun to inspire more dread than joy.

So, I asked myself a question for the first time since the 12th grade: What would Coach Stasko do? The answer was obvious: he’d take a break. He’d go drive his Mustang and see his friends and update his Facebook page and do all the other things a cool, aging, earringed cross-country coach did. He’d chill out, reconnect with other hobbies, and give his legs all the time they needed.

So, that’s what I did. I confess I didn’t stop hiking entirely, but I did put a moratorium on long hikes above treeline, and I cut the time I spend on my legs each week from four days to just one.

Those changes have made all the difference. Over the last month, I’ve started to feel my stoke come back. Now when I think about hiking, I feel more curious than tired. Which, as far as I’m concerned, is a sign that it’s working.

So, do hikers need time off? Physiologically, it depends on your training load. But mentally, it all depends on you: if you feel like you need a break, you probably do. Here are a few symptoms that could mean it’s time for a proper off-season. If any of these apply to you, it might be time to step back and focus on other things for a while.

#8084. Feline Weird? Decoding Strange Cat Behavior

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Cats can be calm and predictable until, suddenly, they are not. Hiding, acting clingy, making unusual noises, or behaving differently can leave a cat parent wondering what on earth is going on.

Sometimes strange behavior is actually completely normal. In other cases, it can be a sign of stress, discomfort, or illness â context is always important. Looking at what has changed and what else is happening at the same time can help make sense of the behavior.

Not every unusual behavior means something is wrong. Cats can sometimes do things that look strange simply because they are just being cats. And cats can just be weird!

For example, contorting its face into an open-mouthed grimace after sniffing something can look pretty strange. Cats may do this while processing an interesting smell through a special scent-detecting organ in the roof of the mouth.

Other odd-looking behaviors can simply be part of a cat's normal personality or daily routine.

If a cat suddenly starts rolling, flipping, rubbing against things, running around, or behaving much more intensely than usual, catnip could be the reason.

Cats respond to catnip in different ways. Some become energetic and playful, others may become more affectionate or even aggressive, and around 40% of cats will have no reaction at all. The effects are temporary, and cats generally settle down after the initial burst of excitement.

If it is clear that a cat has been playing with or eating catnip, the unusual behavior will usually pass on its own. However, if the behavior continues for much longer than expected or there is a chance the cat got into another plant, it is worth contacting a veterinarian.

Cats can be sensitive to changes in their surroundings. Moving furniture, having visitors, introducing another pet, or changing the household routine can all affect behavior. Even changes happening outside the home, like construction work or animals in the yard, can have a significant effect on an indoor cat.

A cat that suddenly starts hiding, becoming more vocal, avoiding certain areas, or acting unusually clingy may be reacting to a change at home. But itâs important to interpret these behaviors in context. Are they eating, drinking, and going to the toilet normally? Are they avoiding jumping up or down? These clues help determine whether a catâs altered behavior is a reflection of external influences or internal health problems.

Giving a cat time to adjust and keeping its surroundings as familiar as possible can help, but if in doubt, a check-up at the vet to rule out pain or illness is never a bad idea.

Cats can also behave differently after losing another pet or a person they were closely attached to.

A grieving cat may become quieter, hide more, eat differently, or seek more attention. Other cats may seem restless or simply act unlike themselves for a while.

Behavior can vary considerably between cats, so there is no single way that a cat will respond to a loss.

A cat that does not have enough stimulation can also start behaving strangely.

Cats need opportunities to play, explore, scratch, climb, and interact with their surroundings. When those opportunities are limited, boredom can sometimes show up as unusual behavior.

Changes such as increased attention-seeking, destructive behavior, or restlessness may be a sign that a cat needs more enrichment.

Unspayed female cats can behave very strangely when they are in heat. They may become more vocal, affectionate, restless, or determined to get outside. An entire female cat that is acting like sheâs possessed every month likely needs to be spayed.

Male cats can also show changes in behavior when responding to females in heat. This can include increased roaming, vocalizing, or marking behavior.

These changes are related to reproductive behavior and can seem very unusual if they are not expected.

A sudden behavior change can be a sign that a cat is uncomfortable or unwell.

Cats donât always show signs of illness in ways we expect. Instead, they may hide more, become unusually quiet, stop interacting normally, or suddenly become irritable when something is wrong. Changes in eating, drinking, litter box habits, or grooming can also provide important clues.

Fleas and ear mites can make a cat suddenly scratch or shake its head more than usual. Dark material in the ears that resembles coffee grounds can also be a sign of a problem.

Urinary problems can cause changes in litter box behavior, including vocalization, while other health problems may lead to changes in appetite, movement, or energy levels.

Some behaviors are more concerning than others.

Obsessive grooming, circling, head-pressing, bumping into things, or marked lethargy are things that should never be ignored or dismissed as âjust another weird cat behaviorâ.

Seizures donât always look like seizures. They may involve shaking, twitching, drooling, gazing into space, or loss of bladder or bowel control. A cat may also behave unusually around the episode.

A seizure warrants an urgent call to the veterinarian.

Likewise, a cat that suddenly seems very unwell, cannot urinate, has severe difficulty breathing, or shows another dramatic change should be assessed promptly.

When a cat starts acting weird, the behavior itself is only part of the story.

Think about when the change started, whether anything has changed at home, and whether there are other signs such as changes in eating, drinking, grooming, litter box use, or energy.

A strange behavior that quickly disappears and has an obvious harmless explanation may not be cause for concern. But when unusual behavior persists, gets worse, or appears alongside other changes, it is worth speaking with a veterinarian.

#8081. First New Cat Species In A Century – and It Has Been Hiding in Plain Sight

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

It turns out, nature still has a few secrets up her sleeve, and apparently, some of them have whiskers.

You would think that, by now, biologists and taxonomists would have named and identified all animal species on the planet, particularly when it comes to mammals. However, a tiny spotted cat in Bolivia has just pulled off something pretty remarkable: it has officially become a new species.

Meet Leopardus tilcayo, or simply the tilcayo. Scientists have formally recognized it as a species of its own, making it the first newly described living feline in more than a century. The last completely new cat species was described way back in 1923.

And here's the fun part: nobody had to trek into some untouched jungle and stumble across an unknown cat.

This little guy was already living in a wildlife sanctuary.

The story began in 2016, when a young man in Bolivia found a kitten on the road. It was raining, and the little cat was covered in mud. Wanting to help, he took it home, believing it was a domestic cat. After about a year, it became clear that the animal was wild and would be better suited to a sanctuary. The cat was eventually brought to Senda Verde Wildlife Sanctuary in Bolivia's Yungas region.

There, researchers began to realize that this was not quite the cat they thought it was.

The tilcayo belongs to the tiger-cat group, a collection of small spotted wild cats found throughout South America. And honestly, this is one ridiculously cute cat.

With its round face, big eyes, tiny body, and light-brown coat covered in irregular, open rosettes, the tilcayo looks a little like someone shrank a leopard down to smaller than your average house cat. Picture a cat thatâs only about 18 inches (46 centimeters) long and weighs around 3 pounds (1.4 kilograms). Thatâs the tilcayo: tiny enough to make an average house cat look downright chunky by comparison.

It's also easy to see why someone might mistake one for a very unusual-looking kitten.

At the Sanctuary, they assumed it was an oncilla, one of the tiger cats already known to science. But the more closely they looked, the less neatly the cat seemed to fit. When biologist Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz first examined the cat, she agreed.

Its small size and distinctive coat pattern stood out, and when they compared it with other Bolivian wild cats, there were enough differences to warrant a closer look. Turns out, this little face was hiding a pretty big scientific surprise.

The real breakthrough came from genetics, and this is where modern technology gets pretty amazing.

Researchers, including Nogales-Ascarrunz, analyzed the complete genomes of 38 cats from the Leopardus genus, using samples from living animals and specimens preserved in museum collections.1 By comparing their DNA, they could spot differences that aren't always obvious from appearance alone.

Two cats can look remarkably similar and still have very different evolutionary histories. DNA gives scientists another way to see those differences, and in this case, it revealed that what had traditionally been grouped as tiger cats actually represented five distinct species.

The researchers named it Leopardus tilcayo, using the local name for the animal. The genetic evidence suggests that its lineage separated from other tiger cats during the Pleistocene epoch.

In other words, the tilcayo didn't suddenly become a new species when scientists identified it. It had been following its own evolutionary path for around 1.4 million years â around one million years longer than Homo sapiens â ie, humans â have been around.

This is where modern genetic tools are so useful. Researchers can uncover aspects of an animal's history that aren't written on its face or visible in its coat. Even specimens collected decades ago and sitting in museum collections may reveal information scientists couldn't access when they were first collected.

The fact that the tilcayo was initially thought to be a regular house cat reminds us that wild kittens can often be mistaken for their domesticated cousins, but that doesnât make them pets.

A tiny, fluffy, spotted kitten may be irresistibly adorable, like it belongs curled up on the couch with you, but a wild kitten has very different nutritional, behavioral, developmental, and welfare needs than a pet cat. The difference between tame and domesticated is thousands of years of instinct, adaptation, and evolution, and just because it looks cute and cuddly doesnât mean itâs a suitable pet.

Identifying the tilcayo is only the beginning, and there is still much to learn about this little cat.

How many are out there? How far do they roam? What does a typical day look like for a Tilcayo?

One adult male is living at the Senda Verde sanctuary, and researchers have documented the species through camera traps and other evidence from the region. Preliminary evidence suggests that small rodents may be part of its diet, while camera-trap observations suggest the cats may be more active at night.

Now researchers need to find out where the tilcayo lives in the wild, how many there are, what kind of habitat they need, and what pressures they face.

At first, discovering that one group of cats is actually five different species might sound like a technical detail. But picture looking at a map and seeing one large population of tiger cats spread across a huge area. It can make the species look relatively widespread.

Each one may occupy a much smaller area and have a much smaller population than scientists originally thought. A cat that looked widespread on paper may turn out to have a far more limited range.

The Tilcayo's home in Bolivia's Yungas forests already faces deforestation, agriculture, fires, and mining. Researchers have shared their findings with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), which assesses species for its global Red List.

The tilcayo is not automatically considered endangered simply because it is a newly recognized species. Scientists still need to find out how many there are, where they live, and how much suitable habitat remains.

But now they know exactly which cat they are looking for. They can begin mapping its range, studying its population, and keeping track of what happens to the forests it depends on.

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the story is that the tilcayo was never exactly hiding.

People had seen this little cat, given it a local name, and even brought one into human care. What was missing was the scientific recognition that it was its own species. It just took close observation and genetic analysis to reveal that the family tree of South America's tiger cats is a lot more complicated than scientists realized.

The tilcayo may be the first new cat species formally described in more than a century, but it probably won't be the last surprise nature has in store. After all, there could be other animals out there that look familiar, have local names, and have been part of people's lives for generations, while science is still busy playing catch-up.

#8080. Chatting About Toxoplasmosis and Pregnancy, Litters of Kitties, and Surprise Smells | Chatty Cattys, Episode 36

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

In this episode of Catster's Chatty Cattys podcast, Dr. Karyn and Nicole dive deep into the fascinating world of feline biology, human pregnancy, and the common misconceptions surrounding cat breeding. From unpacking the real risks of toxoplasmosis to setting the record straight on why cats don't need to "experience motherhood," they share what it truly means to listen to, understand, and care for our feline companions. Instead of advertising a one-size-fits-all approach to pet parenting, the conversation focuses on the importance of understanding a cat's health and emotional reality. The hosts chat about how separating human emotions from animal instincts leads to responsible pet parenting, proving that forcing a feline into a specific human mold rarely ends well.

Tune in to find out how toxoplasmosis actually spreads and why pregnant cat owners don't need to give up their beloved pets. Dr. Karyn breaks down the medical realities of living with cats while expecting, highlighting simple hygiene measures that keep both mom and baby safe. You will also learn about the misconceptions surrounding animal breeding, including why cats do not experience parental bonding the same way humans do and why allowing a cat to have a litter before spaying is a total myth.

Plus, this episode sheds light on hilarious personal pet stories. You will find out what happened when Dr. Karyn woke up to a stinky middle-of-the-night surprise from her cat, how pets react to growing baby bumps, and why male cats sometimes display surprisingly sweet paternal behaviors toward new kittens!

Toxoplasmosis Realities: Dr. Karyn and Nicole address the fears around toxoplasmosis during human pregnancy, clarifying that while the consequences can be serious, actual transmission from cats is extremely rare and easily prevented with basic hygiene, mask/glove usage, or delegating litter box duties.

Undercooked Meat vs. Litter Boxes: The hosts reveal that humans are actually far more likely to contract toxoplasmosis from eating undercooked meat than from handling cat feces, dispelling the common panic that pregnant women must get rid of their cats.

The "Litter of Kittens" Myth: Dr. Karyn debunks the persistent myth that female cats should have a litter of kittens for health reasons or to "experience being a mother," emphasizing that this is human anthropomorphization rather than biological necessity.

Feline Maternal Instincts vs. Human Bonding: The episode explains that mother cats raise kittens purely driven by hormonal instinct; once kittens are weaned, the familial bond ends, and keeping adult kittens with their mother can often lead to territory disputes or bullying.

Personal Pet Confessions: Dr. Karyn shares a gross, funny story about waking up at 4:00 AM to cat anal gland secretions on her face from her cat sneaking into the bedroom, while Nicole talks about how her dogs and cats have reacted to her growing pregnancy bump.

Male Cats Showing Paternal Traits: The hosts highlight how animal behavior can be unpredictable, sharing a story of a male cat adopting and comforting a new male kitten, proving that maternal care isn't exclusive to female pets.

As a certified cat-lover, Radim was excited to join the Catster team on the mission to help all the cat parents in the world by providing useful and helpful information. He used to live with two wonderful cats before embarking on his travels around the world. Radim currently lives in Slovakia, surrounded by nature and his neighbors' cat community.

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

October 16th has been recognized as National Feral Cat Awareness Day since its creation by Alley Cat Allies in 2001. Here at Catster, we believe it takes more than just one day to make a difference, and thatâs why weâre joining Mission: Meow in campaigning to make October National Feral Cat Awareness Month: a time to learn more about feral and community cats and the challenges they face.

These cats may live outdoors and have limited contact with people, but they are still an important part of many communities and deserve care and compassion.

Feral cats are unsocialized domestic cats who typically avoid close human interaction. Some were born outdoors, while others may have become feral after living without regular human contact. Community cats can also include friendly strays and other free-roaming felines who rely on outdoor resources.

One of the most widely used approaches for managing feral cat populations is trap-neuter-return (TNR). Through TNR programs, cats are humanely trapped, spayed or neutered, vaccinated, and returned to their outdoor homes. This can help prevent litters while allowing cats who arenât comfortable living indoors to remain in familiar surroundings. Through surgical sterilization, TNR reduces feral cat numbers without culling or disrupting cat colonies.

National Feral Cat Awareness Month is also an opportunity to learn how to safely interact with community cats, support local TNR efforts, and recognize when a cat may need additional help.

Catster has compiled its resources on feral cats, TNR, community cat care, and related topics to make it easier to find reliable information and learn more about helping cats living outdoors.

#8074. The Best Nonprofits That Support Dads and Fatherhood

The best nonprofits that support dads and fatherhood.

Research has shown that when dads are engaged and present, kids do better. We celebrate dads on Father’s Day because we should celebrate everything that makes children’s lives — and outcomes — better. When children have close relationships with father figures, they tend to avoid high-risk behaviors; have higher-paying jobs and healthy, stable relationships; and have higher IQ test scores. The benefits go on, but one thing’s for sure: Dads matter in the lives of children, and so we should support and celebrate their presence in their kids’ lives.

Here are just a few organizations that champion dads and understand the integral role that fathers play in the lives of their children.

All Pro Dad is a program of Family First that provides tools and resources to dads that allow them to be more present in the lives of their children. Spearheaded by former NFL coach Tony Dungy, NFL player Benjamin Watson, ESPN personality Dan Orlovsky, and many other prominent sports figures, All Pro Dad hosts a yearly interactive get-together for kids and dads at an NFL or NCAA stadium and a monthly school program where dads meet up with their children at school to spend time bonding and relationship building.

The Center for Family Policy and Practice is a nonprofit organization that advocates for fair and equitable laws and policies that affect low-income families and fathers. Focusing on child support, family safety and security, and financial and economic security, the CFPP acts as a think tank to develop solutions to barriers experienced by low-income fathers and fathers of color.

The Child & Family Blog provides research-driven content on the impact of family on social, emotional, and cognitive child development. In addition to covering topics like race, divorce, and inequality, the Child & Family Blog covers research on the importance of fathers and the role they play in both the family dynamic and the development of children.

The Family Equality Council works to ensure that members of the LGBTQ community have the ability to create families and provide support, education, activism and advocacy, and the resources they need to become parents and foster loving, healthy family relationships. The FEP also tracks national and state legislation that affects the ability of LGBTQ couples to become parents and maintain parental rights.

Fathering Together provides anyone who identifies as a father with tools and resources to uplift and support them as they work to create a “more equitable society.” The organization hosts different communities so that dads from every walk of life can reach out to peers for help, support, and advice while working to make the world a better and safer place for their children.

The Fatherhood Project is a Massachusetts-based program that empowers fathers to become more “knowledgeable, active, and emotionally engaged with their children.” Through research-based principles and curricula and programs like Dads Matter, Dads in Recovery, Teen Dads, and Divorcing Dads, the organization aims to help all dads be more present and engaged with their children while focusing on dads in marginalized and underserved communities.

Fathers Incorporated is an Atlanta-based nonprofit that works with federal lawmakers and leaders in the responsible fatherhood movement, faith and business leaders, and family law practitioners to advocate for legislative and community changes that promote fathers’ involvement in the lives of their children. The group focuses on co-parenting, domestic violence, incarceration, child development, child support, and employment and financial stability. Fathers Incorporated provides resources and programs for fathers to engage with their children healthily and raise awareness through programs like the Million Fathers March and Black Dads Count.

Fathers’ Uplift is a one-of-a-kind organization that provides fathers with the tools they need to overcome trauma, addiction, racial barriers, and emotional issues to help them fully engage with their children and families. Fathers’ Uplift provides therapy, coaching, training opportunities, and youth enrichment with the aim of reducing the number of children raised without positive father figures in their lives. It is the only organization in the United States that offers therapy, counseling, and addiction support specifically geared toward fathers and their families with the aim of reuniting families and providing them with the framework to thrive.

The National Fatherhood Initiative is the country’s largest provider of research on the involvement of fathers and the impact fathers have on families. It provides communities with resources and training to increase father engagement with the goal of ensuring that communities and human service organizations have the tools and training they need to be father-inclusive so fathers can be more involved in the lives of their children.

The Native American Fatherhood and Families Association is an Arizona-based nonprofit focusing on nourishing family relationships through its Fatherhood Is Sacred/Motherhood Is Sacred (FIS/MIS), Linking Generations by Strengthening Relationships, and Addressing Family Violence & Abuse programs. Employing culturally sensitive curricula and materials, NAFFA is able to address the specific concerns of the Native American community to reunite families and empower fathers to become family leaders.

The National Partnership for Women and Families understands that families benefit when dads are present and actively engaged. One way the NPWF is creating a more equitable world for women is by spearheading programs, legislation, and calls to action that support fathers by promoting active fatherhood and gender equality.

Established in Brazil in 1997, Promundo has worked globally to engage fathers in the care economy, promote active fatherhood and promote gender equity and justice by engaging men and boys with women and girls. The organization is currently undergoing a rebranding to be more inclusive of all genders. Its new name, Equimundo: Center for Masculinities and Social Justice, “reflects our commitment to fostering gender equity and our roots in social justice. The name change also captures our approach of collaborating with and never overshadowing our diverse partners worldwide.”

This article was originally published on June 7, 2022

#8072. The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era. At one time, men preferred “Sire.” Other times, “Father” was preferable. What we do know is that the most agreed-upon way to refer to dad these days is by calling him, well, ‘dad.’

But why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad? The short answer is that things have gotten a little less formal. But the reason we’ve moved away from formality is that we’ve embraced what’s more linguistically natural for children and parents. ‘Father’ comes from the Proto-Indo-European “pəter” and Old English ‘fæder,’ meaning “he who begets a child,” reflecting the baby-talk sound “pa” as well as a phonetic shift from ‘p’ to ‘f’ in Middle English.

However, ‘dad’ did not evolve from ‘father.’

“It’s from ‘dada,’” says Professor John H. McWhorter, a professor at Columbia University, “a natural sound from children’s mouths as a second stab at consonants after they try the most natural ‘mama.’ Next is often either ‘dada, ‘tata,’ ‘baba’ or … ‘papa.’ Upon which, ‘father’ starts in Proto-Indo-European as “puh-TAIR,” and the ‘puh’ part is this same thing: what started as ‘pa’ in ‘papa.’ The words for Mommy and Daddy are the closest thing to linguistic universals because they are about mouth anatomy in infants rather than thought.”

There are also another key reason why this is reinforced over time. Emie Tittnich, a specialist at the University of Pittsburgh, speaking to Live Science, noted that parents generally refrain from using pronouns like ‘I’ or ‘you’ to avoid confusing their kids with abstract concepts early on. “‘Parents will use [‘mommy’ and ‘daddy’] to help their children learn the role names and also to indicate the relationship, ‘mommy and me,'” says Tittnich. “It usually takes the child awhile to understand that the same person can be called two different names.”

The agreed-upon naturality of these linguistic principles mean that as American society has become more colloquial and secular over time, we move (at least in this instance) away from a term that’s reflective of a status quo based in rigid concepts of class and religion—one of the meanings of ‘fæder’ in Old English is ‘supreme being,’ according to the Online Etymology Dictionary. As a result, we’re generally caught off guard when we hear a child refer to a parent as ‘father.’

However, this is not the case unanimously. We spoke with six dads who prefer — or simply stuck with — ‘father’ instead of ‘dad.’ Some do it as an homage to their own fathers; others do it to sound more authoritative. Others do it because it’s what their kids like. All have their reasons and, maybe, deep inside, some are just big fans of Proto-Indo-European language. Here’s what they say.

I sometimes worry that it sounds a little austere out loud, but it’s just what my father always asked us to call him, and it felt like it was important to me that we carry that on. No one in my family has had a problem with it. I think you can still be a ‘dad’ and be called ‘father,’ if that makes sense. It’s basically semantic, in that way, but it’s also more than semantics. — John, Baltimore, MD

It’s less of a request or a demand or anything, but when we were teaching my oldest what everything is called, we always just said ‘this is your mother’ and ‘this is your father,’ and he liked to say that, too. So we’ve kept it. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t think it was just adorably proper to have our little man coming up to us and saying, “father, mother, may I use the bathroom,” or what have you. But as with everything, I don’t mind anything that seems to feel natural for my kids and makes them happy. — Eric, Austin, Texas

My son didn’t start until he was older. I think he thought it sounded more respectful, or just more professional. We’ve always been a more traditional family, in how we carry ourselves, I guess you would say. So perhaps this was his way of taking that in stride, or contributing to that. My wife teases me about it sometimes. I should clarify, it’s generally him introducing me to other people that way. ‘This is my father, have you met my father?’ etc. — Patrick, Twin Cities, MN

In the past two years, my older daughter, age 21, began calling me ‘father’ and as strange as I found it, I didn’t mine it at all. Now, my four-year-old calls me “father” and I guess I now have a new title. As long as I am not being called ‘Henry,’ I am okay with it. — Henry, Boston, MA

I have eight children—three boys and five girls. I’ve always asked that they call me ‘father’ not to be domineering but because the house could get a little chaotic, as you can imagine, and my wife and I felt that it was a label that was more authoritative and kept things from being too chaotic. ‘Please don’t touch your father’s golf clubs’ just has a better ring to it, I guess. — Elliott, Charlotte, NC

I love that my children call me ‘father,’ because of the sense of responsibility it instills in me. Your ‘dad’ or ‘daddy’ is there to lend you the car, your ‘father’ is there to raise you, and protect you and make sure that you have the tool you need to succeed in life. When my kids call me ‘father,’ it reignites that sense of purpose for me every day, and reminds me it’s up to me to make their world a great place to grow up in. — Sam, Alachua Country, FL

#8070. 8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

Katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite shows for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

You’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

A little online searching will quickly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

Tired of the practically impossible task of packing up the family for a holiday? Here are the best packing cubes for busy families on the go.

For many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

When it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to plan. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

Unleash your little one's love for Lightning McQueen with these top-rated Cars playsets and figures.

As tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:

Of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a big decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

What are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a big factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

The umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!)

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

When you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

The charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or shows, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

The stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Traveling with kids doesn't;t have to mean getting rid of your entire beauty routine.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

These wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

My family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

They come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

The fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

The stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Could your child use a little encouragement to read? Disney is here to help with these fabulous books for kids ages 5 to 9.

Take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!
