Looking for a more understated way to decorate for Christmas? Michelle Obama's minimalist twig-tree look is all the inspiration you need – and you can recreate it at home using branches from your own garden.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Decorating for the holidays doesn't always have to mean a towering evergreen, baubles in every colour and tinsel from floor to ceiling. Sometimes, the simplest ideas make the biggest impact, and Michelle Obama's understated twig tree look is well and truly proof of this!

There is something magical about using natural shapes and soft lighting to create an elegant display, isn't there? And, while a Christmas tree is very much an 'only for December' kind of vibe, the Obamas' approach of using illuminated branches offers a more pared-back alternative, with a gentle glow that can work well beyond the festive season.

It's a look that feels particularly suited to anyone who prefers a more minimalist Christmas, or who wants to introduce a little seasonal magic without buying another large decoration that will spend most of the year in storage. Check it out if you don't believe me:

A post shared by Michelle Obama (@michelleobama)

Love it? The good news is that you don't necessarily need to buy a ready-made twig tree to achieve a similar effect. In fact, with a few suitable branches from your garden, a sturdy vase and a string of delicate LED fairy lights, you can create your own version of Michelle Obama's holiday display for a fraction of the cost.

It's a lovely way to make use of branches left over from routine pruning, giving them a second life as part of your Christmas decorating. And, brilliantly, it's one of the simplest DIY projects going! All you have to do is choose branches with interesting shapes, arrange them so they form a loose, tree-like silhouette, and add lights sparingly enough that the natural structure remains the star of the show.

You don't need specialist crafting skills to recreate Michelle Obama's holiday look. The most important things are choosing branches with an appealing shape and making sure your finished arrangement is stable.

Whether you leave the finished display unadorned or add a handful of small ornaments, this easy DIY is a beautiful way to bring the outdoors in for the holidays.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

With that in mind, then, let's get our Michelle Obama on...

Start by looking for branches with plenty of natural character. A mixture of upright stems and smaller offshoots will give your display a fuller (aka more tree-like) shape, while branches with interesting curves can add a sculptural quality.

You can use fallen branches or suitable cuttings from routine garden pruning. If cutting from a living shrub or tree, make sure you're pruning at an appropriate time and in a way that won't damage the plant. Avoid brittle, rotten or diseased wood, and check branches for insects before bringing them indoors.

Choose a vase or planter with a wide and heavy base to help prevent your tree from tipping over. Position the tallest branches towards the centre and arrange the shorter ones around them, allowing the natural shapes to spread out.

Add small stones or pebbles around the base of the branches to help hold them in place. And take care to step back occasionally to check the overall silhouette, adjusting the stems until the arrangement feels balanced without looking too uniform.

This is where the magic happens. Wrap your LED fairy lights loosely around the branches, starting near the base and working towards the outer stems. Try to distribute the lights evenly, rather than clustering them in one area.

Warm white lights will give the arrangement a soft, inviting glow, while a more delicate micro-LED string can create a subtle, almost starry effect. Battery-operated lights can also be useful if you want to position your display somewhere without a nearby socket.

Shop Fairy Lights For Your DIY Twig Tree:

The trick to nailing that MIchelle Obama look is to make sure you pick some with a flexible wire that is easy to wind around smaller branches. Take care, too, to check that the length is sufficient for the size of your arrangement.

A timer function is a useful extra if you'd like your tree to illuminate automatically in the evenings.

One of the best things about Michelle Obama's holiday display is that it doesn't need much embellishment; you can leave the branches bare apart from the lights for a minimalist finish, or add a few small ornaments if you prefer something more traditionally festive.

A restrained palette of white, silver or muted gold will complement the natural wood without making the display feel too busy. Alternatively, a simple velvet ribbon tied around the vase can introduce a little texture without distracting from the branches.

Once your arrangement is finished, place it somewhere it can be appreciated after dark, and take care to position it on a level surface, away from candles, fireplaces and other sources of heat.

The beauty of this Michelle Obama-inspired DIY is that it doesn't have to disappear as soon as Christmas is over. If you keep the decorations minimal, your illuminated branches can continue to bring a soft glow to your home throughout the winter – and beyond.

#8053. 15 Essential Chapter Books For Elementary School Kids

These new and classic chapter books invite your young ones into complex worlds that they can understand.

There is a special joy a parent gets when watching their child fall in love with a book, but whether you’re browsing your local library, walking through your favorite bookstore, or scrolling through a seemingly endless list of titles online, helping your child find the perfect read can be a daunting task.

But it’s an important one, especially when children are transitioning from picture books to chapter books. With most reaching at least a hundred pages, the right chapter book can not only entertain, but also build up a young reader’s reading endurance — and even their patience. Just as adults are drawn to watching “just one more episode” of their favorite binge-watchable television series, the right chapter book, especially ones with cliffhangers at the ends of chapters, can have your child begging to stay up late to read “just one more chapter.”

And wouldn’t it be great if that book were one that you and your child could enjoy reading together? Whether it’s a graphic novel, a light and silly read, a fantasy with larger-than-life characters and situations, or a story firmly grounded in reality, the right chapter book will have parents just as hooked as their children, creating the perfect bonding experience, especially as kids head back to school.

It may be tempting to suggest an “old reliable” book to your kid. After all, they’re reliable for a reason. But while there is a long list of children’s tales that are still beloved by many — from true classics like L. Frank Baum’s The Wonderful Wizard of Oz and Lewis Carroll’s Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland to comparatively newer titles, such as the works of Roald Dahl (Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Matilda) and Louis Sacher’s Sideways Stories From Wayside School — new books are released each year that seem poised to become classics in their own right, captivating and sparking the imagination of today’s kids.

If you’re feeling overwhelmed by the quantity of books currently on the market, have no idea what kids are reading these days, or are just looking to introduce your child — and yourself — to something new, Fatherly has curated a list of 15 chapter books that were released within the last 10 years, broken down into different age ranges and across different genres, that will become treasured favorites once added to your child’s home library.

Most kids have stepped foot in an elementary school, but how many have spent time in one constantly being threatened by ghosts? Hopefully not too many, but young readers will get a kick out of the Eerie Elementary series, where nearly everyone is in danger at school all the time, and it’s up to a small group of kids to save them through clever problem-solving. While The School Is Alive! is written in an age-appropriate way, it may be a little scary for kids who are prone to being fearful. You know your children best, but most early readers will enjoy having a few mild frights.

This charming story of two unlikely pen pals, a giraffe and penguin, is a great way for children to learn that animals — or, even better yet, people — who look different and come from different parts of the world can still find a lot that they have in common. The narrative unfolds not only through narration and illustrations, but also the correspondence between the animals, making for a fun reading experience. At just over a hundred pages and fewer than 10 chapters, Yours Sincerely, Giraffe is an excellent book for elementary school-aged children and beginning readers looking to build their endurance. Also, don’t miss Megumi Iwasa’s follow-up, Dear Professor Whale, another story of two animals who develop a close long distance friendship.

Jacqueline Jules’ expansive Sofia Martinez series offers excellent reads for all early elementary school-aged kids, but they will especially be embraced by those within the Latinx community. My Family Adventure, the first book in the lineup, centers on Sofia, a 7-year-old with two older sisters, who is eager to stand out and do things her way. Young children will enjoy reading about a character who is among the youngest in her family and who gets in all sorts of fun situations. Sofia’s immediate and extended family dynamics are quite beautiful to see play out, and the series also wonderfully includes common Spanish words and phrases into the narrative for authenticity, with a glossary provided to non-Spanish speakers.

The creator of Captain Underpants returns with a graphic novel book series centered on Dog Man, who, as the name suggests, is part dog, part man, and all hero! He’s also the faithful companion of a not-too-bright police officer, whom Dog Man helps solve problems in creative ways. Like Dav Pilkey’s other works, readers can expect broad humor and story elements that will elicit genuine laughs from your children. This is a great story about loyalty, friendship, and the importance of outside-the-box thinking. While kids may be interested in skipping the author’s note, it’s worth taking a moment to read it with your child, as Pilkey explains how his early struggles with dyslexia ultimately led to his career as a writer. It’s an inspiring bit of personal history that should remind kids that challenges do not have to be permanent barriers to success.

It’s understandable why some kids may not enjoy reading period pieces, but it’s hard to imagine any child not being immediately gripped by author and illustrator Brian Selznick’s beautifully and creatively told story of Hugo Cabret, a young orphan in 1930s Paris who has inherited his family’s interest and skill in all things mechanical. Selznick’s superpower is moving the story forward and deepening our understanding of the characters through his illustrations. Sections of the book are told without words, just as portions of a motion picture might be played out without dialogue, making this an accessible book for readers for lower-level and/or younger readers, while still being a stylistically interesting read that will appeal to older kids and more seasoned readers as well.

This fantasy-adventure story is perfect for kids with vivid imaginations who love fantasy and are often swept away by films like How to Train Your Dragon. While there are plenty of age-appropriate battle sequences, Rise of the Earth Dragon’s greatest strength lies in how the book subtly teaches kids about how to communicate effectively with others and draw on the strength of your friends. Tracey West’s Dragon Masters series is a great entry point for kids who are just starting to explore chapter books, as the vocabulary and storytelling won’t pose too much of a challenge for most early readers.

A gripping, first-person narrative told through the perspective of Ivan, a gorilla that has been held captive for 27 years. Ivan is blissfully unaware of his figurative shackles until he meets and befriends Ruby, a baby elephant recently taken from the wild who changes his world view. It’s easy for young readers to fall in love with the vivid, albeit contained, world that Ivan paints, and adults will enjoy the clear literary kinship between Applegate’s novel and classics like E.B. White’s Charlotte’s Web and Stuart Little. Kids who have trouble parting with the characters they love will enjoy learning that The One and Only Ivan is the first book in a series, and has been recently adapted into a film currently streaming on Disney Plus. This beautiful tale of friendship and possibilities is perfect for kids in upper elementary and early middle school grades.

Summer reading can often feel like a chore, but Lamar Giles’s The Last Last-Day-of-Summer is just the book parents need to get their kids away from the screen and into a book. This quirky sci-fi adventure follows Otto and Sheed, two young Black male cousins, who are working to solve a mystery while traveling through time. The first in the Legendary Alston Boys series, this book’s exciting and funny time-bending narrative makes it the right read for kids — and parents — who enjoy Phineas and Ferb. Children without siblings, and/or kids who have strong bonds with their cousins, will also enjoy seeing Otto and Sheeds’ brotherly relationship unfold.

Archie Morningstar is an 8-year-old boy with a talking cat who stays up past his bedtime to fight crime around the cosmos. We bet you’re intrigued, and your kids will be too! This debut in the Space Taxi series kicks off on “Take Your Kid to Work Day,” when our young hero learns that his dad drives aliens around in a taxi throughout outer space in the twilight hours. This fast paced sci-fi adventure story is filled with humor and, as you might expect from a story centered among the stars, a fair amount of educational information sprinkled throughout. This is a zippy and exciting read for second- through fourth-graders.

Readers who have enjoyed following the adventures of Rafe, the main character in James Patterson’s best-selling Middle School series, will get a real kick out of becoming better acquainted with Junior, Rafe’s faithful canine companion. This spinoff is told through Junior’s perspective, providing a new way to see a well-established literary world. Parents should be warned that there is some animal potty humor — after all, dogs will be dogs, and as all pet owners know, butt sniffs and peeing in the house comes with the territory — but this is a fun, and often silly, story of friendship and loyalty, proving that dog’s really are humans’ best friends.

Representation matters in all forms, and My Pet Slime is a fun read for all kids in upper elementary grades — but especially for those who have allergies. The first book in Courtney Sheinmel’s series centers on Piper, a young girl who wishes she could have a pet. The problem, unfortunately, is that she’s allergic to just about everything. However, thanks to a little literary magic, she ends up becoming the owner of a pet out of slime that has come to life. With bright, colorful illustrations and a wonderful premise, My Pet Slime will resonate with your kids and even teach them a thing or two about caring for a pet in the process.

This fast-paced and funny graphic adventure novel is a great fit for kids in upper elementary school grades. The Boy Who Crashed to Earth is the first in a series centering on Hilo, a seemingly normal kid who is anything but normal — and anything but what he seems to be. The vividly and boldly illustrated book captures larger-than-life moments, like Hilo, who heralds from outer space, battling large robots, with all the excitement they deserve. With a visual and narrative style that seems ready to adapt for an animated show on Nickelodeon, the stories of Hilo and his diverse and well-rounded group of friends will capture the attention of even the most reluctant of readers.

Even though your middle schoolers might feel too old for fairy tales, they will love The School for Good and Evil, Soman Chainini’s fresh take on the stories your children grew up loving. Like most fantasy stories, and most fairy tales, there is quite a bit of peril, violence, and some mild romance. It’s always fun when readers think they can predict what is going to happen next in a story, only to find out that their expectations have been used against them, and The School for Good and Evil delivers on that front in spades.

Some parents may find it difficult to discuss race with their children, but Sharon M. Draper’s Blended does an excellent job of introducing what could be challenging topics in a compelling narrative. The story centers on Isabella, an 11-year-old biracial girl who feels caught between her divorcing parents. Throughout Blended, Isabella encounters several microaggressions — intentional and/or unintentional insults about her race and gender — that end up having an impact on her self-esteem and shifting the way she sees the world. As it’s common for children in upper elementary and middle school grades to feel out of place, Blended provides a mirror for some kids to see themselves in an ultimately uplifting piece of realistic fiction. Parents should be advised that there are some mature themes, like a shooting and police brutality, but everything is presented in an age-appropriate way that will keep your kids glued to the book to find out what happens next.

If your middle schooler has fallen out of love with reading, or is itching for books that feel less kiddie books, then Ghost, the first in Jason Reynolds’ four-part Track series may be perfect for them. It’s a gripping coming-of-age story of Castle Cranshaw, nicknamed “Ghost,” who seems destined to be the star of his middle school track team, if only he could outrun his trauma brought about by a toxic and abusive parent first. While Ghost is somewhat mature in its themes, and — mild spoiler alert! — its unresolved ending will frustrate some, it’s a page-turning story of friendship and overcoming, or perhaps, outrunning, one’s obstacles.

This article was originally published on July 24, 2023

#8052. Book-To-Screen Adaptations Coming In 2027 That Are Worth The Read First

If you just can’t wait to learn the endings... you don’t have to.

Lately it feels like we’re getting all kinds of exciting new casting announcements, from the two leads in the screen adaptation of Rebecca Yarros’ Fourth Wing to Florence Pugh fronting the movie adaptation of Matt Haig’s The Midnight Library. But for now, those projects have release dates of “TBD.” So what incredible books will we get to see play out on the big screen in the near future? Here are all the best book-to-screen adaptations coming in 2027, so you can read the book beforehand if that’s your jam.

Author Tomi Adeyemi’s rich storytelling will come alive just two weeks into the New Year, when her novel Children of Blood and Bone comes to theaters and IMAX. The film will star Thuso Mbedu as Zélie, Damson Idris, Amandla Stenberg, Regina King, Cynthia Erivo, Idris Elba, and the incredible Viola Davis, to name just a portion of the cast.

There are three books in Adeyemi’s Legends of Orïsha triology, all available now, if you want to read through to the end between now and mid-January.

If you have Apple TV, you’ll want to start Neuromancer when it drops on Jan. 22. Based on William Gibson’s sci-fi cyberpunk novel published in 1984, the 10-episode series will follow Case, a hacker-slash-hustler, and Molly, a cyborg mercenary, through a dangerous heist that will pit them against AI (timely), massive corporations, and all the powers-that-be.

Greta Gerwig’s take on Narnia is coming and it can’t get here soon enough, TBH. Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew is based on the 1955 novel The Magician’s Nephew by C.S. Lewis, the sixth published (but first in the timeline of the story) novel in the children’s series The Chronicles of Narnia.

This movie is getting a true theatrical release in February, then hitting Netflix to stream at home on April 2, 2027. Either way, we can’t wait to see Meryl Streep and Daniel Craig in these magical roles.

Feb. 12 is going to be a big day at the box offices. In Kristen Hannah’s novel by the same name, she captures the story of World War II from the perspective of two sisters, who will no doubt be played beautifully by actual sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning. Go into this theater armed with tissues, and read Hannah’s book now if you’d like to know why.

Spoiler alert! At the end of Season 1, Shane and Ilya’s relationship is revealed, setting up the central tension of Season 2. What will the fallout be, and how will the pair weather it together? All we’ll say is that apparently “intimacy rehearsals” are well underway...

While a more specific release date hasn’t been announced yet, if you’d like to read ahead, Season 2 of the show is based on The Long Game, which is Book 6 in author Rachel Reid’s Game Changers series.

A summer read turned summer blockbuster? We’re here for it. Starring Phoebe Dynevor and Patrick Schwarzenegger as January and Gus, we get to watch these two authors who have no business falling in love do exactly that. The rest of the cast seems stellar too: think Andie MacDowell, Kristin Davis, Tig Notaro, and Kevin Bacon.

Parents often lament that kids don’t come with instruction manuals. This isn’t to say there’s a lack of guidance available for those wanting to refine their parenting skills. As far back as 1946, when American pediatrician Benjamin Spock’s The Common Sense Book of Baby and Child Care sold 500,000 copies in its first six months of publication, the parenting book industrial complex has been humming right along.

As the school year gets ready to kick off, many parents will be looking for a helpful read as they start a post-summer reset. With so many options to sort through, we’ve hand-picked nine essential parenting books that provide cutting-edge insights across an array of topics — without talking down to parents.

At the beginning of A Place to Belong, Amber O’Neal Johnston challenges parents to embrace self-interrogation in the pursuit of inclusivity. She fully acknowledges the intentionality and hard work that are required to cultivate a truly inclusive home, but she also captures the real urgency of this particular moment in history, if we want to start undoing the toxic effects of divisiveness and injustice.

Johnston lays out a compelling blueprint in A Place to Belong for how to help kids grow in self-acceptance and radical inclusivity. She includes examining family culture, acknowledging the challenges and injustices other cultures face, and evaluating the literary and media lenses parents provide through which their kids then interpret the world around them. And she’s a passionate proponent for parents normalizing difficult conversations with their kids.

While it’s a message delivered with grace, Johnston’s call to inclusivity isn’t an easy task to adopt. But she’s tread the road with her family, and gives a clear-eyed view of how she came to the realization that accepting such an undertaking was preferable to accepting the alternative.

There’s no shame in parents wanting what’s best for their kids. Where things tend to go off the rails is when parents take too intense of a hands-on approach to every aspect of their child’s lives, stunting their capacity for independence and problem-solving.

But parents who want to foster independent kids need to rely on more than their gut feelings to discern appropriate levels of parental support. Stixrud and Johnson offer insights from research to give parents evidence-based strategies for raising resilient kids who don’t fear failure and provide practical advice to help address the roots of childhood anxiety.

Real talk. Parenting can feel like such a high-stakes endeavor at times, and when it does it can absolutely suck the joy out of parents and kids alike. Sociologist Janice Johnson Dias, Ph.D., understands that reality and sets out in Parent Like It Matters to help parents cultivate joy in their daughters without lowering the expectation that they can create sustainable social change.

Dias bolsters autobiographical storytelling and insights from academic research with assignments at the end of each chapter that provide a roadmap for parents to better care for themselves, get to know their daughters more fully, and raise girls who are purposeful, courageous and joyful.

Are you ever afraid of how judgy other parents would get if they knew how often you lost it with your kids — or how much energy you burn to keep yourself from losing it with your kids? Well, chances are, you’re not alone. Which doesn’t mean that parents shouldn’t strive to become more patient, but it does suggest we’d all be better off if we were honest about how hard it can be to keep our cool.

Naumberg gives voice to these struggles with an honest hilarity to help parents break the shame cycle of feeling like a failure whenever they can’t conjure the patience necessary to keep a compassionate poker face when their kids are driving them nuts. It’s a disarming — though also direct and to-the-point — approach that provides parents the space to identify their triggers and make a plan for avoiding and diffusing them.

Tina Payne Bryson and Daniel Siegel have released dozens of helpful books, articles, and Ted Talks since the release of The Whole Brain Child, at their latest book is particularly relevant in that it explains how parents can be more present in an increasingly distracted world. It’s also strikingly reassuring in its emphasis that parenting mistakes and missteps are repairable and that it’s never too late to regain your child’s trust and help them develop emotional intelligence.

#8050. 47 Cozy Fall Movies To Cue Up After Your Annual 'You’ve Got Mail' Rewatch

Grab your favorite nubby blanket and light a candle. These comfort watches hit that sweet sweater-weather spot.

It’s become a ritual for me: Every October, without fail, I put on You’ve Got Mail. It’s almost a seasonal reflex, like buying every pumpkin-spice-flavored product at Trader Joe’s. Between Kathleen Kelly’s quaint little bookshop and Joe Fox’s bouquet of newly sharpened pencils, it makes me sink right into the season. It’s the cinematic equivalent of a cable-knit sweater.

But the fall is long, and a girl cannot sustain herself on one movie alone (she’s tried, trust me). So, for those of us who’ve already knocked out our annual rewatch (or two, or three), here are a bunch of other cozy fall movies to snuggle up with. From the Nora Ephron extended universe and bookish period pieces to the movies that somehow make Thanksgiving chaos look like something you actually want to revisit each year, these cozy fall movies have you covered.

The OG! You’ve Got Mail is a remake of this Ernst Lubitsch classic, with Jimmy Stewart and Margaret Sullavan as bickering coworkers in a Budapest shop who are (you guessed it) secretly each other’s anonymous pen pals.

Nora Ephron wrote it, and Meg Ryan and Billy Crystal made it iconic. I mean, the Central Park autumn montage?! The cutesy “Waiter, there is too much pepper on my paprikash” moment. Cozycore all the way. Plus, you get the salad scene (yes, yes, yes) and a great “can men and women really just be friends” debate built in.

Ah, let’s travel back in time to the first Hanks-Ryan pairing under Ephron’s direction. Sure, this is technically more of a winter-into-Valentine’s watch, but I’d argue it still belongs in any comfort rotation that includes You’ve Got Mail.

Ephron’s final film on the list pairs Meryl Streep in top form as Julia Child with Amy Adams, also in top form, as a blogger cooking her way through Mastering the Art of French Cooking. Did I mention Stanley Tucci plays Julia’s beloved husband Paul? Perfection. Just watch it with snacks or you’ll be making boeuf bourguignon at 10 p.m.

Not Ephron, but pure peak-Meg: She plays a stressed-out New York marketing exec who, oopsie, falls for a 19th-century duke (played by Hugh Jackman, in waistcoats) who’s tumbled through time. Is it ridiculous? Obviously. Is it delightful? Also obviously.

Both versions work, but I really enjoyed Greta Gerwig’s version. It’s basically a warm hug in a bonnet! It’s got Saoirse Ronan as Jo, Emma Watson as Meg, Florence Pugh as Amy, Eliza Scanlen as Beth, Laura Dern as Marmee, Meryl Streep as Aunt March, and enough Massachusetts autumn to make you want to up and move to Concord.

The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society (2018)

Lily James plays a writer in post-WWII London who starts corresponding with a quirky book club on a tiny English Channel Island as she pursues a new book idea. She ends up bonding deeply with the islanders... and learning a lot about, well, a lot along the way.

Misty fields. Long coats. The hand flex. You know what I’m talking about. Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen made this moody-weather Austen adaptation the one to beat.

Some may argue this is at times too sad to be a cozy movie, but who made that rule? I think sadness and coziness can be two sides of the same coin. Here, Julia Roberts plays a progressive art history professor at 1950s Wellesley, with Julia Stiles, Kristen Dunst, Maggie Gyllenhaal, and Ginnifer Goodwin as her students. It’s got peak fall academia vibes thanks to plenty of plaid skirts, brick buildings, and falling leaves.

For 40 years, Big Mama kept her Chicago family together with one rule: Sunday dinner, no exceptions. But when she gets sick and her three grown daughters — played by Vivica A. Fox, Vanessa Williams, and Nia Long — have to step in and keep the family together, things get... sticky. It’s got big feelings and even bigger plates.

Jodie Foster directed this underrated gem starring Holly Hunter as a woman who loses her job and flies to her parents’ home in Baltimore for Thanksgiving with her incredibly chaotic family. The ‘90s cynicism is strong with this one, so be aware of that going in. But also: Robert Downey Jr. steals every scene he’s in.

If you’ve ever felt like the black sheep in your family, you’ll definitely relate to Katie Holmes’ title character as she tries to host Thanksgiving in her tiny NYC apartment... when her oven dies. It’s funny, it’s tender, and it’s very real if you’ve ever tried to impress your hard-to-impress family.

Can you really get any more classic than this? Steve Martin and John Candy are just trying to get home for Thanksgiving, but make it an unhinged buddy-comedy road trip movie. It has a way of hitting even harder once you’re the one in the family booking the holiday travel.

Remember my previous note that being a sad movie and being a comfort movie are not mutually exclusive? Here’s another one in that category. Steve Carell is a widowed advice columnist who falls for a woman (Juliette Binoche) during a fall family weekend in Rhode Island... only to learn she’s dating his brother. He’s definitely going through it, but it’s Carell so his suffering is naturally also comedic. Add in a big family house, board games, touch football, and it’s extremely cozy.

This one’s a two-fer on the coziness scale because you get an idyllic Connecticut town and plenty of drool-worthy food scenes. The movie follows three waitresses (played by Julia Roberts, Annabeth Gish, and Lili Taylor) who spend one last summer-into-fall figuring out what comes next in life and love, all while slinging the town’s famous secret-sauce pizza.

Is this the ultimate whodunit for sweater weather? It certainly feels like a contender. It’s really a recipe for cozy mystery success when you throw together a dead patriarch, a sprawling New England mansion, Daniel Craig’s Southern-fried detective, and Chris Evans in cable-knit.

Robin Williams gave us one of the most memorable mentors of all time with John Keating, an unconventional English teacher at a stuffy 1950s Vermont prep school. It’s tweed blazers and reading poetry in caves and crisp autumn walks. Fair warning: It’s a tearjerker, and you’ll forevermore get misty-eyed whenever you hear “O Captain! My Captain!”

Yep, another sad-but-oh-so-life-affirming Robin Williams movie to add to your fall rotation. Here, Matt Damon plays a South Boston janitor at MIT who happens to also be a math genius. Williams plays the therapist who finally gets through to him (and, let’s be real, to all of us). Come for the Boston accents and the Southie bar scenes; stay for the “it’s not your fault” scene that’ll wreck you.

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom (2026)

Aardman’s flock is back, and this time (for the first time) it’s Halloween! When the clumsy Farmer wrecks the sheep’s prized pumpkin patch, Shaun goes all mad scientist trying to fix it. It unsurprisingly spirals from there and, before you know it, a hair beast is roaming the woods. This creature-feature parody may be new, but I'd be shocked if it didn't earn classic status.

Wes Anderson’s stop-motion adaptation of the Roald Dahl book is literally so fall-coded — it’s all oranges, browns, and golds! The kids will love it, but so will the adults in the room. George Clooney even voices the title fox.

Our sweet Paddington, you’ve always been a bringer of cozy vibes. Give me all the marmalade and pop-up books and, yes, even Hugh Grant as a gloriously vain villain. Everyone in the family will be a fan of this sweet pick.

Food is comfort, and comfort is cozy, therefore Ratatouille is cozy comfort at its finest (and Pixar at its most heartwarming). It’ll make even the adults watching cry over a bowl of stewed root vegetables, which somehow feels right for fall.

#8049. Ask Dr. Paola – HELP! My Cat Refuses to Eat Wet Food! (October 5, 2026)

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a new pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â

I feed my 7-year-old, neutered indoor male cat, Sigi, canned food and dry kibble. He prefers the kibble and leaves most of his wet food. I have tried three different brands, and he holds out until I give him the dry food.

I prefer the ingredients in the wet food to the kibble, which is the same brand as one of the canned foods. He has maintained his weight, and heâs not skinny. I do give him some treats in the evenings.

It sounds like Sigi has made his position very clear: kibble wins, and apparently, he is prepared to negotiate accordingly! The reassuring part is that he is maintaining a healthy weight and body condition. While it makes perfect sense to prefer the ingredients and higher moisture content of canned food, the most important consideration is that his main diet is complete and balanced, meaning it has the appropriate number of calories and all the nutrients he needs to maintain his body.

Wet food does have an advantage because it provides considerably more moisture and usually fewer calories per gram than dry food. For a neutered indoor cat like Sigi, keeping portions measured is especially important because these cats need fewer calories. I suggest measuring his daily kibble rather than allowing unlimited grazing, as this also helps you learn what he normally eats and notice any changes in appetite sooner. It is important to remember that those evening treats count toward his calorie intake and shouldn't exceed 10% of his daily allowance.

For cats eating a primarily dry-food diet, drinking plenty of water becomes a priority, and there are several ways you can encourage Sigi to spend a little more time at the water bowl each day. Providing multiple water sources in different locations gives cats a choice of drinking spots, which might vary throughout the day, depending on activity in the house. Ceramic or stainless steel bowls are more hygienic than plastic and provide a fresher taste that cats prefer. Many cats prefer to drink from moving water, so a cat drinking fountain is another great idea.

If you would still like to increase his wet food, you could make the transition very gradually rather than turning dinner into a battle of wills. Try warming a small amount of canned food to enhance its aroma, adding a little warm water, or experimenting with different textures. You could also try a nutritionally complete and balanced fresh food formulated specifically for cats.

Some cats find the aroma and texture of fresh food more appealing, so it can be another option to explore rather than trying to convince Sigi that canned food is the only acceptable alternative to kibble.

Most importantly, avoid trying to out-stubborn a cat by withholding his preferred food until he gives in. Cats that eat too little for several days can develop serious health problems, including hepatic lipidosis. The goal isnât to win the wet-food argument, but to find a nutritionally appropriate diet that Sigi actually enjoys eating. Wet or fresh food would be a nice addition, but mealtimes do not need to become a battle.

With cats, sometimes a little compromise goes a long way!

#8048. It’s Not Too Late For A “Fall Reset.” Here’s How To Make One Actually Stick.

September came and went, huh? Here’s how to hit refresh anyway, without adding one more thing to your plate.

I keep reading about fall resets and, well, sure... I want one. Who doesn’t, really? A fall reset is a chance to turn a metaphorical fresh page on your personal story without any of that New-Year’s-Resolution pressure. But as a busy mom, I already feel like I’m failing at this. With one kid settled at college and another finally back in the back-to-school routine, I blinked and somehow September came and went. The calendar changed, the weather cooled, and I kept hitting reset on my reset. It’s not exactly an auspicious start!

While a fall reset sounds great in theory, in reality, it can be hard to make it happen amid chaotic mornings, after-school practices, homework, tutoring sessions, weekend sports events, making dinner, keeping a home clean, and, oh yeah, my own work. Suddenly, something that should be a fresh little personal improvement project is feeling big and weighty and like just one more item on my endless to-do list. So for help, I turned to Dr. Rachel Goldman, a New York City-based clinical psychologist, author of When Life Happens: The Mindset Shift You Need to Manage Stress, Build Confidence, and Break Free, and a mom of two herself.

“A fall reset is so much more realistic than New Year's resolutions because transitions are already happening around us,” Dr. Rachel, as she’s known, tells me. “January is overwhelming because there's just so much pressure to make a New Year's resolution, but fall is natural. Everybody is going back to school, the season is changing… it's just a natural time to be thinking about a refresh or reset.”

The key to a successful reset, Dr. Rachel continues, is to keep your goals in perspective. “I think people think a reset means that you have to overhaul your whole life,” she says, “and I always like to take it back and pause, and ask, ‘What do I need or want out of this season? And then identify one thing.’”

Maybe you want a consistent bedtime. Maybe you want to add movement into your day. Maybe you want family dinners to actually happen more nights than not. But landing on one small tweak to your current routine is more approachable and realistic than thinking you're going to refresh your whole life — “because that tends to work for like a week, right?” she says. (It’s like she knows us!)

For me, landing on two reset “wish list” items has made this undertaking feel so much more doable. I realized that part of what’s been holding me back is that I couldn’t even put my finger on exactly what I wanted to change after a difficult summer. So, my two things are committing to a renewed focus on work after a purposeful pause, and building more opportunities for joy and connection into my days.

Starting small can also mean baby-stepping your way into your goal, Dr. Rachel says. If you want to build a daily meditation practice but you’re starting from scratch, block off 10 minutes to start, not an hour. If you want to begin journaling, start by writing just a few thoughts a day in your notes app, not setting a 20-minute writing goal from the get-go. My goal of fostering more connection might look like sending at least one "thinking of you!” message to a friend, or aiming to schedule one coffee meet-up a week.

Dr. Rachel also recommends visualizing what you want your season to look like. It’s an exercise she does with clients, asking them to close their eyes and imagine a magic wand just gave them the season they want. She then asks them to describe what they’re seeing, smelling, and feeling.

Verbalizing what the result of your reset goal looks like in your real life can help you clarify just what, exactly, you need to do. Did you picture an idyllic morning walk with a friend and smell the fresh air, hear the conversation, and taste the coffee you’re sipping as you stroll? Having that strong image in mind can help you actually get it on the calendar and make it happen.

Of course, it’s that last part (the action) that’s critical. “I can’t take credit for this quote, but I always say that a goal without a plan is just a wish,” Dr. Rachel says. “So if you want to hit the reset button and you have a goal, you have to put the plan in place.”

If you want more free time, that might mean actively delegating things off of your to-do list, rather than adding something in. If your goal is to build movement or connection into your day, block off an hour on your calendar for a walk or a class, or coffee with a friend.

Finally, remember that a reset goal — even one you’ve visualized, planned, and scheduled — isn't set in stone. It’s totally fine to reevaluate and tweak as you go along, Dr. Rachel says. So if your reset goal is working for you and starting to become a habit, it might be a good time to add another. If not, take a moment to rethink your reset and change course (or just give yourself a break) without guilt.

“The most sustainable reset is actually being flexible enough to adjust when life happens,” Dr. Rachel says. “Maybe you intended to go to the gym, but you're not feeling well. Or maybe your kid is home sick, or you had a really busy week. If your reset goal becomes too rigid, that can become problematic. So remaining flexible and kind to yourself is really important.”

#8047. 40 Years Ago, One Underrated Chapter Book Helped Kids Talk About Trauma

It might not be as well-known as the Ramona series, but Dear Mr. Henshaw could be Beverly Cleary’s most important book

It’s an undeniable fact that Beverly Cleary was a huge part of the way several generations of kids learned to read. She has been since Henry Huggins arrived in 1950, and remains a top pick for voracious young readers beyond her passing in 2021 at the age of 104. Library shelves forever enshrine her Ramona and The Mouse and The Motorcycle books, rightfully revered as timeless classics. Despite being generations apart from when they were first penned, children continue to connect with Cleary’s earnest style that never forgets to throw in some laughs. Among her dozens of books, there’s one underrated story that can be viewed as the most empathetic book the author ever wrote, covering a topic rarely tread upon in kids' literature written during that era.

First published four decades ago, in 1983, Dear Mr. Henshaw centers on a boy from California named Leigh Botts, who aims to be a writer when he grows up. Beginning in second grade, the youngster starts a correspondence with famous children’s book author Boyd Henshaw, which continues over several years. During this time, Leigh is coping with his parents' recent divorce, trying to make sense of the confusing emotions caused by this trauma.

Mr. Henshaw responds to Leigh’s sixth-grade assignment to write a letter to an author with his own set of ten questions. The aspiring author slowly and reluctantly answers probing inquiries like “Who are you?” or “What is your family like?” As time marches forward, Leigh discovers he enjoys writing to Mr. Henshaw, and the letters become a form of therapy, eventually transitioning into a personal diary addressed to “Pretend Mr. Henshaw.” Leigh finds comfort in this safe space, openly addressing his fears and concerns, like why his dad doesn’t say he misses him when they talk on the phone (if he remembers to call), and how Leigh doesn’t like being home alone after his mom leaves for work.

This original illustration from Paul O. Zelinsky depicts Leigh writing to Mr. Henshaw, hesitant at first, but quickly warming up to the idea.

While Leigh responds to his correspondence, the readers of Dear Mr. Henshaw never see a single word from the adult author. The character is merely a guide to Leigh opening up, processing his feelings, and permitting himself to have this outlet. Between his time writing letters and the lessons from his teachers, Leigh’s abilities as a writer simultaneously mature while his emotional vocabulary grows. By the end, he’s able to face his negligent father, understand his mother’s pain, and realize the divorce wasn’t his fault, while also having his first taste of success as a published author. No matter how hard he wishes, Leigh’s world will never be the way it was, but like the butterflies he finds during his walks along the shore (similar to the real Monarch Butterfly Grove in Pismo Beach), Leigh grows into something new and different, comfortable with who he's become.

According to Beverly Cleary, Dear Mr. Henshaw is the most serious book she wrote during her lifetime. The story came about because two different boys wrote letters to her around the same time, asking why she hadn’t written about a boy whose parents were divorced. The spark was lit, and the book flowed from her head onto paper.

Cleary’s books were not typically as solitary as Dear Mr. Henshaw, and rarely delve into serious trauma. It’s an outlier with its somber tone and grounded situation, although Cleary’s signature humor from across her catalog of work is present. Leigh doesn’t live in a bustling cul-de-sac surrounded by kids, but rather isolated in “a really little house,” with his neighbors being a gas station and a thrift shop. He’s lethargic to find meaning in anything that goes on around him, trapped between unfamiliar spaces, physically and emotionally. After he adds writing to his routine, his sense of abandonment fades to allow personal growth that even adult readers can admire and aspire towards.

Dear Mr. Henshaw covers many of the anxieties children feel during a divorce. It’s not unusual for them to go through their own makeshift stages of grief, ranging from being mad and sad, denying the events are real while hoping everything will return to how things were before, and eventually accepting the new status quo. Kids can react to this outwardly through anger and tantrums, while other children will internalize it and never show what they’re truly feeling. Cleary reassures the reader that whatever they’re going through is nothing to feel ashamed about, and one can heal from the invisible wounds on their heart.

Divorce is rarely an easy transaction, no matter how old you are. Processing the good memories alongside the bad is a difficult experience, and often a source of confusion and frustration. Dear Mr. Henshaw encourages the reader not to be afraid to explore what hurts them because the only way to grow is to face it in a healthy and introspective way.

Despite earning a Newbery Medal when it was released, Dear Mr. Henshaw remains overshadowed by Cleary’s more popular and light-hearted stories. It received a sequel eight years later with Strider, centered on Leigh and his friend Barry sharing custody over a stray dog they discover on a beach. While it didn’t reach the level of notoriety its predecessor had, it’s a perfect follow-up for children continuing their own journeys through divorce.

Cleary’s books were predominantly a slice of idealized Americana, but the concept of change can be found in many of them. Dear Mr. Henshaw is a magnificent book as relevant today as it was 40 years ago, inspiring readers to look inward and answer the tough questions preventing them from finding clarity in their lives.

Empty food cans usually head straight for the recycling bin. But with a quick wash and a few nail holes, they can have a second life in the garden.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Canned beans, tomatoes, and soup move through plenty of kitchens at a steady clip, and the empties usually get a quick rinse before they go out with the recycling. At that point, old tin cans still have plenty of life left. They’re stiff, hold soil and water without leaking, and cost nothing after being discarded.

Cans make for one of the easiest garden recycling projects, and the basic projects need nothing fancier than a hammer, a nail, and a can opener. One can might hold a pepper seedling in March, then lose its bottom at transplant time and slip right back over that same plant as a cutworm collar. That’s a lot of mileage out of something headed for the curb.

I start my stash in fall. Soup and chili season brings in a steady supply, and a box of clean cans in the shed will be ready when seed starting rolls around in late winter. Some can go to work right away, too – as lanterns on chilly evenings or as a winter home for hollow stems cut back during fall cleanup.

Clean cans first. Hot, soapy water and a bottle brush get the food out, and a soak loosens the label and glue. The edges are the real hazard. If you’ve got a smooth-edge can opener, like this Oxo Good Grips one on Amazon, use it, since it cuts through the side seam and leaves a dull lip. Regular openers leave a sharp ring. Pinch any jagged bits flat with pliers or take a file to them, and wear gloves for this part.

Won’t they rust? They will, eventually. On most cans, the “tin” is only a thin coating over steel, and rain and wet soil wear through it over time. That takes a while, and a can with a few orange spots still holds soil and water just fine for seasonal jobs. I paint the outside of any can that’ll sit out for a long stretch, and punch drainage holes so water doesn’t sit in the bottom. A can too far gone can usually still go in with the metal recycling.

Without further ado, in this latest installment of our Dirt Cheap Gardening series, here are my eight favorite ways to upcycle tin cans.

Thin plastic cell packs can split or tip over, but a tin can is heavier and less likely to get knocked around. You can use cans to start seeds or root cuttings. Turn one upside down on a scrap board and tap a nail through the bottom in several spots to make drainage holes – a basic 16-ounce claw hammer, like this Irwin one from Amazon, is plenty for the job.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Fill your tin can pots with a light, sterile seed-starting mix, such as Espoma Organic Seed Starter from Walmart, instead of garden soil. Metal doesn’t breathe like terracotta, so feel the mix before you water. When it’s time to transplant, cut the bottom out with the can opener and push the root ball up and out.

A tin can can help protect seedlings from a few garden pests, although it won’t keep them all away. Burying a can around a young plant may make it harder for slugs to reach, but they may still climb over it, so don’t rely on it as a dependable barrier.

Where a can collar is more useful is against cutworms. These caterpillars hide in the soil by day and chew through young stems at ground level after dark. Cut a can open at both ends, slip it over the seedling, and press it 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) into the soil, leaving a couple of inches above ground. Put it in place when you plant, while the seedling is most vulnerable.

You can also hang cans near vulnerable plants as a makeshift bird scare. Moving, clattering cans may startle birds, but the effect can wear off as they get used to them, so treat it as a short-term deterrent. Perhaps try alternating tin cans with a predator decoy, like the Dalen Lifelike Great Horned Owl Decoy Bird Repellent on Amazon.

My potting benches end up buried under twine, plant labels, and hand tools. A few cans fix that for free. Drop a ball of garden twine (like this PerkHomy green jute twine from Amazon) into one can, and it won’t roll off the bench anymore. Put labels and pencils in the next can, and pruners and a trowel in the one after that. Mark each one with a weatherproof Garden Marker pen (on Amazon) so you don’t have to guess later. Nail them to the shed wall through the back.

Bare hands make a mess of granular fertilizer, bone meal, and compost, and a clean can scoops them out without bending or cracking the way a plastic cup might. Make it do double duty. Pour a measured cup of water in, scratch a line at the waterline with a nail, and you’ve got a rough measuring cup for any rates listed in cups. Keep a second can just for compost.

Fertilizer residue can speed up rust, so knock the scoop clean after each use, store it dry, and never bring it back into the kitchen.

Thyme, chives, and oregano stay compact enough to grow in a can on a sunny windowsill or balcony rail. Get the drainage holes in first, then paint the outside. Home Depot stocks Rust-Oleum Stops Rust spray paint in gloss white, and white is the better pick for a patio since dark cans heat up fast in full sun.

Skip painting the inside, and let the paint cure before you plant. This time of year, aim for a south- or west-facing window. In summer, a can on a hot patio can dry out quickly.

Punched-tin lanterns throw speckled light across a patio table, and they’re a nice touch now that it gets dark earlier. Freeze a can full of water first. The ice keeps the walls from denting while you tap a nail through them in dots, swirls or stars. Once it thaws, dry it and paint it if you like, then drop in a battery-operated LED tea light, which you can get from Walmart in a pack of 12. An LED carries far less fire risk than a candle if wind tips a lantern into dry leaves. Thread wire through two holes near the rim to hang it.

Many native bees are solitary and nest alone in narrow tunnels rather than hives. A tall can filled with hollow stems gives them just that. Fall cleanup supplies the material. Bamboo, reeds, and the hollow or pithy stems of sunflowers, sumac, or raspberries all work in mixed widths. Cut them a little shorter than the can so the rim shelters the openings, keep a closed node at the back when possible, and pack them in tight. Keep the bundle dry over winter.

Around the last spring frost, mount the can on its side about 5 feet (1.5 m) up, facing southeast. Replace the stems every one to three years to keep mites and fungal disease from building up.

The other ideas on this list use the cans, but this one makes use of the lids by turning them into plant labels. Flatten each lid carefully, then write the plant name on it with a permanent marker. You can attach it to a wooden stick or tie it to a plant support with garden twine. The metal stands up to rain better than paper labels, and you’re giving a useful second life to something that might otherwise go in the recycling. Be careful handling the edges, which can be sharp.

Clean cans don’t take up much room on a shed shelf, and they keep a lot of little purchases off the shopping list. Start a stack this fall, and by seed-starting season there’ll be one ready for nearly every job!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8045. I Am The Desperate Mom Friend Organizer You’re Going to Like More Than You Think

I am, at times, a human exclamation point. I have, at times, hated everything about myself for being this person.

I am “such a mom,” the comic foil in every situation, like Brooke in The Five Star Weekend or really any next door neighbor in any ‘90s-era sitcom. Some people can’t stand this mom which means they probably can’t stand me, an extroverted, excited, earnest mom trying too hard and fumbling around for a good sun hat. I have no fewer than four sun hats and, much like Brooke, would absolutely overpack for a weekend in Nantucket if I was ever invited to Nantucket. The problem is I’m not sure if I would be invited to Nantucket by a cool group of moms. I think I would get on their nerves.

My friends — who, I promise, are kind and true and do, in fact, have my best wishes at heart — have wished I was different too. I’ve been secretly and then openly mortified to hear other friends secretly and then openly mocking me. “Jen and her little parties,” that kind of thing. I’ve pretended to laugh as I passed around a charcuterie board and pretended that it didn’t embarrass me to be seen as this kind of caricature, a human meme. I tried to take up less space when I worried I was too much, too present, too excited to take the wheel.

I took a break from being me for about three months, an eternity for me. No plans for the weekend, no plans for a Wednesday, no plans for a rainy Sunday afternoon when I would normally ask a few girlfriends over to play Rummikub and eat various dips. It felt like I was grounding myself from my life; it gave me flashbacks to being a grounded 16-year-old finding out the best party ever happened on a Friday when I was alone in my room. During that break, I started to plan too many things for myself: Volunteering in a local little theater where I then decided I should write a one-woman show about being a single mom and maybe I could sell fun T-shirts as merch and have a macaroni and cheese break halfway through the show. Made by me.

I broke my fast. I became me again but what’s more, my little break made me realize this part of me is kind of great. I realized my friends and I did nothing for three months. Everyone just hibernated, waiting for me to break my fast and become a cheerleader again.

Much like John Candy in Planes, Trains, and Automobiles, I like me. And what’s more, other people like me too. My friends noticed that I wasn’t arranging things. They got bored. They reached out to make sure I was okay. When I broke my fast with sunset pizza and wine at the beach, everyone breathed a sigh of relief.

The truth is, they need me. The truth is, being an organizer is who I am. The truth is, no one really wants me to change.

Jen McGuire is a contributing writer for Romper and Scary Mommy. She lives in Canada with four boys and teaches life writing workshops where someone cries in every class. When she is not traveling as often as possible, she’s trying to organize pie parties and outdoor karaoke with her neighbors. She will sing Cher’s “If I Could Turn Back Time” at least once, but she’s open to requests.

#8044. 45 Years Ago, One Kids Book Series Taught A Generation How To Make Bad Decisions

Imagine if you could tell Bilbo Baggins to leave the ring behind for Gollum, have Leslie not swing on the rope to Terabithia on that rainy day, or remind Jonas to pack warmer clothes at the end of The Giver. Most fiction is concrete, with the authors dictating what happens next. But that changed when two writers figured out a way for the reader to control a character because the reader was that character. We’re talking about Choose Your Own Adventure, of course. The first published installment arrived in 1979, with The Cave of Time — though as we’ll see that wasn’t really the first book. For decades, Choose Your Own Adventure was an atypical experiment in literary determinism that resulted in one of the most-read book franchises ever created.

For a generation, these interactive novels transported readers through space and time to form their own stories, putting them in the cockpit of planes, the gi of a judo master, or even the fins of a shark. By the end of the 90s, CYOA closed the chapter on its story, but nearly twenty-five years later, the company is back in action. Here’s how it all began, ended, and began again.

A few variations of the cover to “Sugarcane Island,” the first ever CYOA book

Interactive books weren’t a completely new idea before Choose Your Own Adventure (CYOA), but its predecessors weren’t mainstream popular. There was a romance novel from the 1930s, where the reader decides which suitor the protagonist marries, with dozens of possible endings. Several high-concept stories arrived by the 50s and 60s, like Raymond Queneau’s surreal Story As You Like It or Robert Coover’s explicit and unsettling The Babysitter. Celebrated for their uniqueness, none of these caught on beyond their novelty and were purely adult fare. It wasn’t until a lawyer teamed up with a young writer to find a way to bring this idea to bookshelves across the country.

Edward Packard came from a family deep in the legal business, but practicing law was never something he truly cared about. While his passion was writing, Ed’s children's books were never picked up by publishers. His fate changed one evening in 1969 while making up a bedtime story for his two daughters about a character named Pete. Struck by writer's block, Packard couldn’t figure out how to progress the tale and asked his kids what should happen next. When both girls answered differently, he realized Pete was never the protagonist – it was his kids living those adventures firsthand in their imaginations. Immediately, Packard knew he was onto something.

Ray Montgomery had just started Vermont Crossroads Press in 1970, after cutting his teeth writing roleplaying scenarios for Clark Abt, a pioneer in educational games. The Yale and NYU grad had aspirations larger than his employer and ventured out to make a name for himself in publishing. When Packard walked into his office with a draft of Sugarcane Island in 1976, Montgomery saw great potential that perfectly aligned with his interests. “I Xeroxed 50 copies of Ed’s manuscript and took it to a reading teacher in Stowe,” Montgomery said in an interview from 1981. “His kids — third grade through junior high — couldn’t get enough of it.”

Sugarcane Island became the best-selling book of the upstart publisher, moving over five thousand copies, but they were still an unknown entity in a crowded landscape.

It was this point where things started to get messy for Packard and Montgomery. Both writers saw a potential for larger success beyond the small Vermont publishing house, and the two pursued greener pastures, independent from each other's ventures. Packard published two CYOA-style books in 1978 under the Harper imprint, Lippincott. Meanwhile, Montgomery’s agent managed to obtain a six-book deal from Bantam in 1979, and the two writers came together to officially launch the CYOA experience as we know it today.

Similar to the origin story of Sugarcane Island, Packard turned to his kids for story ideas. His daughter, Andrea, told him about her summer escapade, spelunking, and her desire to wander solo to explore more. She imagined a tunnel that could transport her to another time or place, and her dad loved it! Andrea scribbled more notes and ultimately ideated the first published CYOA book, “The Cave of Time.”

Interior from “The Cave of Time” with two of the multiple endings available to readers

While hiking through Snake Canyon, you come upon a cave you’ve never noticed before. You step inside and can potentially travel to medieval times, a prehistoric era, the Ming Dynasty, and other periods. Along the way, you can find your fortune through a foolish king, dine with cavemen, battle the Loch Ness Monster, try to escape the sinking Titanic, or any number of unpredictable possibilities. Some endings are bittersweet, others hopeful, and some are just plain grim.

A fortuitous mistake resulted in Bantam overprinting this inaugural entry, and the publisher remedied its overstock by donating 100,000 books to schools and libraries throughout America. This charitable act guaranteed their target audience would have no problem discovering the book, transforming CYOA into a household name practically overnight.

50 books later, readers returned to the cave for another adventure, making it one of the few retro CYOA titles to have a sequel. For her efforts, Andrea received a credit in the book and a percentage of royalties that still come to her mailbox decades later.

The opening page of every CYOA book warns readers they are responsible for their own fate. There’s no backtracking allowed (in theory), creating a flexible narrative where the outcome changes each time a page is turned. More often than not, the wrong turn leads to fatal consequences. But, really, who hasn’t flipped backward to reconsider a choice?

Few books offer the chance to be the master of a protagonist’s destiny, have wild adventures in a pocket-sized format, and combine those parts with the element of risk and uncertainty from a single decision. Some books have as many as 40 endings, and that finality could happen as early as the first ten pages. While most readers sought the happily ever after conclusion, others found pleasure in seeing how many ways they could fail in the grizzliest way possible.

Nope, this is definitely not going to end well. Don Hedin illustration from “The Forbidden Castle.”

“My philosophy was that it should be like life,” Packard once said, with the intent of including moral realism in the reader's experience. Smart choices were typically better than impulsive, haphazard decisions, but morally virtuous ones weren’t guaranteed to be the wisest, and you often paid for heroics with self-sacrifice. Cheating was discouraged, but technically, if you didn’t take your finger off the page, it wasn’t a final decision.

There was one time when being mischievous paid off, and that famous case was the twelfth book, Inside UFO 54-40. This is the only book in the series that explicitly rewards cheating. In order to find the secret alien planet, the reader must forego the typical CYOA patterns and stop playing along. Only by reading the book straight through would they stumble on a page unmarked by any choices to discover this paradise. “You did not make a choice, or follow any directions, but now, somehow, you are descending from space—approaching a great, glistening sphere.” The lesson was ambiguous, but a valuable one - sometimes, disobeying the rules is its own reward.

Stacks of CYOA books are common in any library or bookstore no matter where you live

CYOA books dominated stores around the world during the ’80s and ’90s, with hundreds of millions of books sold in 38 languages. But as the new millennium approached, Montgomery and Packard found themselves at a crossroads with no page to turn.

Video games were taking over, as screen time replaced reading. Sales dwindled until the company flew the white flag in 1998, ending with book #184, Mayday, which Packard co-wrote with the person responsible for the very first title in the franchise, his daughter Andrea.

In 2003, Montgomery and his wife Shannon Gilligan (who met while working on an Atari game based on the CYOA books) bought the rights to the franchise and revived it through Chooseco. Montgomery passed away in 2014, writing Gus vs. the Robot King, but Gilligan has kept the brand thriving as CEO while bringing it to new places.

Cover to Murder at the Old Willow Boarding School

Today, CYOA sells an average of a million books annually, evolving to reach a more inclusive readership and touching on issues that affect modern society. Their bestseller remains a four-pack filled with Classics, but Chooseco transitioned into graphic novels like Eighth Grade Witch and offers longer CYOA books with titles like Time Travel Inn and Murder at the Old Willow Boarding School, which introduced their first nonbinary character. Readers ages 5 to 8 can dip their toes into the Dragonlark series, and even younger ones can start their adventure with the adorable board book The Abominable Snowman, with lethal endings absent from these kid-friendly editions. There are also board games, a math book, an upcoming Tarot card set, and a proposed book series for nostalgic adults with more mature themes — but nothing too explicit.

Packard wrote a trio of books in the CYOA style under the name U-Ventures in 2010 and continues to write fiction while maintaining his blog.

Montgomery always hoped the CYOA series would be a stealth reading program to excite kids into becoming voracious bookworms. Years later, his dream continues to be a reality and may soon rekindle that same love within adults who grew up on these books.

There are surprising plans beyond the traditional format that Gilligan couldn’t divulge in 2023, but even as technology evolves, nothing beats the experience of reading a physical book and not knowing what awaits the reader when they turn it over.

At Toy Fair 2023, Shannon Gilligan said: “Touching a page and moving it makes the brain think you’ve been somewhere on some super subtle level.” And even though she said Choose Your Own Adventure is at the “dawn of a relaunch,” the truth is, we’ve all been on this adventure for years.

This article was originally published on Jan. 5, 2024

#8043. The Youth Have Spoken: They Want More Neurodivergence & Friendship In Their TV Shows

A study of 1,500 teens found they want less romance and more friendship on their screens.

Gen Z this and Gen Alpha that — it’s easy to look at younger generations and judge the things about them we don’t understand. This is especially true when we observe kids’ and teens’ relationships with their devices. But a new study, the Teens and Screens Report from the Center for Scholars & Storytellers at UCLA, reveals that younger generations don’t feel much different about technology and the media they consume than we do.

Here’s what talking to 1,500 adolescents about what they want in their entertainment content illuminated for researchers, from AI hesitancy to a desire for more stories centering platonic relationships.

Every year, the Center for Scholars & Storytellers (CSS) at UCLA performs a study to find out what tweens and teens want to see in the TV shows, movies, and media made for and about them. Researchers interviewed more than 1,500 adolescents ages 10-24 “about their perceptions, opinions, and beliefs regarding popular media, including TV shows, movies, video games, AI, and social media,” a press release about the report reads.

The high-level takeaway: While there are more and more ways to consume stories today, teens still want to consume “traditional” media. However, they want more diverse perspectives in their TV show and movie options.

Among Gen Xers and Millennials, a “story” typically means a TV show or a movie. For the surveyed adolescents, YouTube videos, video games, and 30-second videos also count as storytelling platforms.

“YouTube ranked as the top medium for storytelling, with nearly four out of five respondents saying that short-form videos can tell a story. TV shows, movies, and video games followed closely behind. TikTok scored the highest among social media platforms,” the press release reads.

We tend to think of kids and teens as hapless would-be victims of AI (no one would willingly watch brain rot, right?). But the same optimism and fear adults seem to feel about the technology were also present among the study group. Participants’ ages tended to be the best predictor of how they felt about AI.

Forty-four percent of 10- to 13-year-olds described AI-generated programs as “fascinating,” while only about 10% used the word “doom” in their description (ominous). That split was completely reversed in the 19-year-old group, where doom was the No. 1 feeling participants had about AI (27.4% of them).

In contrast to last year’s results, live-action content took the top spot this year as the preferred choice for adolescent and young adult audiences compared to animation (58% to 42%). In a world where AI is beginning to touch everything, we’re all craving things we know are real.

Sure, some kids do have their favorites, but when it comes to quality content and storytelling, the youth are not looking to the Charlie D’Amelios and Salish Matters of the world. They want real actors on their screens (just maybe not A-listers they’ve already seen a thousand times).

Very few participants said they would cast an influencer in a movie or TV show; 40% said they would rather cast an unknown actor over anyone else. Whether this is because they like the idea of young people being given the opportunity to break into the industry or they want fresh faces from more diverse backgrounds, they were loud and clear about this preference.

According to the CSS’s report, only 2.8% of speaking or named characters in the top 100 movies of 2025 had a disability. Younger audiences say that’s simply not enough — they “overwhelmingly” want to see more neurodivergent characters in their media, the study found.

“A whopping 55 percent of all adolescents and young adults surveyed feel this way, with that percentage increasing to well into the 70s among youth who identify as LGBTGIA+ or have a disability themselves,” says the report. “Additionally, only 22.7% of respondents believe that current media portrayals of neurodivergence ‘ring true to real life’ most of the time.”

Speaking of real-life relatability, for the fourth year of the report in a row, kids and teens have declared they want to see more friendship and less romance in their stories.

Participants were asked this question: “What specific topics would you like to see in the TV shows and/or movies you watch?” The top three responses, in order, were:

Nearly 58% of participants also said they want to see more representation of platonic friendships in their media, with 52% feeling that romantic relationships are far more central to the lives of fictional characters than they are for real people their age. Those respondents also said they want to see people in different-gender friendships who simply prioritize their platonic relationship rather than it turning into a romantic one.

And in what feels like a win for parents, teens in this age group ranked wanting to see more drugs, alcohol, and drinking dead last.
